name: Malpelo Barnacle Blenny
shortDescription:
The Malpelo barnacle blenny (Acanthemblemaria stephensi) is a tiny chaenopsid blenny reaching only 5 cm. It has a small, elongated body with a distinctive cirrus above each eye and typically peeks out from empty barnacle shells or worm tubes with just its head visible. Found exclusively around Malpelo Island in the eastern Pacific Ocean, this endemic species inhabits coral reef surfaces at depths of 5 to 25 meters.

It is a planktivore, darting out from its tube dwelling to snatch passing zooplankton before quickly retreating to safety. Named in honor of marine biologist John S. Stephens Jr., this tiny fish is one of the special endemic species that makes diving at the remote Malpelo Island UNESCO World Heritage Site so unique. Despite its small size, finding these curious little faces peering from their barnacle homes is a delightful experience for visiting divers.
divingRegions: Eastern Tropical Pacific
bestSeason: Year-round; Malpelo expeditions typically run from January to May
photographyTips: Use super-macro for frame-filling portraits as they peer from barnacle holes; patience is key as they pop in and out rapidly.

name: Yellow-Banded Perch
shortDescription:
The yellow-banded perch (Acanthistius cinctus), also known as the yellowbanded wirrah, is a species of serranid fish in the family Serranidae. Adults reach up to 45 cm in length and display a dark brown to grey body with 5-6 prominent yellow or golden vertical bands across the flanks. They have a robust, laterally compressed body with a large head and mouth.

This species inhabits rocky reefs, reef drop-offs, and caves at depths of 10-100 meters along the coast of eastern Australia and northern New Zealand. They are typically solitary and territorial, often found resting in or near caves and overhangs. Yellow-banded perch are carnivorous, feeding on small fish, crustaceans, and other invertebrates.

They are relatively approachable and curious, often allowing divers to observe them closely. Their bold banding pattern makes them immediately recognizable and a rewarding find on temperate rocky reefs.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, New Zealand
bestSeason: Year-round; best visibility February-May in Australia
photographyTips: Often found resting near cave entrances; use a strobe to bring out the vivid yellow banding against the dark reef background.

name: Yellowfin Sea Bream
shortDescription:
The yellowfin sea bream (Acanthopagrus latus) is a medium-sized sparid fish reaching up to 45 cm. It has a silvery body with a yellowish tinge and notably bright yellow pelvic and anal fins that give the species its common name. Found in the western Pacific and eastern Indian Ocean from Japan to India and the Persian Gulf, it inhabits coastal reefs, estuaries, and brackish waters at depths of 1 to 50 meters. This omnivorous species feeds on mollusks, crustaceans, worms, and algae.

It is an important food fish in Asian cuisines and a popular recreational fishing target. Divers in Asian coastal waters encounter schools of yellowfin bream around reef structures and harbor pilings, where their yellow fins flash attractively against the darker water.

name: Eyestripe Surgeonfish
shortDescription:
The bluebanded surgeonfish (Acanthurus dussumieri), also known as the eyestripe surgeonfish, is a large surgeonfish reaching about 54 cm, found across the Indo-Pacific from East Africa and the Red Sea to Hawaii and the Tuamotu Islands. Its body is brown to olive-gray covered with fine longitudinal blue lines and dots, with a distinctive yellow bar behind the eye and a bright yellow patch surrounding the sharp retractable tail spine. The tail is lunate with a blue-white margin.

This species is primarily herbivorous, grazing on algae and detritus from sandy and rubble areas of reef flats and lagoons, often in small groups. It tends to prefer sandy zones adjacent to coral reef areas rather than the reef itself, making it a common sight on reef flats and in shallow lagoon environments. Found from 1 to 131 meters, though most commonly in shallow water less than 20 meters. The bluebanded surgeonfish is a steady, approachable species that can be observed closely by patient divers, especially in areas where it is habituated to human presence.

bestSeason: Year-round on tropical reef flats and lagoons
photographyTips: Profile shots showcase the fine blue lines and yellow tail spine marking; shoot on sandy reef flats in natural light for an open, bright composition.

name: Yellowmask Surgeonfish
shortDescription:
The yellowmask surgeonfish (Acanthurus mata), also known as the elongate surgeonfish, is a species of surgeonfish in the family Acanthuridae. Adults reach up to 50 cm with an elongated body displaying olive-brown coloration with fine blue horizontal lines across the body and a distinctive bright yellow to orange band across the face and around the eye. This species inhabits steep outer reef slopes and channels at depths of 5-100 meters across the Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea and East Africa to the central Pacific. Yellowmask surgeonfish are planktivorous, feeding on zooplankton in the water column above the reef, often in large loose aggregations.

They are typically found in deeper water than most surgeonfish species, making them more commonly encountered by experienced divers comfortable at greater depths. Their elegant proportions, distinctive facial marking, and schooling behavior make them a rewarding sighting.
divingRegions: South Africa, Polynesia, Coral Triangle, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, French Polynesia, South Pacific Islands, India & Sri Lanka, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round; common on deep outer reef slopes
photographyTips: Found at moderate to greater depths; use available light to capture the subtle blue lines and distinctive yellow face mask.

name: Goldrim Surgeonfish
shortDescription:
The goldrim surgeonfish (Acanthurus nigricans), also known as the whitecheek surgeonfish, is a medium-sized tang reaching about 21 cm in length. It has a dark brownish-black body with a distinctive white band below the eye, a yellow rim on the dorsal and anal fins, and a white-edged caudal peduncle spine typical of surgeonfish. The tail fin is dark with a yellow or gold submarginal band.

This species is found throughout the central and western Pacific, from Christmas Island to Hawaii, Pitcairn, and the Marquesas. It inhabits coral reefs and rocky substrates, typically at depths of 1-20 meters, where it grazes on filamentous and small fleshy algae. It is usually seen singly or in small groups, moving methodically across the reef as it feeds.

Like other surgeonfish, it possesses a sharp, scalpel-like spine at the base of the tail that can be erected for defense against predators or during territorial disputes. Its bold coloration and consistent presence on reef flats make it a regular sighting for divers across its range.
divingRegions: Polynesia, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef, French Polynesia, Eastern Tropical Pacific
photographyTips: Standard or macro lens for portraits showing the white cheek bar; approach slowly as they are moderately wary. Capture the golden fin edging with proper strobe positioning.

name: Orange-Band Surgeonfish
shortDescription:
The orange-band surgeonfish (Acanthurus olivaceus), also known as the orangespot surgeonfish, is a medium-sized tang reaching about 35 cm in length. Adults are olive-grey to brown with a distinctive bright orange horizontal band or spot behind the eye that extends toward the pectoral fin, the feature that gives the species its name. The tail is lunate with pale margins.

Juveniles are strikingly different, displaying a uniform bright yellow coloration with no orange marking. The transition from juvenile to adult occurs gradually as the fish matures. This species is found throughout the Pacific, from Christmas Island to Hawaii and the Marquesas, inhabiting reef flats, lagoons, and outer reef slopes.

It forms large grazing schools that sweep across the reef, feeding on detritus, film algae, and diatoms from sandy and rubble substrates. Like all surgeonfish, it possesses a sharp, retractable blade at the base of the tail used for defense. The orange-band surgeonfish is one of the most abundant tangs in Hawaiian waters and a common sight for divers across its range.

photographyTips: Standard lens for school shots showing the synchronized grazing behavior; macro for the distinctive orange band detail. Capture the yellow juvenile if spotted for life-stage comparison.

name: Pacific White-Spotted Eagle Ray
shortDescription: Eastern Pacific eagle ray, split from A. narinari in 2014. Range: Sea of Cortez to Peru including offshore Cocos, Galápagos, and Revillagigedo seamounts.
longDescription: The Pacific white-spotted eagle ray (Aetobatus laticeps) is the eastern Pacific species in the Aetobatus complex following the 2014 taxonomic split (Last, White & Naylor). Range: Gulf of California (Sea of Cortez) south to Peru, including offshore seamounts and oceanic islands — Cocos, Galápagos, and the Revillagigedo Archipelago (Socorro, Roca Partida, Clarion, San Benedicto). Distinguished morphologically from its Atlantic (A. narinari) and Indo-Pacific (A. ocellatus) sisters by a broader head and stockier disc.
divingRegions: Eastern Tropical Pacific, Mexican Tropical Pacific, Sea of Cortez, Cocos Island, Galápagos, Revillagigedo Archipelago
bestSeason: Year-round; aggregations more common at offshore seamounts during liveaboard season Nov-May

name: Spotted Eagle Ray
shortDescription: Graceful spotted eagle ray often seen gliding over sandy flats or cruising reef walls. The polka-dot pattern is unmistakable.
longDescription: The spotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari sensu stricto) is the Atlantic species in the Aetobatus complex following the 2014 taxonomic split. Range: western Atlantic from Massachusetts and Bermuda south through the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico to Brazil; eastern Atlantic from Macaronesia and West Africa to Angola. The Indo-Pacific population is now Aetobatus ocellatus (ocellated eagle ray) and the eastern Pacific population is Aetobatus laticeps (Pacific white-spotted eagle ray). Distinctive pale-spotted dark blue-grey dorsum and long whip-like tail with venomous barbs.
divingRegions: North Atlantic, Caribbean, US East Coast
bestSeason: Year-round in tropical waters, summer months in temperate regions
photographyTips: Approach slowly and calmly, shoot from below to capture their distinctive spotted pattern against blue water, use wide-angle lens to capture full wingspan, be patient as they often circle back if not startled

name: Naru Eagle Ray
shortDescription: A medium-sized eagle ray of the northwest Pacific, found off southern Japan, South Korea, China, Hong Kong, and Vietnam. Recognized as a distinct species from the longheaded eagle ray (A. flagellum) in 2013.
longDescription:
The Naru eagle ray (Aetobatus narutobiei) is a cartilaginous fish of the eagle ray family found in the northwest Pacific off southern Japan, South Korea, China, Hong Kong, and Vietnam. It occurs from shallow coastal flats to depths of 59 m (194 ft), but always in water warmer than 15 °C (59 °F).

Until 2013, this species was considered a population of the longheaded eagle ray (Aetobatus flagellum), but it differs in genetics, morphology, size, and range — the smaller longheaded eagle ray is restricted to the Indian Ocean. The Naru eagle ray reaches up to 1.5 m (4.9 ft) in disc width, with uniformly greenish-grey to brownish upperparts. Its life history and ecology have been most thoroughly studied in Japanese waters, particularly Ariake Bay.
divingRegions: Northwest Pacific (southern Japan, South Korea, China, Hong Kong, Vietnam)
photographyTips: Wide-angle lens; shoot from below against open water; uniformly greenish-grey dorsum lacks the spotting of related species — emphasize disc shape and trailing whip-tail.

name: Ocellated Eagle Ray
shortDescription:
The ocellated eagle ray (Aetobatus ocellatus) is a large eagle ray found throughout the Indo-Pacific region. Recent taxonomic revision split this species from Aetobatus narinari, with A. ocellatus representing the Indo-Pacific population. Adults reach a disc width of up to 3 meters and display a dark dorsal surface adorned with white spots that often have darker centers (ocelli), a white underside, and an extremely long whip-like tail.

They possess a distinctive flat, duck-bill shaped snout used for digging in sand to find mollusks, crustaceans, and worms, which they crush with powerful fused dental plates. They are often encountered cruising over sandy flats adjacent to coral reefs at depths of 1-60 meters, sometimes in groups. Their graceful, wing-like swimming motion is one of the most elegant sights on any dive. They occasionally leap fully out of the water in spectacular aerial displays.
longDescription: The ocellated eagle ray (Aetobatus ocellatus) is the Indo-Pacific species in the Aetobatus complex following the 2014 taxonomic split. Distributed from the Red Sea and east African coast through the Indo-Pacific to Hawaii, southern Japan, the Great Barrier Reef, and New Caledonia. Distinguished from its Atlantic sister A. narinari by smaller, more numerous white ocelli on the dark blue-grey dorsum. Schools form along reef edges and over sandy lagoons; long whip-tail with venomous spines.
divingRegions: Bay of Bengal, Polynesia, Eastern Australia, Hawaii, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef, Northern Australia, French Polynesia, South Pacific Islands, Coral Triangle
photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens; position yourself along their travel path on sandy channels between reef sections for dramatic approach shots.

name: King Ragworm
shortDescription:
The king ragworm (Alitta virens) is one of the largest polychaete worms in the northeastern Atlantic, reaching 30-90 cm in length. Adults display a striking iridescent green-blue to bronze sheen along their segmented body, with each segment bearing a pair of paddle-like parapodia used for locomotion and respiration. They possess powerful eversible jaws that can deliver a noticeable nip.

They inhabit sandy, muddy, and mixed substrates in estuaries and shallow coastal areas at depths of 0-20 meters, constructing semi-permanent mucus-lined burrows. They are omnivorous scavengers and predators feeding on algae, other worms, and organic detritus. They emerge from their burrows at night to forage, and during breeding season they swarm at the surface in mass spawning events. Their impressive size, iridescent coloring, and active behavior during night dives make them a fascinating encounter for divers exploring temperate sandy habitats.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, US East Coast
photographyTips: Use a macro lens on night dives when they emerge from burrows; their iridescent sheen is best captured with side-angled strobe lighting.

name: Pelagic Thresher Shark
shortDescription:
The pelagic thresher shark (Alopias pelagicus) is a medium-sized shark reaching up to 3.3 meters, with roughly half its length comprising the extraordinarily elongated upper caudal fin lobe. It has a dark blue-grey back, white underside, and large eyes. Found in tropical and subtropical waters of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, it inhabits open ocean and seamount environments at depths of 0 to 300 meters.

This species uses its whip-like tail to herd and stun small schooling fish before consuming them. At specific locations such as Monad Shoal in the Philippines, pelagic threshers visit cleaning stations at dawn, allowing divers to observe them at close range while cleaner wrasses remove parasites. These reliable dawn encounters have made Malapascua Island one of the world's premier shark diving destinations.

name: Convict Cichlid
shortDescription:
The convict cichlid (Amatitlania nigrofasciata), also known as the zebra cichlid, is a freshwater cichlid in the family Cichlidae. Adults reach about 15 cm with a laterally compressed body displaying grey to bluish coloration with 8-9 prominent black vertical bars, giving it a convict-like striped appearance. Females often show orange coloration on the belly.

This species is native to freshwater streams, rivers, and lakes at depths of 0-5 meters in Central America from Guatemala to Honduras, with introduced populations in many regions worldwide. Convict cichlids are famously aggressive parents, forming monogamous pair bonds and fiercely guarding their eggs and fry. Both parents participate in nest defense, attacking intruders many times their own size.

They are omnivorous, feeding on algae, insect larvae, and small invertebrates. Their bold behavior and dramatic parental care make them fascinating to observe in clear Central American rivers.

name: Bullhead Catfish
shortDescription:
The black bullhead (Ameiurus melas) is a medium-sized freshwater catfish reaching about 45 cm and 3 kg, native to North America from the Great Lakes and Mississippi basin to the Gulf Coast. It has been widely introduced to Europe. The body is robust and scaleless, colored dark olive to black on the back and sides with a lighter belly.

It has eight prominent barbels around the mouth used as sensory organs for locating food in murky water. Stout, serrated spines in the dorsal and pectoral fins can deliver a painful sting. Black bullheads are incredibly tolerant of poor water quality, surviving in warm, muddy, low-oxygen environments where other fish cannot.

They are primarily nocturnal bottom feeders, consuming insects, crustaceans, mollusks, plant matter, and carrion. Freshwater divers often encounter them in ponds, lakes, and slow rivers, where they rest on muddy substrates during the day. Males guard and fan egg masses in nests they construct under logs or banks.
divingRegions: North American Inland, European Inland
bestSeason: Spring through autumn; most active in warmer water temperatures
photographyTips: Macro or mid-range lens for close-up portraits showing barbels; they are often stationary during the day, making photography straightforward.

name: Yellow-Tailed Grunter
shortDescription:
The yellow-tailed grunter (Amniataba caudavittata), also known as the flagtailed terapon, is a species of grunter in the family Terapontidae, native to Australia and Papua New Guinea. Adults reach about 27 cm with a robust, compressed body displaying silvery-grey coloration and a distinctive yellow caudal fin marked with horizontal dark stripes. This species is remarkably euryhaline, inhabiting both freshwater and marine environments including estuaries, rivers, mangrove creeks, and coastal lagoons at depths of 0-5 meters from Cape Leeuwin in Western Australia along the north coast to Bowen, Queensland.

They produce grunting sounds by grinding their pharyngeal teeth, amplified by the swim bladder. Yellow-tailed grunters feed on insects, crustaceans, mollusks, and plant matter. Their ability to thrive in diverse salinities makes them one of the most adaptable Australian fish species, encountered in habitats ranging from freshwater billabongs to coral reef flats.

name: Skunk Anemonefish
shortDescription:
The skunk anemonefish (Amphiprion akallopisos) is a small clownfish found in the western Indian Ocean. Adults reach 8-11 cm and display a uniform peach to pinkish-orange body with a single narrow white stripe running along the dorsal midline from the upper lip to the tail, resembling a skunk's stripe. They lack the vertical head bars typical of many other clownfish species, giving them a clean, elegant appearance.

They live in symbiosis with host anemones, primarily Heteractis magnifica and Stichodactyla mertensii, at depths of 3-25 meters on coral reefs. Like other clownfish, they are protandrous hermaphrodites with a dominant female leading each group. They feed on zooplankton and algae near their host anemone.

Their gentle demeanor and subtle beauty make them a favorite subject for macro photographers visiting Indian Ocean dive destinations. They are commonly encountered in the Maldives, Seychelles, and along the East African coast.

photographyTips: Use a macro lens and include the host anemone for context; their pale coloring requires careful exposure to avoid overexposure of the white stripe.

name: Barrier Reef Anemonefish
shortDescription:
The barrier reef anemonefish (Amphiprion akindynos) is a species of clownfish in the family Pomacentridae, primarily found on the Great Barrier Reef of Australia. Adults reach about 12-13 cm with a light to dark orange-brown body, two white vertical bars, and a whitish tail. The species name 'akindynos' is Greek for 'safe,' referring to the protection the fish receives from its host anemone's stinging tentacles.

This species inhabits coral reefs at depths of 1-25 meters, living in obligate symbiosis with host sea anemones. They feed on algae, zooplankton, and small invertebrates. Like all clownfish, they are protandrous hermaphrodites, with the dominant individual in each anemone being female and the next-largest being the breeding male. Their bold, territorial behavior and endearing relationship with their host anemone make them captivating subjects for underwater observation and photography.
divingRegions: Great Barrier Reef, South Pacific Islands
bestSeason: Year-round; best conditions on GBR September-December
photographyTips: Use a macro lens for close-up portraits; capture them with their host anemone for the full symbiotic story.

name: Twobar Anemonefish
shortDescription:
The twobar anemonefish (Amphiprion allardi), also known as Allard's clownfish, is a colorful clownfish reaching up to 15 cm. It has a vivid orange body with two broad white bars edged in black crossing the head and mid-body. Found in the western Indian Ocean from Kenya to Durban, South Africa, and east to Mauritius, it inhabits coral reefs at depths of 2 to 30 meters.

This species lives in symbiosis with bubble-tip anemones (Entacmaea quadricolor), rarely venturing far from its host. It feeds on zooplankton, algae, and small invertebrates. Like other clownfish, it lives in hierarchical groups where the largest individual is the dominant female. Its restricted western Indian Ocean range makes it a special find for divers exploring the reefs of East Africa.

name: Yellowtail Clownfish
shortDescription:
The yellowtail clownfish (Amphiprion clarkii), also known as Clark's anemonefish, is the most widely distributed clownfish species, found from the Persian Gulf to Micronesia and Japan to Australia. Reaching about 15 cm in length, it displays remarkable color variation across its range, from nearly black with white bands and a bright yellow tail to orange, brown, or yellow-bodied forms. Two or three white vertical bands cross the body.

It is the least host-specific of all clownfish, associating with at least ten species of sea anemones, which it protects from anemone-eating fish in exchange for shelter among the stinging tentacles. Clownfish produce a mucus coating that prevents the anemone's nematocysts from firing. Like all clownfish, they are protandrous hermaphrodites: all individuals begin as males, with the dominant fish in a group transitioning to female. The female is the largest and most aggressive member of the hierarchy. Yellowtail clownfish are bolder than many species and will charge at approaching divers while making audible popping sounds.
longDescription: Clark's anemonefish (Amphiprion clarkii) ranges throughout the Indo-West Pacific from the Persian Gulf and East Africa east to Melanesia, north to southern Japan, and south to northwestern Australia. The most widely distributed clownfish, hosting in nearly all ten of the symbiotic anemone species used by the genus.

name: Maldivian Anemonefish
shortDescription:
The Maldivian anemonefish (Amphiprion nigripes) is a small, colorful clownfish endemic to the Maldives and Sri Lanka. Adults reach 7-11 cm in length and display a vibrant orange body with a single white vertical bar behind the eye and distinctive black pelvic and anal fins, which give it the species name 'nigripes' (black feet). They live exclusively with the magnificent sea anemone (Heteractis magnifica) and are found on coral reefs at depths of 2-25 meters.

Like other clownfish, they are protandrous hermaphrodites living in social groups with a dominant female. They feed on zooplankton and algae and rarely venture far from their host anemone. Their restricted range makes them a special sighting for divers visiting the Maldives, where they are one of the most commonly encountered and photographed reef fish. Their bold orange color contrasting with the purple or brown anemone creates a striking visual combination.

name: Psychedelic Wrasse

imageCredit.artist: Ludwig Jerry, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service

shortDescription:
The psychedelic wrasse (Anampses chrysocephalus) is a stunningly colored wrasse endemic to the Hawaiian Islands. Males reach 15-18 cm and display one of the most remarkable color patterns in the reef fish world: a dark body covered in brilliant white spots and lines creating a psychedelic pattern, with a vivid orange-red head and matching red tail. Females (known as redtail tamarin wrasse) display a more subdued dark brown body with white spots and an orange-red tail.

They inhabit coral reefs and rubble areas at depths of 5-40 meters. They are protogynous hermaphrodites, with dominant females transitioning to the spectacularly colored male form. They feed on small benthic invertebrates picked from reef surfaces.

Their extreme beauty has made them one of the most sought-after aquarium fish, leading to collection pressure. For divers, encountering a male psychedelic wrasse on a Hawaiian reef is a highlight, as their unique color pattern is unlike any other fish species.

photographyTips: Use a macro or mid-range lens; males are territorial and may circle back, allowing multiple photo opportunities — strobes are essential to capture the vivid colors.

name: Natal Spurfowl Wrasse
shortDescription:
The natal wrasse (Anchichoerops natalensis) is a large, robust wrasse reaching up to 60 cm in length. Males are spectacularly colored with a deep blue-green head, orange body, and intricate facial markings, while females and juveniles display a more subdued brownish coloration. Endemic to the Indian Ocean coasts of South Africa and Mozambique, it inhabits rocky reefs and kelp-lined areas at depths of 5 to 40 meters.

This species is a protogynous hermaphrodite, with dominant females transforming into colorful males. It feeds on sea urchins, crabs, and shellfish, using its strong jaws to crush hard-shelled prey. As a game fish and dive attraction along the South African coastline, it is popular with both anglers and underwater photographers. Its bold colors and approachable behavior on rocky reefs make it a highlight of temperate South African diving.
divingRegions: Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round; best visibility from April to September along the South African coast
photographyTips: Use wide-angle to capture the full body in its rocky reef habitat; males are especially photogenic with their vivid coloration.

name: Black Cod
shortDescription:
The black cod (Anoplopoma fimbria), more accurately called sablefish, is a deep-water fish reaching up to 120 cm in length and 25 kg in weight. Despite its common name, it is not a true cod but belongs to its own family (Anoplopomatidae). It has a sleek, elongated body with a dark grey to black coloration on the back and upper sides, fading to lighter grey below. The skin is smooth and velvety, and two dorsal fins are well separated.

Black cod are found throughout the North Pacific from California to Alaska and across to Japan, primarily inhabiting deep continental slopes at depths of 200-2,000 meters, though juveniles and some adults occur in shallower waters accessible to divers. They are long-lived fish, surviving over 90 years, and are slow to mature, not reproducing until 5-7 years of age. Their flesh is extremely rich in omega-3 oils, making them one of the most prized commercial fish in the Pacific. Divers in the Pacific Northwest occasionally encounter juveniles around kelp forests and rocky reefs in waters as shallow as 20-30 meters.
divingRegions: Pacific Northwest, California & Baja
bestSeason: Year-round; juveniles more accessible to divers in summer and autumn in shallower waters
photographyTips: Standard lens for full-body shots; their dark coloration requires careful strobe positioning to reveal detail. Deep-water encounters require advanced diving certification.

name: Mediterranean Feather Star

imageCredit.artist:
Massimiliano De Martino

Original uploader was Yoruno at it.wikipedia

shortDescription:
The Mediterranean feather star (Antedon mediterranea) is a beautiful crinoid echinoderm found throughout the Mediterranean Sea. Adults have 10-20 feathery pinnate arms reaching 10-15 cm in length, displaying vivid colors from deep red and maroon to yellow, orange, and brown. They perch on elevated positions such as gorgonian sea fans, rocky outcrops, and sponges at depths of 5-200 meters, extending their arms into the current to filter-feed on plankton and suspended organic particles.

Unlike their stalked sea lily relatives, feather stars are free-moving and can swim using coordinated arm movements. They use small hook-like cirri on their base to grip substrates. Their elegant form, vibrant colors, and prominent positions on the reef make them eye-catching subjects for underwater photography. They are one of the most commonly encountered echinoderms on Mediterranean dives and add a tropical touch to temperate underwater landscapes.
divingRegions: Mediterranean
photographyTips: Use a macro lens for arm detail or mid-range when perched on sea fans; their vivid colors contrast beautifully with the blue water background.

name: Yellow Encrusting Sponge
shortDescription:
The yellow encrusting sponge (Aplysina aerophoba) is a conspicuous marine sponge found throughout the Mediterranean Sea and eastern Atlantic. It forms bright yellow tubular or encrusting colonies on rocky substrates, typically with chimney-like oscula (exhaust openings) at the tops of tubes. Colonies can cover substantial areas of rock face and grow up to 20 cm tall. The vivid yellow color turns dark purple-black when the sponge is removed from water and exposed to air.

It is a filter feeder processing large volumes of seawater to extract bacteria and organic particles. This sponge contains bioactive compounds of pharmaceutical interest and provides habitat for numerous small invertebrates within its porous structure.

photographyTips: Wide-angle or macro depending on colony size; the vivid yellow provides great color contrast against dark rocky substrate; look for small critters living in the tubes.

name: Penpoint Gunnel
shortDescription:
The penpoint gunnel (Apodichthys flavidus) is a slender, eel-like fish reaching up to 46 cm in length. It comes in several striking color morphs including bright green, maroon, and orange, matching the seaweed in which it hides. Found along the Pacific coast from the Bering Sea to southern California, it inhabits intertidal and shallow subtidal rocky areas, tide pools, and kelp beds at depths of 0 to 10 meters.

Its common name refers to a dark, pen-nib-shaped mark at the base of the anal fin spine. This species coils its body among seaweed fronds and eelgrass, feeding on small crustaceans and mollusks. Both parents guard egg masses, with the female coiling around the eggs in a protective embrace. Its vivid color variations and snake-like movements through tide pool vegetation make it a fascinating find for shore divers and tide pool explorers.

name: Black-Spotted Pufferfish
shortDescription:
The black-spotted pufferfish (Arothron nigropunctatus) is a medium-to-large pufferfish reaching up to 33 cm, found throughout the Indo-Pacific. Its body is round and robust, typically grey to yellowish-brown, covered in distinctive black spots that vary in size and density between individuals. Some specimens display a striking yellow or golden color morph.

Like all pufferfish, it can inflate its body by swallowing water when threatened, becoming nearly spherical and difficult for predators to swallow. It possesses tetrodotoxin in its skin and organs, making it highly toxic if consumed. This species inhabits coral reefs and lagoons, often seen resting on coral heads or slowly swimming along reef edges.

It feeds on algae, sponges, tunicates, and small invertebrates, using its fused beak-like teeth to crush hard-shelled prey. Known for its docile and inquisitive nature, it often allows divers to approach closely, making it a favorite subject for underwater photographers. Its expressive face and slow, deliberate swimming style give it a personality-rich appearance.

photographyTips: Approach slowly for close-up portraits; use a macro lens to capture the textured skin and expressive face. Strobe lighting brings out the contrast of black spots.

name: Forbes Sea Star
shortDescription:
The Forbes sea star (Asterias forbesi) is a medium-sized starfish found in the northwestern Atlantic. Adults reach 12-20 cm in diameter and typically have 5 arms, occasionally 4 or 6, with a small orange madreporite (sieve plate) visible on the dorsal surface. Coloration ranges from tan and olive to brown and reddish-purple, with a lighter underside covered in rows of tube feet.

They inhabit rocky shores, jetties, pilings, and sandy substrates at depths of 0-50 meters. They are voracious predators of bivalve mollusks, gripping both shell halves with their tube feet, prying them apart, and inserting their stomach to digest the prey externally. They can regenerate lost arms over several months.

They play a significant ecological role in controlling mussel and oyster populations. Divers commonly encounter them on rocky substrates and man-made structures throughout the northwestern Atlantic, where their predatory behavior on bivalves can be directly observed.

name: Sand Smelt

imageCredit.artist:
This illustration was made by Citron
You must credit this : Citron / CC-BY-SA-3.0

shortDescription:
The sand smelt (Atherina presbyter) is a small, slender fish reaching about 20 cm in length, found in shallow coastal waters of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean. It has a translucent, elongated body with a bright silver lateral stripe running from behind the eye to the tail, and a green-grey back. Its scales are relatively large and easily shed. Sand smelts form dense schools in shallow water, from harbors and estuaries to rocky coastlines and sandy beaches, typically within a few meters of the surface.

They feed on zooplankton, small crustaceans, and larval fish, and are in turn a crucial food source for larger predatory fish, seabirds, and marine mammals. Their schooling behavior creates beautiful visual effects as hundreds of fish move in synchronized patterns, their silver flanks catching and reflecting sunlight in shimmering displays. Divers and snorkelers in European and Mediterranean waters routinely encounter these schools near pier pilings, rocky walls, and seagrass beds. They spawn in spring and summer, attaching eggs to algae and seagrass with adhesive filaments.

imageCredit.attribution: (c) Hamid Badar Osmany, some rights reserved (CC BY)

shortDescription:
The frigate tuna (Auxis thazard) is a small tuna in the family Scombridae. Adults reach up to 65 cm and 1.7 kg with a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body, dark blue above with a distinctive pattern of oblique wavy lines on the scaleless area behind the corselet, and silvery below. This species inhabits tropical and subtropical open waters worldwide at depths of 0-200 meters, often near the surface. Frigate tuna are fast, schooling predators that hunt in packs, feeding on small fish, squid, and crustaceans.

They are found throughout the world's tropical oceans and are commonly encountered by divers at offshore reefs, seamounts, and around floating objects. Their rapid swimming speed and schooling behavior create dynamic underwater scenes. They are also important prey for larger predators including marlins, sharks, and dolphins.

It aggregates in large numbers in open water above reefs. It feeds on zooplankton. It is not strongly territorial. In the darkness of deep water, it becomes invisible save for its post-dorsal white spot, giving the illusion of glowing in the dark. It is oviparous, and the males of the species guard and aerate the eggs.

name: Orange-Stripe Triggerfish
shortDescription:
The orange-stripe triggerfish (Balistapus undulatus), also known as the undulate triggerfish, is a medium-sized triggerfish reaching up to 30 cm in length. It has a deep, compressed body with a striking coloration: dark green to olive-brown background covered with diagonal orange lines on the body and face, and orange or yellow markings around the mouth. The caudal peduncle features forward-pointing orange spines used in territorial disputes.

Like all triggerfish, it possesses a locking dorsal spine that it erects when sheltering in crevices, making it nearly impossible to extract. This species is found throughout the Indo-Pacific on coral reefs, particularly in areas with mixed coral and rubble. It feeds on coral tips, sponges, tunicates, algae, and a variety of invertebrates, using its powerful jaws and teeth to crush hard-shelled prey. The orange-stripe triggerfish is notoriously territorial and aggressive, particularly during the breeding season when females guard egg nests and will charge at divers who venture too close.

name: Axilspot Hogfish
shortDescription:
The bastard hogfish (Bodianus axillaris), also known as the turncoat hogfish or coral hogfish, is a medium-sized wrasse reaching about 20 cm in length. Adults display a bicolored pattern with the front half of the body dark maroon-brown and the rear half white, separated by a sharp boundary. A prominent black spot marks the base of the pectoral fin.

Juveniles look completely different, with a dark brown to black body adorned with bright orange-red spots and a yellow-edged ocellus on the soft dorsal fin. This dramatic color transformation as the fish matures can confuse observers into thinking they are different species. Found throughout the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to the Pacific Islands, it inhabits coral-rich reef slopes and walls, typically between 10 and 40 meters.

Juveniles often act as cleaner fish, picking parasites from larger species at cleaning stations. Adults are more solitary and feed on small invertebrates, crustaceans, and worms. The species is a protogynous hermaphrodite, with females transforming into males.
divingRegions: Maldives & Chagos, Polynesia, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, French Polynesia, Micronesia, South Pacific Islands, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Macro lens for both juvenile and adult forms; document the dramatic color difference between life stages. Capture juvenile cleaning behavior at stations for behavioral shots.

name: Hawaiian Hogfish
shortDescription:
The Hawaiian hogfish (Bodianus bathycapros) is a wrasse species endemic to the Hawaiian Islands. Adults reach 20-30 cm and display a reddish-pink to maroon body with a white or pale lower half and a distinctive dark spot on the dorsal fin. They are found on deeper rocky reefs, ledges, and drop-offs at depths of 20-100 meters, making them a reward for deeper recreational and technical dives.

They feed on benthic invertebrates including crustaceans, mollusks, and echinoderms, which they pick from reef surfaces with their protrusible mouth. They are protogynous hermaphrodites, with larger individuals being male. Their Hawaiian endemism, attractive coloration, and association with deeper reef habitats make them a noteworthy sighting that experienced divers in Hawaii specifically seek out. They add a splash of color to the deeper reef environments where they are typically found.
divingRegions: Hawaii
photographyTips: Use a mid-range lens on deeper dives; strobes are essential to restore the reddish-pink coloration that appears dark without artificial light at depth.

name: Saddleback Hogfish
shortDescription:
The bastard hogfish (Bodianus bilunulatus), also known as the saddleback hogfish, is a species of wrasse in the family Labridae. Adults reach up to 55 cm with a white to yellowish-white body and a large black saddle marking on the posterior portion. Juveniles are strikingly different, often showing a bright yellow and black pattern.

This species inhabits coral reefs and lagoons at depths of 5-60 meters throughout the Indo-Pacific, from East Africa to Hawaii. They are typically solitary, feeding on sea urchins, crustaceans, mollusks, and brittle stars. Juveniles often act as cleaner fish at cleaning stations where they remove parasites from larger reef fish. Their dramatic color transformation from juvenile to adult makes them particularly interesting for underwater naturalists.
divingRegions: South Africa, Hawaii, Lord Howe & Norfolk, Western Australia, Southern Japan, Micronesia, Japan, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round; juveniles performing cleaning behavior are most active during daytime
photographyTips: Approach slowly and look for them near coral heads; a mid-range lens captures the bold black and white contrast well.

name: Island Hogfish
shortDescription:
The island hogfish (Bodianus insularis) is a species of wrasse in the family Labridae found in the eastern Atlantic Ocean. Adults reach about 35 cm with a robust body displaying reddish to pinkish coloration. This species is restricted to islands associated with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, including St. Helena, Ascension Island, and surrounding seamounts.

It inhabits rocky reefs and reef slopes at depths of 5-50 meters. Island hogfish feed on benthic invertebrates including sea urchins, crustaceans, and mollusks. Their geographic isolation has led to their evolution as a distinct species from related Bodianus hogfishes. Due to the remoteness of their habitat, they are rarely encountered by recreational divers, making any sighting noteworthy. The species name 'insularis' reflects their island-restricted distribution.

name: Red Pigfish
shortDescription:
The red pigfish (Bodianus vulpinus) is a large wrasse endemic to New Zealand, found around both the North and South Islands as well as the Kermadec Islands. Growing to about 55 cm, adults display a stunning deep red to orange-red body, sometimes with darker mottling on the upper flanks. Males tend to be more intensely colored than females and develop a more robust head profile.

This species inhabits rocky reefs, particularly around kelp forests and reef walls, at moderate depths. It is a carnivore with strong jaws adapted for crushing hard-shelled prey including sea urchins, crabs, mollusks, and brittlestars. Red pigfish are known for their inquisitive nature, often approaching divers closely and making them popular reef companions during dives.

They are protogynous hermaphrodites, with females capable of changing sex to male. This species is relatively long-lived and slow-growing. Its vibrant coloration against the backdrop of New Zealand's lush kelp forests makes it one of the most photogenic temperate reef fish in the region.

name: Butterfly Perch
shortDescription:
The butterfly perch (Caesioperca lepidoptera) is a marine fish in the family Anthiadidae found in temperate waters of Australia and New Zealand. Adults reach up to 47 cm with a laterally compressed, deep body displaying pinkish coloration, blue margins on the fins, a blue band behind the eye, and a distinctive large black spot toward the posterior end. This species inhabits rocky reefs, outcrops, and drop-offs at depths of 4-100 meters. Butterfly perch are schooling planktivores that form aggregations above high-profile reef structures, feeding on zooplankton in the water column.

They are one of the most commonly encountered schooling fish on temperate Australian reefs and can form impressive aggregations. Their attractive pink coloration and schooling behavior make them a highlight of many temperate diving experiences in southern Australia.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, New Zealand, Western Australia, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia
bestSeason: Year-round; large schools most common in spring and summer
photographyTips: Wide-angle lens captures their beautiful pink schools above reef formations; natural light enhances their soft pink coloration.

shortDescription:
The big blue octopus (Callistoctopus macropus), also known as the white-spotted octopus, is a medium-sized octopus with an arm span reaching about 150 cm found in the Mediterranean and tropical Indo-Pacific. Despite the common name 'big blue,' it is typically reddish-brown to maroon covered with distinctive white spots. It is nocturnal, emerging at night to hunt small crustaceans and mollusks on sandy and rocky substrate.

During the day it hides in crevices, under rocks, or in empty shells. It is commonly encountered on night dives in the Mediterranean, where it is one of the most frequently seen octopus species. Its striking spotted pattern and approachable nature make it a popular photography subject.

shortDescription:
The elephant fish (Callorhinchus milii), also known as the Australian ghostshark, is a cartilaginous fish belonging to the chimaera order. It reaches about 1.2 meters in length and is immediately recognizable by its fleshy, trunk-like protrusion on its snout, called a proboscis, which is covered in electroreceptors used to detect prey buried in sandy and muddy bottoms. Its body is silvery with dark brown patches and a large dorsal fin preceded by a venomous spine.

Unlike true sharks, chimaeras have smooth skin without scales, a single gill opening on each side covered by an operculum, and upper jaws fused to the skull. Elephant fish are found in temperate waters of the southern hemisphere, typically over continental shelves. They feed on shellfish, crustaceans, and small bottom-dwelling organisms.

During spring, they move into shallow bays and estuaries to lay large, leathery egg cases on sandy bottoms. Their ancient lineage dates back over 400 million years, making them living fossils of significant evolutionary interest.
divingRegions: Southern Australia, New Zealand, Southwestern Australia
bestSeason: Spring (October-December in southern hemisphere) when they move into shallow bays to breed
photographyTips: Approach carefully along the sandy bottom; use a wide-angle lens to capture the distinctive proboscis and overall body shape in context.

name: Northern Fur Seal
shortDescription:
The northern fur seal (Callorhinus ursinus) is a marine mammal in the family Otariidae. Adult males reach up to 2.1 m and 270 kg, while females are considerably smaller at about 1.4 m and 50 kg. They have a dense, dark brown to black underfur with longer guard hairs, small external ear flaps, and large, expressive eyes.

Males develop a thick neck and mane during maturity. This species inhabits the North Pacific Ocean, with major breeding colonies on the Pribilof Islands (Alaska), Commander Islands (Russia), and smaller colonies on other North Pacific islands. They spend most of their life at sea, diving to depths of up to 200 meters to feed on fish and squid. Northern fur seals are highly curious and playful, often approaching and interacting with divers in entertaining displays of underwater acrobatics. Their large, dark eyes and agile swimming make underwater encounters with them a thrilling and memorable experience.
divingRegions: California & Baja
bestSeason: Summer (June-August) near breeding colonies; year-round at sea
photographyTips: Wide-angle lens essential for their playful underwater approaches; they often initiate interaction, creating dynamic photo opportunities.

name: Star-Eye Parrotfish
shortDescription:
The star-eye parrotfish (Calotomus carolinus), also known as Caroline's parrotfish or the stareye parrotfish, is a medium-sized parrotfish reaching up to 50 cm. It has a mottled brown to reddish body with distinctive bright radiating lines around each eye creating a star-like pattern. Found across the Indo-Pacific from East Africa to Hawaii and the eastern Pacific, it inhabits coral reefs, rocky areas, and algae-covered substrates at depths of 1 to 46 meters.

Unlike many parrotfish that use beak-like fused teeth, this species has individual teeth and feeds by tearing rather than scraping algae from surfaces. Its more subdued coloring compared to other parrotfish, combined with the unique eye pattern, makes it an interesting find for divers familiar with reef fish identification. It is often seen grazing individually or in small loose groups across reef flats.
divingRegions: Polynesia, Hawaii, Great Barrier Reef, Southern Japan, Eastern Tropical Pacific, Micronesia, South Pacific Islands, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round; commonly seen on shallow reef and reef flat dives
photographyTips: Use macro to capture the distinctive star-eye pattern; moderate approach speed as they can be skittish.

name: Jonah Crab
shortDescription:
The Jonah crab (Cancer borealis) is a large, heavily built crab found along the northwestern Atlantic coast. Adults reach a carapace width of 15-22 cm and display a yellowish to reddish-brown, roughly oval carapace with coarsely toothed edges. Their robust claws have black tips and are powerful enough to crack open mollusks and sea urchins.

They inhabit rocky reefs, boulder fields, and offshore banks at depths of 0-800 meters, though most commonly encountered by divers between 5-50 meters. They are omnivorous predators and scavengers feeding on mollusks, sea urchins, crustaceans, and algae. They are often found sheltering in rock crevices and under boulders during the day, emerging at night to forage.

Their large size and imposing claws make them an impressive sight for divers in New England and Maritime Canadian waters. They have become increasingly important commercially as an alternative to declining American lobster stocks.

name: Nervous Shark
shortDescription:
The nervous shark (Carcharhinus cautus) is a small requiem shark in the family Carcharhinidae. Adults reach up to 150 cm with a typical carcharhinid body shape, grey-brown coloration above, white below, and slightly darker fin tips. The species name 'cautus' means cautious in Latin, reflecting this shark's extremely wary behavior around humans.

This species inhabits shallow coastal waters, mangrove-lined creeks, and inshore reefs at depths of 0-20 meters in tropical Australia and Papua New Guinea. Nervous sharks feed on small fish, crustaceans, and cephalopods. They are viviparous, giving birth to litters of 1-6 pups. True to their name, they are one of the most skittish shark species, frequently fleeing from divers at considerable distance.

This behavior makes them challenging but rewarding to observe in the wild. They pose no threat to humans and are themselves listed as Near Threatened due to habitat degradation.

photographyTips: Extremely wary of divers; use a long zoom lens and remain very still, as they flee quickly from any perceived disturbance.

name: Devonshire Cup Coral
shortDescription:
The Devonshire cup coral (Caryophyllia smithii) is a solitary, non-reef-building stony coral found throughout the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean. Adults grow to about 3 cm in diameter and 1.5 cm tall, with a cup-shaped calcareous skeleton surrounded by up to 80 translucent tentacles that can be white, green, pink, or orange with contrasting tips. Unlike tropical reef corals, it does not rely on symbiotic algae and thrives in low-light conditions on rocky walls, overhangs, and wrecks at depths of 1-100 meters.

It feeds by capturing small planktonic organisms with its stinging tentacles, which are typically extended at night or in areas with strong currents. Each polyp is a separate individual, though they often occur in dense aggregations covering rock surfaces. Their delicate beauty and variety of colors make them one of the most rewarding macro photography subjects in temperate waters, particularly when tentacles are fully extended.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean, North Sea & Baltic
bestSeason: Year-round, tentacles more often extended in winter
photographyTips: Use a macro lens with a snoot or focused strobe to isolate individual polyps; tentacles are more likely to be extended during current flow or at night.

longDescription: The Upside-Down Jellyfish has turned the jellyfish lifestyle literally on its head. It rests bell-down on shallow sandy flats, farming zooxanthellae algae in its oral arms much like corals farm symbiotic algae. It can still sting — releasing mucus clouds containing stinging cells into the water above it.

name: Longnose Sucker

The longnose sucker (Catostomus catostomus) is a streamlined freshwater fish reaching up to 64 cm. It has an elongated body with a distinctive long snout and a ventral, fleshy-lipped mouth adapted for bottom feeding. Coloring is dark olive to brown above and pale below, with males developing a vivid red lateral stripe during spawning season.

Found across northern North America from the northern United States to Alaska and northern Canada, and in parts of Siberia, it inhabits clear, cold lakes and rivers at depths of 0 to 30 meters. This species feeds by sucking up algae, invertebrates, and detritus from rocky and gravel substrates. Its abundance and large size make it a commonly encountered fish during freshwater dives in northern lakes and rivers, where groups can be observed methodically working over rocky bottoms.

name: Resplendent Pygmy Angelfish
shortDescription:
The resplendent pygmy angelfish (Centropyge resplendens) is a small, vividly colored marine angelfish in the family Pomacanthidae. Adults reach only about 6 cm in length. They display a stunning bright blue body with brilliant orange-yellow areas on the head, dorsal region, and fins.

This species is endemic to Ascension Island in the remote mid-Atlantic Ocean, making it one of the rarest angelfish in the world. It inhabits rocky and coral reef areas at depths of 15-40 meters, where it feeds primarily on algae, detritus, and small invertebrates. The resplendent pygmy angelfish is typically solitary or found in small harems with one dominant male and several females.

Like other Centropyge species, they are protogynous hermaphrodites. Their extreme rarity and limited range, combined with their dazzling coloration, make them one of the most sought-after sightings for dedicated fish-watching divers.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, South Atlantic Islands, Caribbean, US East Coast
photographyTips: Use a macro lens and patience; these tiny, shy fish dart into crevices quickly, so pre-focus on their territory and wait for them to emerge.

Inhabits coral and rocky reefs from a few metres to ~170 m, where it sits motionless on or near substrate, ambushing small fishes and crustaceans. name: Blue-Spotted Grouper
shortDescription:
The blue-spotted grouper (Cephalopholis cyanostigma), also known as the bluespotted hind, is a species of grouper in the family Serranidae. Adults reach up to 55 cm with a robust, reddish-brown body covered with numerous small, bright blue spots surrounded by pale circular markings. This species inhabits coral reefs, reef slopes, and rocky areas at depths of 3-45 meters across the western Pacific, from Indonesia and the Philippines to the Great Barrier Reef and Japan. Blue-spotted groupers are typically solitary and territorial, often found perched on coral heads or resting in crevices during the day.

They are ambush predators feeding on small fish and crustaceans. Like other Cephalopholis groupers, they are protogynous hermaphrodites. Their vivid blue spots against the reddish-brown body create a stunning appearance that makes them one of the more photogenic small grouper species.
divingRegions: Coral Triangle, Great Barrier Reef, Sunda Shelf
photographyTips: Often perched on coral heads; use a macro or mid-range lens to capture the intricate pattern of blue spots on the reddish body.

name: Coney Grouper
shortDescription:
The coney grouper (Cephalopholis fulva) is a small, beautifully colored grouper reaching about 40 cm in length, found throughout the western Atlantic and Caribbean. It displays remarkable color variability, occurring in several distinct phases: the most common reddish-brown phase covered with small blue spots, a bright yellow phase (xanthic), a bicolor phase with dark upper body and pale lower body, and an entirely dark phase. All phases feature two prominent black spots on the chin and two on the caudal peduncle. This protogynous hermaphrodite inhabits coral reefs from just below the surface to about 150 meters, though most commonly found between 10-45 meters.

It is a sit-and-wait predator, perching motionless on coral heads or reef edges before lunging at passing small fish and crustaceans. Coneys are among the most commonly encountered groupers on Caribbean dives and are relatively tame, often allowing close approach. They frequently visit cleaning stations where small gobies and shrimp remove parasites. Their multiple color phases make identification interesting and photography rewarding.
divingRegions: Caribbean, Brazil Coast
bestSeason: Year-round; look for the rare yellow phase for something special
photographyTips: Macro to standard lens; approach slowly as they often hold position on their perch. Document different color phases for comparison. Strobes bring out the blue spot detail.

name: Swell Shark
shortDescription:
The swell shark (Cephaloscyllium ventriosum) is a small, docile catshark reaching about 1 m found in the eastern Pacific from central California to southern Mexico and Chile. It has a flattened head, mottled brown and tan patterning with dark and light saddle markings providing excellent camouflage. When threatened, it curls into a U-shape, grabs its tail fin with its mouth, and swallows water to inflate to nearly double its normal size, wedging itself tightly into crevices.

It is biofluorescent, glowing bright green under ultraviolet light. A nocturnal species, it is commonly found resting in rocky caves and crevices during the day by divers in California kelp forests.
divingRegions: California & Baja
photographyTips: Look in caves and under ledges during day; UV lights reveal biofluorescence; wide-angle for full body in cave settings; do not harass into inflating.

name: Hornwort
shortDescription:
Hornwort (Ceratophyllum demersum) is a rootless, free-floating submerged aquatic plant found in freshwater habitats worldwide. It grows in dense, bushy masses with branching stems reaching 1-3 meters in length. The leaves are dark green, stiff, and forked into narrow, toothed segments arranged in whorls around the stem, giving the plant a foxtail-like appearance.

Unlike most aquatic plants, hornwort lacks true roots and either floats freely or anchors itself loosely to the substrate by modified leaves. It reproduces primarily through fragmentation and can grow rapidly, forming extensive underwater meadows. These stands provide critical habitat for aquatic organisms including juvenile fish, invertebrates, and amphibian larvae. The plant is an efficient oxygenator and water purifier, absorbing excess nutrients and helping to prevent algal blooms.

Freshwater divers encounter hornwort in lakes, ponds, slow rivers, and springs, where it creates beautiful underwater landscapes reminiscent of terrestrial forests in miniature. It tolerates a wide range of water conditions and can be found from tropical to temperate latitudes.

photographyTips: Wide-angle for underwater meadow scenes with sunlight filtering through; macro for leaf detail and the small invertebrates sheltering among fronds.

name: Blue-Cheeked Butterflyfish
shortDescription:
The hooded butterflyfish (Chaetodon larvatus) is a medium-sized butterflyfish reaching about 12 cm in length, endemic to the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and Gulf of Oman. It is immediately recognizable by its pale orange body with dark chevron-shaped markings, a distinctive bright blue or bluish-grey patch covering the cheek area, and a dark hood-like marking over the head. This species inhabits coral-rich reef slopes, walls, and outer reef areas at depths from 3 to 12 meters, where it feeds almost exclusively on Acropora coral polyps. Blue-cheeked butterflyfish are typically found in pairs or small groups, maintaining long-term pair bonds.

Their dependence on healthy coral makes them indicators of reef quality. As a Red Sea endemic, they are one of the species that diving visitors most want to see and photograph. Their distinctive coloration, predictable pairing behavior, and coral-rich habitat combine to make them one of the most beautiful and photogenic butterflyfish species in the world.
divingRegions: Red Sea, Arabian Sea
bestSeason: Year-round; Red Sea diving conditions are excellent throughout the year
photographyTips: Macro or mid-range lens; pairs against colorful coral backgrounds create stunning compositions. Their shallow depth range means excellent natural light.

name: Rapanui Butterflyfish
shortDescription:
The Rapanui butterflyfish (Chaetodon litus), also known as the Easter Island butterflyfish, is a small reef fish reaching up to 15 cm. It has a pale grey to white body with a black eye bar, yellowish fins, and a distinctive black spot near the rear dorsal area. Endemic to the seas around Easter Island, approximately 3,500 km off the coast of mainland Chile, it inhabits brown algae-covered volcanic boulders at depths of 1 to 25 meters.

This species feeds on worms, crustaceans, barnacles, and other benthic invertebrates. As one of the most geographically restricted butterflyfish in the world, finding this species is a unique privilege reserved for divers visiting the remote island. Its subtle beauty and extreme rarity make it a prized sighting for fish enthusiasts and underwater photographers.
divingRegions: Easter Island
bestSeason: Year-round; Easter Island diving best from October to April
photographyTips: Use macro for detailed portraits showing the subtle coloration; they can be shy, so approach slowly among the volcanic boulders.

name: St Helena Butterflyfish

imageCredit.artist: holger_heye, einige Rechte vorbehalten (CC BY-NC), hochgeladen von holger_heye

shortDescription:
The St. Helena butterflyfish (Chaetodon sanctaehelenae), locally known as the cunningfish, is a species of butterflyfish in the family Chaetodontidae. Adults reach about 15 cm with a compressed body displaying a yellowish to brownish coloration with darker vertical barring.

This species is endemic to the remote mid-Atlantic islands of St. Helena and Ascension Island, making it one of the rarest butterflyfishes in the world. It inhabits rocky reef areas at depths of 3-30 meters around these volcanic islands. The local name 'cunningfish' derives from its ability to nibble bait from fishing hooks while avoiding capture.

Like other butterflyfishes, it feeds on small invertebrates and coral polyps. With fewer than a handful of diving operations reaching these remote islands, the St. Helena butterflyfish remains one of the least observed reef fish species by recreational divers.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, South Atlantic Islands
photographyTips: A standard macro or mid-range lens captures this rare endemic; document location and behavior for scientific value.

name: Pacific Double-Saddle Butterflyfish
shortDescription:
The Pacific double-saddle butterflyfish (Chaetodon ulietensis) is a medium-sized butterflyfish reaching about 15 cm in length, found across the Pacific from Southeast Asia to French Polynesia. It has a white to pale body with fine diagonal lines ascending from the belly, and two bold dark saddle-shaped markings on the upper body: one across the mid-back and one at the rear dorsal area. A dark band passes through the eye, and the caudal fin is yellow with a dark bar. This attractive pattern makes it easily identifiable among the many butterflyfish species.

It inhabits coral-rich reef slopes, lagoons, and outer reef faces, typically at depths of 3-30 meters. Like many butterflyfish, it is usually seen in long-term pair bonds, with both individuals swimming and feeding together. Its diet consists primarily of coral polyps, small invertebrates, and algae. The Pacific double-saddle butterflyfish is a reliable indicator of reef health, as it depends on living coral for food and shelter. It is generally shy but can be approached slowly for photography.
divingRegions: Polynesia, Coral Triangle, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, French Polynesia, South Pacific Islands
photographyTips: Standard or macro lens for pair portraits; approach slowly as they tend to turn away. Wait near a coral head they are feeding on for cooperative behavior.

name: Spotted Snakehead
shortDescription:
The spotted snakehead (Channa punctata) is a freshwater fish in the family Channidae, native to the Indian subcontinent. Adults reach about 30 cm with an elongated, cylindrical body, a large flattened head with a wide mouth, and a continuous dorsal fin. Coloration is olive-green to brown with irregular dark spots and blotches.

This species inhabits ponds, swamps, canals, and slow-moving rivers at depths of 0-3 meters throughout India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, and Myanmar. Spotted snakeheads possess an accessory breathing organ that allows them to breathe atmospheric air, enabling them to survive in stagnant, oxygen-poor waters and even travel short distances over land. They are voracious ambush predators feeding on fish, frogs, insects, and crustaceans. As one of the most resilient freshwater fish in South Asia, they are found in virtually every type of freshwater habitat and are an important food fish throughout their range.

name: Long-Necked Turtle
shortDescription:
The eastern long-necked turtle (Chelodina longicollis), also known as the common snake-necked turtle, is a freshwater turtle in the family Chelidae, endemic to eastern Australia. Adults reach about 25 cm carapace length with a neck reaching approximately 60% of the shell length. The carapace is generally dark brown to black, with a broad cream to yellow plastron edged in black.

Their remarkably long neck allows them to strike sideways to capture prey. This species occupies a broad range of freshwater habitats at depths of 0-5 meters across eastern Australia, from southeastern Queensland through New South Wales to South Australia, including Tasmania. They are more abundant in shallow, ephemeral wetlands. Long-necked turtles are carnivorous ambush predators feeding on aquatic invertebrates, fish, tadpoles, crustaceans, and carrion. When threatened, they emit a strong-smelling musk from glands on the bridge of the shell, earning them the nickname 'stinker.'
divingRegions: Australasian Inland
bestSeason: Year-round; most active spring through autumn
photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens in clear freshwater to capture the distinctive long neck; they are often tolerant of careful approach.

name: Golden Grey Mullet
shortDescription:
The golden grey mullet (Chelon auratus) is a medium-sized mullet species found throughout the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Adults reach 30-45 cm in length and display a streamlined, silvery body with a distinctive golden-yellow spot on the gill cover, which gives the species its name. They form large schools in shallow coastal waters, estuaries, harbors, and lagoons at depths of 0-20 meters. As detritivores and herbivores, they feed by scooping up sand and mud from the bottom, filtering out algae, organic detritus, and small invertebrates.

They are highly tolerant of varying salinity levels and frequently enter freshwater rivers. Their schooling behavior creates impressive underwater scenes, particularly when sunlight filters through shallow water illuminating the silvery flanks. Divers commonly encounter them in Mediterranean harbors and coastal sites, where they have become habituated to human presence and can be approached closely.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean, Caribbean, US East Coast
bestSeason: Year-round, most abundant in warmer months
photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens to capture schooling behavior in shallow, well-lit water; the golden gill spot is best highlighted with side lighting.

name: Common Snapping Turtle
shortDescription:
The common snapping turtle (Chelydra serpentina) is one of the largest freshwater turtles in North America, with a carapace reaching up to 50 cm in length and weights exceeding 16 kg, though some individuals grow much larger. It has a rough, dark brown to black carapace with three keeled ridges, a large head with powerful hooked jaws, a long serrated tail, and notably small plastron that leaves much of its body exposed. Unable to withdraw fully into its shell like other turtles, it relies on its aggressive temperament and powerful bite for defense on land, though it is generally docile and retreating underwater.

This species inhabits virtually any freshwater body including lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, and marshes throughout eastern North America from Canada to the Gulf of Mexico. It is an opportunistic omnivore, feeding on fish, frogs, birds, small mammals, aquatic plants, carrion, and invertebrates. Snapping turtles can live over 100 years and are important apex predators in freshwater ecosystems. Freshwater divers frequently encounter them resting on muddy bottoms or slowly cruising along submerged logs.
longDescription: Surface to 10 meters (freshwater)
divingRegions: North American Inland, Florida Inland
bestSeason: Spring through autumn; June nesting season for observing females on land near water bodies
photographyTips: Wide-angle for full-body shots; maintain a respectful distance from the head as their bite is powerful. They are more docile underwater than on land but should not be provoked.

name: Marron
shortDescription:
The marron (Cherax cainii), also known as the smooth marron, is a large freshwater crayfish in the family Parastacidae, endemic to southwestern Australia. Adults can reach up to 38 cm and over 2 kg, making them the third-largest freshwater crayfish species in the world. They have a robust body with large, smooth-edged claws and coloration varying from dark brown to olive-green, with some individuals displaying striking blue tones. Marron inhabit permanent freshwater rivers, streams, and dams at depths of 0-5 meters in southwestern Western Australia.

They are omnivorous, feeding on decomposing plant material, algae, small invertebrates, and detritus. Marron require well-oxygenated water with adequate shelter such as submerged logs and undercut banks. They are an iconic Western Australian species, important both culturally and as an aquaculture product. Their impressive size and endemic status make encounters in clear Western Australian rivers a memorable freshwater diving experience.

photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens to capture their impressive size; look for them under logs and in burrows in clear river pools.

name: Variable Nudibranch
shortDescription:
The variable nudibranch (Chromodoris magnifica) is a strikingly beautiful sea slug found across the tropical Indo-West Pacific, from Indonesia and the Philippines to Australia and the western Pacific. Adults reach approximately 5-6 cm in length. The body displays a vivid blue to blue-white central region bordered by a bright orange or yellow mantle margin, with a white band separating the two colors. The rhinophores and gill plume are typically orange to yellow.

As suggested by its common name, color intensity and pattern can vary between individuals and populations, though the basic blue-white-orange theme remains consistent. They inhabit coral reefs and rocky substrates at depths of 5-30 meters, where they feed on specific sponge species. Like other chromodorid nudibranchs, they sequester toxic compounds from their sponge prey, which provides chemical defense against predators.

Their bold warning colors advertise this toxicity. Variable nudibranchs are hermaphroditic and lay distinctive spiral egg ribbons on the reef. They are among the most commonly photographed nudibranchs in the Indo-Pacific, and dive guides actively search for them to delight macro photography enthusiasts visiting sites in Indonesia, the Philippines, and Papua New Guinea.
divingRegions: Coral Triangle, Great Barrier Reef, Northern Australia
bestSeason: Year-round; more commonly spotted during calm conditions
photographyTips: Macro lens with dual strobes; black background technique works beautifully with these colorful subjects; focus on the rhinophores; shoot slightly above to show the mantle border.

longDescription: A classic Indo-Pacific chromodorid (~3–4 cm). White body with three parallel black lines running the length of the mantle and a bright yellow or orange marginal band. Feeds on sponges and is a signature Coral Triangle macro subject.

name: Nudibranch (Chromodoris Orientalis)
shortDescription:
Chromodoris orientalis is a striking nudibranch reaching about 3-4 cm in length, found throughout the western Pacific from Japan to Indonesia and the Philippines. Its mantle is white to pale cream with a complex pattern of dark brown to black lines, spots, and reticulations that are unique to each individual. The mantle margin is edged with a thin orange or yellow line, and the rhinophores and gills are typically dark brown to black.

This species belongs to the chromodorid family, known for their vivid coloration which serves as a warning to predators of their chemical defenses derived from the sponges they feed upon. It is typically found on coral reefs and rocky substrates where its preferred sponge prey grows, at depths from the shallows down to about 30 meters. Like all nudibranchs, it is a hermaphrodite and lays ribbon-like egg masses in spiral patterns on the substrate. Its slow, deliberate crawling movement and eye-catching pattern make it a popular subject for macro photography, particularly at famous muck diving destinations in Indonesia and the Philippines.

bestSeason: Year-round in tropical waters; spring in temperate Japanese waters
photographyTips: Use a macro lens with a diopter for maximum detail; shoot at the slug's eye level and include the substrate for context. Dual strobes prevent harsh shadows.

name: Two-Spot Demoiselle
shortDescription:
The two-spot demoiselle (Chrysiptera biocellata), also called the twinspot damselfish, is a small, attractive reef fish reaching up to 12 cm. It has a brownish body with two prominent dark ocelli (eye-spots) on the upper body and dorsal fin. Found across the Indo-Pacific from East Africa to the western Pacific, it inhabits coral rubble, rocky reef areas, and algae-covered substrates at depths of 1 to 12 meters. This territorial species aggressively defends small patches of algae that it cultivates for food, chasing away much larger fish and even approaching divers.

It feeds on algae and small invertebrates within its territory. Its bold personality despite its small size, combined with the distinctive twin spots, makes it an entertaining and identifiable reef resident.

bestSeason: Year-round; visible on most shallow reef dives

name: Rapanui Damselfish
shortDescription:
The Rapanui damselfish (Chrysiptera rapanui), also known as the Easter damselfish, is a small, vibrant reef fish reaching up to 7 cm. It has a bright blue to purple body with variable orange-yellow markings. Found only around Easter Island (Rapa Nui) in the southeastern Pacific and the Kermadec Islands in the southwestern Pacific, it inhabits coral and rocky reefs, surge pools, and shallow reef areas at depths of 1 to 20 meters. This territorial species feeds on algae and small invertebrates.

Its restricted range makes it one of the most special endemic species that divers can encounter on the remote reefs of Easter Island. Despite its small size, its vivid coloring and energetic territorial behavior make it a delightful companion on every dive around Rapa Nui.

name: Slinger Seabream
shortDescription:
The slinger seabream (Chrysoblephus puniceus) is a colorful sparid fish endemic to the southwestern Indian Ocean, primarily found along the South African coast. Adults reach 55-85 cm and display a reddish-pink body with bluish tints, pink fins, and a distinctive slender blue bar below the eyes. They inhabit offshore rocky reefs at depths of 10-130 meters, most commonly between 20-80 meters.

They are protogynous hermaphrodites, with females transforming into males at approximately 5 years of age or 38 cm in length. They feed on crustaceans, cephalopods, and small fish. They are an important sport and commercial fish in KwaZulu-Natal waters.

For divers exploring South African reefs, particularly Aliwal Shoal and the Protea Banks, encountering slingers on deeper reef dives adds a flash of pink to the reef scene. Their restricted distribution makes them a special sighting unavailable elsewhere in the world.
divingRegions: South Africa, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Use a mid-range lens on deeper reef dives; strobes are essential to restore the beautiful pink-red coloration at depth.

name: Mayan cichlid
shortDescription:
Cichlasoma urophthalmus, now reclassified as Mayaheros urophthalmus and commonly known as the Mayan cichlid, is a robust freshwater cichlid reaching up to 27 cm. It has an oval body with variable coloration from olive-brown to reddish, featuring 6 to 8 dark bars and a distinctive ocellus (eye-spot) on the caudal peduncle. Native to the Atlantic slope of Central America from Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula to Nicaragua, it inhabits cenotes, lagoons, rivers, and coastal brackish waters at depths of 0 to 20 meters.

During breeding, both males and females develop intense red coloration on the belly and flanks. This species has undergone extensive taxonomic revision, having been placed in multiple genera including Cichlasoma, Nandopsis, Herichthys, and most recently Mayaheros. Cenote divers in Mexico frequently encounter breeding pairs displaying vivid red coloration in crystal-clear freshwater pools, where they aggressively guard their territory against all intruders.
divingRegions: Florida Inland, Mexico & Central America Freshwater, Indonesian/Malay Inland
bestSeason: Year-round; breeding pairs most colorful in warmer months
photographyTips: Use macro for breeding color detail; natural cenote light provides excellent illumination for portraits of these colorful fish.
