name: Walking Catfish
shortDescription:
The walking catfish (Clarias batrachus) is a freshwater catfish in the family Clariidae, native to Southeast Asia. Adults typically reach 30-50 cm with an elongated, scaleless body, dark brown to grey coloration, flattened head with four pairs of barbels, and a continuous dorsal fin running nearly the entire body length. This species possesses a specialized suprabranchial organ that allows it to breathe atmospheric air and survive out of water for extended periods.

They can use their pectoral fins to 'walk' across land between water bodies, giving them their common name. Found at depths of 0-5 meters in ponds, swamps, rice paddies, and slow-moving rivers throughout Southeast Asia and as an invasive species in Florida. Walking catfish are omnivorous, feeding on fish, invertebrates, plant matter, and detritus.

Their ability to survive in oxygen-poor water and move overland makes them remarkably adaptable. They are an important food fish in Southeast Asia.
divingRegions: Florida Inland, East Asia Inland, Indonesian/Malay Inland, Philippines Inland, SE Asia Freshwater
photographyTips: Best photographed in murky freshwater habitats; use a wide-angle lens with strobe to illuminate their elongated body and distinctive barbels.

name: Brown Seaweed Sculpin
shortDescription:
The brown seaweed sculpin (Clinocottus globiceps), also known as the mosshead sculpin, is a small marine sculpin in the family Cottidae. Adults reach about 19 cm with a large, rounded head, mottled brown to greenish coloration, and bushy cirri (small fleshy projections) on the head that resemble seaweed. This species can change color to match surrounding algae, ranging from brown to green to reddish.

They inhabit rocky intertidal and shallow subtidal zones at depths of 0-18 meters from Kodiak Island, Alaska, to central California. Mosshead sculpins are masters of camouflage, sitting motionless among algae-covered rocks where they blend perfectly with their surroundings. They feed on small crabs, amphipods, isopods, and other invertebrates.

Their ability to breathe air and tolerate exposure at low tide allows them to exploit intertidal habitats. Finding one requires careful observation, as their camouflage is remarkably effective.
divingRegions: California & Baja
bestSeason: Year-round; best seen in tidepools at low tide
photographyTips: Super-macro lens recommended; scan seaweed-covered rocks very carefully to spot their perfectly camouflaged forms.

name: Sea Butterfly (Clio pyramidata)
shortDescription: A pelagic sea butterfly with a translucent pyramidal shell. Swims by flapping wing-like parapodia and is one of the dominant zooplankton pteropods in temperate-to-tropical seas.
longDescription: A planktonic sea butterfly with a translucent pyramidal aragonite shell up to 21 mm long, swimming with wing-like parapodia in the open ocean. Cosmopolitan across temperate to tropical seas, with documented records from polar to equatorial waters and from the surface down to 3,700 m. Performs diel vertical migrations and feeds on phytoplankton and microzooplankton trapped in mucous webs. The thin aragonite shell is highly vulnerable to ocean acidification, making the species a sentinel indicator for climate change in pelagic ecosystems.
divingRegions: Worldwide (subtropical to subpolar pelagic waters; observable on blackwater dives)
bestSeason: Year-round; surface abundance peaks during seasonal phytoplankton blooms
photographyTips: Almost exclusively a blackwater-diving subject — drift over deep water at night with focusing lights and a macro lens (60–100 mm equivalent). Use a small aperture (f/16–f/22) for depth of field on the transparent shell, and a single off-axis strobe to bring out iridescence without blowing highlights. Move slowly: the parapodia beat in hovering bursts and the animal is easily disturbed by camera-mounted lights.

shortDescription:
The sea angel (Clione limacina) is a small pelagic sea slug in the family Clionidae. Adults reach about 3-5 cm with a gelatinous, translucent body completely lacking a shell. They swim using two wing-like extensions of their foot called pteropodia, which beat rhythmically like angel wings. Internal organs, including the pink to orange gonads, are visible through the transparent body.

This species inhabits cold waters of the Arctic Ocean and North Atlantic at depths of 0-500 meters, drifting in the water column as part of the zooplankton. Sea angels are specialized predators that feed almost exclusively on sea butterflies of the genus Limacina, using tentacle-like structures called buccal cones to capture and extract their prey from its shell. Their ethereal, otherworldly appearance as they pulse through dark, cold waters creates one of the most magical encounters possible for cold-water divers. They are increasingly studied as indicators of ocean acidification impacts.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, California & Baja, US East Coast
bestSeason: Year-round in Arctic waters; spring blooms bring more to surface
photographyTips: Requires macro capability in cold water; gentle lighting reveals the translucent body and visible internal organs.

name: Cook's Turban Shell
shortDescription:
Cook's turban shell (Cookia sulcata) is a large marine gastropod in the family Turbinidae, endemic to New Zealand. The shell reaches 50-90 mm in diameter with a thick, heavy, conical-turbinate shape displaying prominent spiral ridges and a pearly iridescent interior visible around the aperture. The exterior is typically brownish to greenish with encrusting organisms.

The animal itself has a large, muscular foot with a thick, calcareous operculum for sealing the shell opening. This species inhabits rocky shore intertidal and subtidal zones at depths of 0-15 meters around New Zealand's coastline. Cook's turban shells are herbivorous, grazing on turfing and other small algae growing on rocky surfaces.

They are an ecologically important species in New Zealand's temperate reef ecosystems and are culturally significant to Maori as a traditional food source. Their large, attractive shells make them easy to spot on reef walks and dives.
divingRegions: New Zealand
bestSeason: Year-round; New Zealand summer (December-March) for best conditions
photographyTips: Use a macro lens to capture the pearly interior of the shell; photograph them on algae-covered rocks in their natural habitat.

name: Slimy Sculpin
shortDescription:
The slimy sculpin (Cottus cognatus) is a small, bottom-dwelling freshwater fish reaching up to 12 cm. It has a broad, flattened head, large fan-like pectoral fins, and a dark mottled brown body that provides excellent camouflage against rocky substrates. Found across northern North America from Alaska and Canada to the northern United States, it inhabits cold, clear streams, rivers, and lake bottoms at depths of 0 to 20 meters.

This species lacks a swim bladder and rests on the substrate, using its large pectoral fins to brace against currents. It feeds on aquatic insects, small crustaceans, and fish eggs. Males guard eggs in nests under rocks. Its cryptic appearance and sedentary nature make it a challenge to spot but a rewarding find for divers exploring cold, clear freshwater environments.

name: Rock Scallop
shortDescription:
The rock scallop (Crassadoma gigantea) is a large bivalve mollusk found along the Pacific coast of North America. Adults reach 15-25 cm in diameter and cement their lower valve permanently to rocky substrates, unlike their free-swimming relatives. When open, they reveal a vivid orange mantle edge lined with rows of tiny, iridescent blue-green eyes that detect shadows and movement, triggering the shell to snap shut when predators approach. The shell exterior becomes encrusted with coralline algae, sponges, and other organisms, providing camouflage.

They inhabit rocky reefs, kelp forests, and boulder surfaces at depths of 2-80 meters, filter-feeding on plankton and organic particles. Their sedentary lifestyle and camouflaged exterior make them easy to overlook, but once spotted, the brilliant orange and blue eye display is stunning. They can live for over 50 years, and large specimens become permanent features of their reef environment.
divingRegions: California & Baja
photographyTips: Use a macro lens to capture the row of blue eyes along the orange mantle edge; approach slowly to photograph before the shell snaps shut.

name: American Crocodile
shortDescription:
The American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus) is a large reptile reaching up to 6 meters, though most adults are 3 to 4 meters. Distinguished from alligators by its narrow, V-shaped snout and lighter olive-grey coloring, it is one of the most widespread crocodilian species in the New World. Found from southern Florida through the Caribbean and Central America to northern South America, and along the Pacific coast from Mexico to Peru, it inhabits coastal areas, mangrove swamps, river mouths, and brackish lagoons at depths of 0 to 5 meters.

Unlike most crocodilians, this species tolerates and regularly enters saltwater. It feeds on fish, turtles, crabs, birds, and occasionally larger prey. In recent years, underwater encounters with American crocodiles have become possible at specific managed sites such as Chinchorro Bank in Mexico and Gardens of the Queen in Cuba, where experienced guides facilitate safe close-up observation of these magnificent ancient predators in their natural habitat.
divingRegions: Caribbean
bestSeason: Year-round; November to March for best conditions at managed encounter sites
photographyTips: Use wide-angle for dramatic close-up compositions; over-under split shots are highly effective; always follow guide safety protocols.

name: Freshwater Crocodile

longDescription: Australia's smaller, more slender crocodile (compared to the massive saltwater croc). Primarily a freshwater species found in rivers, lakes, and billabongs, but enters tidal estuaries and occasionally coastal waters in the Northern Territory and Queensland.
divingRegions: Australasian Inland
bestSeason: April to October (dry season, clearer water)
photographyTips: Slender snout distinguishes from saltwater croc — include the head in profile for identification

name: Philippine Crocodile
shortDescription: One of the most critically endangered crocodilians in the world, with fewer than 100 adults left in the wild. Found in freshwater lakes and coastal marshes of the Philippines. A sighting would be extraordinary.
longDescription: One of the rarest crocodilians on earth, with fewer than 100 mature individuals surviving in the wild. Endemic to the Philippines and threatened by habitat loss and hunting. Conservation breeding programs are attempting to prevent its extinction.

photographyTips: Extremely rare — any sighting should be reported to the Philippine Crocodile Conservation Programme

longDescription: Famous among divers for the unique crocodile diving experiences at Banco Chinchorro, Mexico — one of the few places in the world where divers can safely observe large crocodilians in clear, shallow water with experienced operators.

name: Common Sunstar
shortDescription:
The common sunstar (Crossaster papposus) is a large, spectacular starfish with 8-16 arms (typically 10-12), reaching up to 34 cm across. It is found in the North Atlantic and North Pacific on rocky substrates from the low intertidal to about 300 m. Its upper surface displays a striking concentric ring pattern in red, orange, pink, and white, with each arm having bands of contrasting color.

It is a voracious predator of other starfish, sea cucumbers, and sea anemones, and is notably a predator of the common starfish. Its multi-armed, sun-like shape and vivid patterning make it one of the most photogenic invertebrates in temperate waters.
divingRegions: Arctic, Pacific Northwest, North Atlantic, Northern Japan, North Sea & Baltic
photographyTips: Macro for pattern detail; wide-angle with strobe to capture full disc; vivid colors show best with artificial light; rocky reef backgrounds provide good contrast.

name: Dusky Morwong
shortDescription:
The dusky morwong (Dactylophora nigricans) is a distinctive temperate reef fish reaching up to 70 cm. It has a deep body with bold dark brown to black vertical bars on a lighter background, thick lips, and characteristically elongated lower pectoral fin rays. Found in the temperate waters of southern Australia from Western Australia to New South Wales, it inhabits rocky reefs, kelp forests, and sponge gardens at depths of 5 to 40 meters.

This species feeds on small invertebrates and algae, using its thick lips to graze on reef surfaces. It is often seen in pairs or small groups cruising through kelp-draped rocky reefs. Its striking banding pattern and bold profile make it an attractive subject for underwater photographers exploring the rich temperate reefs of southern Australia.

name: Mediterranean Hermit Crab
shortDescription:
The Mediterranean hermit crab (Dardanus arrosor) is one of the largest hermit crab species in European waters. Adults reach 8-12 cm in body length (excluding shell) and display a reddish-orange body with hairy legs and prominent blue eyes. They carry appropriated gastropod shells on their backs for protection, upgrading to larger shells as they grow.

They are often seen with calliactis anemones attached to their shells in a mutualistic relationship: the anemone provides stinging-cell protection while benefiting from food scraps from the crab's meals. They inhabit rocky reefs, sandy bottoms, and mixed substrates at depths of 5-100 meters, scavenging on dead organic matter, small invertebrates, and algae. Their large size, vivid coloration, and shell-carrying behavior make them endearing and photogenic subjects. Watching them interact with their anemone partners or attempting to switch shells provides fascinating behavioral observations during Mediterranean dives.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean
photographyTips: Use a macro or mid-range lens; capturing the hermit crab emerging from its shell with anemone decorations creates engaging compositions showing the mutualistic relationship.

name: Reticulated Dascyllus
shortDescription:
The reticulated dascyllus (Dascyllus reticulatus) is a small damselfish reaching about 9 cm found across the Indo-Pacific. It has a grey to brownish body with dark scale margins creating a net-like (reticulated) pattern, and a prominent dark blotch at the base of the pectoral fin. It is closely associated with branching corals, particularly Pocillopora and Acropora, where small groups shelter among the branches.

It feeds on zooplankton above the coral, retreating into the branches when threatened. Like other damselfish, it is territorial and will defend its coral head aggressively. Juveniles may initially settle among anemone tentacles before moving to coral heads.

name: Marbled Stingray
shortDescription:
The marbled stingray (Dasyatis marmorata) is a medium-sized stingray found in the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Adults reach a disc width of 50-60 cm and display a distinctive marbled pattern of dark brown blotches and spots on a lighter brown background on the dorsal surface, making them one of the most attractively patterned stingrays in their range. The underside is white.

They possess a long, whip-like tail with a venomous spine. They inhabit sandy and muddy bottoms on the continental shelf at depths of 12-100 meters, often partially buried in sediment during the day. They feed on benthic invertebrates including worms, crustaceans, and mollusks excavated from the substrate.

Their beautiful marbled pattern distinguishes them from the more uniformly colored common stingray. Divers encounter them on sandy areas adjacent to rocky reefs in the Mediterranean and along the West African coast, where their camouflage makes them a satisfying find for observant divers.

photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens and approach slowly over sand; capture the marbled pattern from above to show the distinctive markings that distinguish this species.

name: Twinspot Lionfish
shortDescription:
The twinspot lionfish (Dendrochirus biocellatus), also known as the Fu Manchu lionfish, is a small venomous scorpionfish in the family Scorpaenidae. Adults reach only about 10 cm with an ornately colored body featuring reddish-brown to dark brown coloration with intricate banding, two distinctive ocelli (eyespots) on the soft dorsal fin, and two elongated barbels on the upper jaw resembling a mustache. The pectoral fins are large and fan-like.

This species inhabits coral reefs, rubble areas, and rocky crevices at depths of 1-40 meters across the Indo-Pacific from East Africa to Samoa. Twinspot lionfish are secretive and nocturnal, hiding in small crevices during the day and emerging at dusk to hunt small shrimp and crabs. Their elaborate camouflage and venomous dorsal spines provide defense. Despite their small size, they are among the most ornate and sought-after lionfish species for macro photographers.

name: Central American River Turtle
shortDescription:
The Central American river turtle (Dermatemys mawii), also called the hickatee, is a large freshwater turtle reaching 60 cm carapace length and 22 kg. It has a smooth, dark brown to olive carapace and a pale, yellowish plastron. Found from southern Mexico through Belize to northern Guatemala, it inhabits rivers, large lagoons, and flooded forests at depths of 0 to 10 meters. This almost entirely aquatic species rarely basins and is primarily herbivorous, feeding on fallen leaves, fruits, and aquatic plants.

It is the only living species in the family Dermatemydidae, representing an ancient lineage. Critically endangered due to overhunting for its meat, encountering one during a river or cenote dive is an exceptionally rare and significant wildlife experience that highlights the importance of freshwater habitat conservation.
divingRegions: South American Inland
bestSeason: Year-round; best encountered during rainy season when rivers are flowing
photographyTips: Use wide-angle with available light; their dark coloring requires careful exposure compensation against lighter water backgrounds.

name: Sea Pike
shortDescription:
The sea pike (Dinolestes lewini) is an elongated, predatory fish endemic to the temperate waters of southern Australia. Growing to about 60 cm in length, it has a slender, pike-like body with a pointed snout and a large mouth filled with small sharp teeth. The body is silvery with a greenish to brownish tint on the upper flanks. Sea pike typically form schools ranging from small groups to large aggregations of hundreds of individuals, often seen cruising along reef edges, through kelp forests, and over rocky reef systems.

They are active predators that feed on smaller fish, crustaceans, and squid. The schools can create spectacular scenes for divers as they move in coordinated formations, often splitting and reforming around kelp fronds and rocky outcrops. Sea pike are found from southern Western Australia around the southern coast to New South Wales, including Tasmania.

They inhabit a range of depths but are most commonly encountered at moderate reef depths. Their streamlined shape and schooling behavior make them visually dramatic subjects for wide-angle underwater photography.

bestSeason: Year-round; schools are most impressive in areas with good current flow
photographyTips: Use wide-angle lens to capture the full school effect; position yourself against a kelp forest or reef backdrop; shoot upward into the school for dramatic silhouettes against the surface

Endemic to southern Africa from Namibia to KwaZulu-Natal, it inhabits rocky reefs, kelp forests, and shallow coastal waters at depths of 0 to 40 meters. This omnivorous species feeds on algae, small invertebrates, and mussels.

It is one of the most commonly encountered fish by shore anglers and divers along the South African coast. Schools of blacktail are a regular sight on shallow rocky reef dives, where their silvery bodies and the distinctive tail markings create lively underwater scenes.

name: Brain Coral Colony
shortDescription:
Brain coral (Diploria labyrinthiformis), also known as grooved brain coral, is a massive reef-building coral that forms large, dome-shaped colonies reaching up to 2 meters in diameter. Its surface is covered with a complex pattern of meandering ridges and valleys that closely resemble the convolutions of a human brain, giving it its common name. The living tissue covers the entire colony surface, with individual polyps arranged along the valleys between ridges.

During the day, the polyps are retracted and the colony appears as a solid stone-like structure. At night, polyps extend their tentacles to feed on zooplankton drifting in the current. Brain corals are among the slowest-growing corals, adding only a few millimeters per year, meaning large colonies may be several hundred years old.

They are important reef framework builders in the Caribbean and western Atlantic, providing structural habitat for countless reef organisms. Their fluorescent pigments can create beautiful color displays under UV or blue light. Brain corals are relatively resilient compared to branching species but are still threatened by coral bleaching, ocean acidification, and disease.

bestSeason: Year-round; night dives reveal polyp feeding behavior
photographyTips: Use a macro lens for the intricate labyrinthine texture; UV or blue light photography reveals stunning fluorescence. Wide-angle captures massive old colonies in reef context.

name: Discodoris Atromaculata Nudibranch

imageCredit.artist: Anders Finn Jørgensen from Copenhagen, Denmark

shortDescription:
Discodoris atromaculata is a large dorid nudibranch found in the Mediterranean Sea and eastern Atlantic. Adults reach 6-12 cm and display a broad, oval body with a cream to pale yellow background covered in irregular brown to dark chocolate spots, resembling a leopard or cow pattern. The mantle surface has a distinctive velvety texture with tiny tubercles.

They inhabit rocky reefs and cave walls at depths of 5-50 meters, feeding primarily on the sponge Petrosia ficiformis, on which they are often found resting and are well camouflaged. They lay their eggs in distinctive flat, ribbon-like spirals on rock surfaces. Their large size compared to many other Mediterranean nudibranchs makes them relatively easy to spot, and their attractive spotted pattern makes them a popular macro photography subject. They are one of the most frequently encountered nudibranch species throughout the Mediterranean basin.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean
photographyTips: Use a macro lens; look on or near Petrosia ficiformis sponges where they feed, and include the sponge in the frame for ecological context.

name: Banded Sea Urchin
shortDescription:
The banded sea urchin (Echinothrix calamaris), also called the double-spined urchin, is a distinctive sea urchin found throughout the Indo-Pacific. Adults reach a test diameter of about 5-10 cm with two distinct types of spines: short, fine, venomous spines that are banded in yellow-brown to dark colors and can deliver a painful sting, and longer, thicker primary spines that are typically banded in light and dark colors or may be uniformly colored. They inhabit coral reef crevices, under ledges, and in rocky holes at depths of 1-70 meters, emerging at night to graze on algae and organic material.

Their dual-spine defense system provides both physical and chemical protection against predators. The venomous secondary spines can penetrate wetsuits and skin, causing intense pain. Despite the hazard, their dramatic appearance with the contrasting banded spines makes them interesting subjects for careful observation and photography on tropical reef dives.

bestSeason: Year-round, more visible on night dives
photographyTips: Use a macro lens and maintain safe distance from the venomous spines; look in reef crevices and under ledges where they shelter during the day.

name: Red Sea Whip
shortDescription:
The red sea whip (Ellisella ceratophyta) is a gorgonian soft coral that can grow up to 2 meters tall. It has a single, unbranched or minimally branched whip-like form with a deep red to orange coloration and small polyps extending from the central axis. Found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to the western Pacific, it inhabits reef walls, current-swept slopes, and drop-offs at depths of 10 to 40 meters.

This species anchors to hard substrate and extends into the current to filter-feed on plankton. Its slender form often hosts commensal organisms including whip coral shrimp and gobies that match the coral's color, making each whip a miniature ecosystem worth examining. Sea whips swaying in ocean currents create dramatic underwater scenes, especially when backlit against blue water, and the tiny commensal creatures they host are among the most sought-after macro subjects.
divingRegions: Coral Triangle, Micronesia, South Pacific Islands, Japan
bestSeason: Year-round; best seen on current-swept reef walls

name: Dragon Moray Eel
shortDescription:
The dragon moray eel (Enchelycore pardalis) is one of the most visually striking moray eels in the world, reaching about 90 cm in length. Its body is adorned with a vivid pattern of orange to reddish-brown spots and mottling on a lighter background, reminiscent of a dragon's skin. Its most distinctive features are the elongated, tubular nostrils that project forward like horns, and its dramatically curved, glass-like fangs that are visible even when the mouth is closed, giving it a fearsome dragon-like appearance. These curved teeth are adapted for catching slippery prey such as fish and octopus.

The dragon moray inhabits rocky and coral reefs in the Indo-Pacific, though it is most reliably encountered at certain Japanese dive sites (particularly Izu Peninsula), Hawaii, and scattered locations in the central Pacific. It is a shy, nocturnal species that hides deep in crevices during the day, making sightings relatively rare and highly prized. Its spectacular coloring and ferocious appearance make it one of the most sought-after subjects in underwater photography.

photographyTips: Macro lens essential for the incredible facial detail; patience is key as they peer from deep crevices. Focus on the horned nostrils and curved fangs for dramatic portraits.

name: Mayfly Larva
shortDescription:
The green drake mayfly larva (Ephemera danica) is a burrowing aquatic nymph reaching about 2.5 cm in length, found in rivers and streams across Europe. Its body is elongated and cylindrical with a pale yellowish-brown coloration, distinctive upward-pointing mandibular tusks used for digging, and feathery gills along the abdomen that wave rhythmically to maintain water flow for respiration. Mayfly nymphs are among the most sensitive freshwater invertebrates, requiring clean, well-oxygenated water, making them excellent bioindicators of water quality.

They spend one to two years burrowing in sandy and silty stream beds, feeding on fine organic particles and algae. When conditions are right, nymphs rise to the surface en masse for their final metamorphosis, emerging as short-lived winged adults that famously live only one to three days, during which they mate and die. These mass emergences can involve millions of individuals and attract feeding frenzies from fish and birds. Freshwater divers may observe nymphs burrowing in the substrate or swimming with a distinctive undulating motion using their tail filaments.
longDescription: 0-3 meters (freshwater rivers and streams)
divingRegions: European Inland
bestSeason: Year-round for nymphs; May-June for observing pre-emergence behavior and mass hatches
photographyTips: Macro lens with extension tubes for extreme close-ups of the gills and tusks; gentle handling in a photo tank may be needed for clear shots of such small subjects.

Epiactis thompsoni, known as the red-striped anemone, is a marine invertebrate in the family Actiniidae. It is found in the rocky intertidal zones of southern New Zealand and the Southeast Australian Shelf.

name: Sling-jaw Wrasse
shortDescription:
The sling-jaw wrasse (Epibulus insidiator) is a remarkable Indo-Pacific wrasse reaching about 35 cm, famous for having the most protrusible jaws of any fish. It can extend its mouth forward by up to 65% of its head length to snatch prey from crevices, a unique hydraulic jaw mechanism that operates in milliseconds. Found from the Red Sea to the central Pacific, it occurs in two main color morphs: bright yellow and dark brown.

It inhabits coral-rich reef areas from 1-42 m, feeding on small fish and crustaceans plucked from between coral branches. Divers who witness its feeding strike experience one of the most remarkable biomechanical displays in the fish world.
divingRegions: Polynesia, Coral Triangle, Hawaii, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, French Polynesia, South Pacific Islands, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Mid-range or macro lens; patience may reward you with a jaw extension strike; both color morphs photograph well; side profiles best show the jaw mechanism.

name: Rock Hind Grouper
shortDescription:
The rock hind grouper (Epinephelus adscensionis) is a medium-sized grouper reaching up to 61 cm. It has a tan to olive body densely covered with reddish-brown spots, with several larger dark blotches along the back and a distinctive saddle-like blotch on top of the caudal peduncle. Found in the western and eastern Atlantic from Massachusetts to Brazil and from Ascension Island to West Africa, it inhabits rocky reefs, coral heads, and ledges at depths of 2 to 120 meters. This territorial species often rests on rocky outcrops and ledges, relying on its spotted camouflage for protection.

It feeds on crabs, fish, and octopus. Its accessible depth range and tendency to hold position on reef structures make it a commonly encountered and easily photographed grouper species on Caribbean and Atlantic dives.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, South Atlantic Islands, Caribbean, Brazil Coast, US East Coast
bestSeason: Year-round; commonly encountered on Caribbean reef dives
photographyTips: Use macro for spot detail or wide-angle showing the fish on its rocky perch; they are generally approachable if you move slowly.

name: Hong Kong Grouper
shortDescription:
The Hong Kong grouper (Epinephelus akaara) is a small to medium-sized grouper reaching up to 50 cm. It has a reddish-brown body densely covered with small orange-red spots, giving it an exceptionally attractive appearance. Found in the western Pacific from Japan to Vietnam and the South China Sea, including Hong Kong waters, it inhabits rocky and coral reefs at depths of 5 to 50 meters.

This species is one of the most highly valued reef fish in Chinese cuisine, making it extremely vulnerable to overfishing. It is now classified as endangered by the IUCN. Conservation efforts including marine protected areas are crucial for its survival. Encountering one on a dive in Hong Kong or Japanese waters is increasingly rare, making each sighting a significant wildlife observation.
divingRegions: Southern Japan, Japan
bestSeason: Year-round; best in marine protected areas
photographyTips: Use macro for spot detail; approach carefully as they are increasingly wary due to fishing pressure.

name: Longtooth Grouper
shortDescription:
The longtooth grouper (Epinephelus bruneus), known as kue in Japanese, is a large grouper reaching up to 128 cm and 33 kg. It has a brownish body with faint darker markings and characteristically elongated canine-like teeth. Found in the western Pacific from Japan and Korea to Vietnam and the South China Sea, it inhabits rocky reefs, reef edges, and deep rocky habitats at depths of 10 to 200 meters. This apex predator feeds on fish, crustaceans, and cephalopods.

It is one of the most highly prized fish in Japanese cuisine, with specimens fetching extremely high prices. This species is slow-growing and long-lived, making it vulnerable to overfishing. Encountering a large longtooth grouper on Japanese reef dives is increasingly rare and correspondingly special.

bestSeason: Year-round; best encountered during warmer months
photographyTips: Use wide-angle with strobe to capture the full body profile; their large size and slow movements allow careful composition.

name: Easter Island Grouper
shortDescription:
The Easter Island grouper (Epinephelus cifuentesi) is a large serranid fish reaching up to 90 cm in length, endemic to the remote waters of Easter Island (Rapa Nui) and nearby Sala y Gomez in the southeastern Pacific. It has a robust, typical grouper body shape with a dark brownish to olive coloration marked with faint darker spots and blotches. The species inhabits rocky reefs and caves around these volcanic islands, typically at depths between 10 and 60 meters.

Like other groupers, it is a protogynous hermaphrodite, starting life as female and potentially transitioning to male at larger sizes. It feeds on fish, crustaceans, and cephalopods, using its large mouth to create a suction force that inhales prey whole. Due to the extreme isolation of its habitat, this species is encountered by relatively few divers, making it a prized sighting for those who travel to Easter Island. The remote location has provided some natural protection from commercial fishing pressure, though the species remains vulnerable due to its limited range and slow reproductive rate.
divingRegions: Eastern Tropical Pacific
bestSeason: Year-round; austral summer (December-March) offers warmest water temperatures
photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens for environmental portraits in the dramatic volcanic reef scenery; approach patiently as they may retreat to caves.

name: Goldblotch Grouper
shortDescription:
The goldblotch grouper (Epinephelus costae) is a medium to large grouper found in the Mediterranean Sea and eastern Atlantic. Adults reach 60-80 cm and display a grey-brown body with a distinctive golden-yellow blotch on the upper flanks near the dorsal fin, along with faint darker vertical bars that may appear and fade. They inhabit rocky reefs, caves, and wrecks at depths of 10-200 meters, most commonly between 20-100 meters. As ambush predators, they feed on fish, cephalopods, and crustaceans, lying in wait near reef structure before striking.

They are protogynous hermaphrodites, starting life as females and transitioning to males. Like other grouper species, they tend to be territorial and often occupy the same shelter for extended periods. Their curious nature and the golden blotch marking make them readily identifiable. They are less commonly encountered than the dusky grouper in the Mediterranean, making each sighting noteworthy.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean
photographyTips: Use a mid-range lens on deeper reef dives; strobes are essential at depth to reveal the distinctive golden blotch marking.

name: Rock Cod
shortDescription:
The rock cod (Epinephelus erythrurus), also known as the cloudy grouper, is a medium-sized grouper reaching about 50 cm in length. It has a robust, typical grouper body shape with a large head and mouth, and coloration that varies from pale brown to reddish-brown with irregular dark brown blotches and spots across the body. The fins are often edged with red, and the tail margin is rounded or slightly convex.

This species inhabits rocky reefs, coral outcrops, and estuarine environments throughout the Indo-West Pacific, from East Africa to the western Pacific. It is found from shallow coastal waters to about 50 meters depth, preferring areas with ample structure for shelter and ambush hunting. Like other groupers, it is a protogynous hermaphrodite, beginning life as female.

It feeds on crabs, shrimp, and small fish, using its cavernous mouth to create a powerful suction that inhales prey whole. Rock cod are territorial and typically found alone near their home crevice or overhang. They are approachable by patient divers and will often peer out from their shelter with apparent interest.

bestSeason: Year-round; most active during dawn and dusk feeding periods
photographyTips: Standard or macro lens; approach slowly and settle near their shelter. They often peer out from holes, creating natural framing opportunities for portraits.

name: Blacksaddle Grouper
shortDescription:
The blacksaddle grouper (Epinephelus howlandi) is a medium-sized grouper reaching up to 45 cm. It has a pale body marked with several large, dark saddle-shaped blotches and small dark spots. Found in the western and central Pacific from the Great Barrier Reef to the Marshall Islands and from Japan to New Caledonia, this species inhabits outer reef slopes and channels at depths of 10 to 60 meters.

It is a solitary predator feeding on small fish and crustaceans. Like other groupers, it is a protogynous hermaphrodite, beginning life as female and potentially changing sex to male. Its attractive patterning and tendency to hold still near coral outcrops makes it a cooperative subject for patient underwater photographers.

divingRegions: Eastern Australia, New Zealand, Western Australia, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia
photographyTips: Use wide-angle lenses for full body shots, focus on distinctive callosities pattern, capture breaching behavior with fast shutter speed, maintain legal distance requirements

name: North Atlantic Right Whale
shortDescription: The most endangered large whale — fewer than 350 remain. Named 'right whale' because it was the 'right' whale to hunt (slow, floats when dead). Now critically threatened by ship strikes and fishing gear.
longDescription: The most endangered large whale — fewer than 350 remain. Named 'right whale' because it was the 'right' whale to hunt (slow, floats when dead). Now critically threatened by ship strikes and fishing gear.
divingRegions: North Atlantic, US East Coast
photographyTips: Wide angle — respect distance and regulations

name_i18n.ja: タイセイヨウセミクジラ

name: North Pacific Right Whale
shortDescription: One of the rarest large whales — fewer than 500 remain. Virtually identical to the North Atlantic right whale but genetically distinct.
longDescription: One of the rarest large whales — fewer than 500 remain. Virtually identical to the North Atlantic right whale but genetically distinct.
divingRegions: Arctic, Pacific Northwest, Northern Japan, Japan
photographyTips: Wide angle — respect distance

name: Black Reef Leatherjacket
shortDescription: Eubalichthys bucephalus, commonly referred to as the black reef leatherjacket, is a species of fish in the family Monacanthidae. Its range includes the East Central, Southeast, Southwest, and West Central Australian Shelves.

name: Gunn's Leatherjacket
shortDescription: Eubalichthys gunnii, known as Gunn's leatherjacket, is a species of fish in the family Monacanthidae. It is found in the Southeast and Southwest Australian Shelves.

name: Black Reef Leatherjacket
shortDescription: Large leatherjacket with mosaic-like markings, endemic to southern Australia. Often hovering near kelp fronds.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Western Australia, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia
bestSeason: Year-round, with better visibility typically in summer months
photographyTips: Approach slowly as they can be skittish; use macro lens for detail shots of their textured skin; best photographed against contrasting backgrounds to highlight their dark coloration

name: Rocky Aeolid
shortDescription: Eubranchulus rupium, the green balloon aeolid, is a species of sea slug or nudibranch, a marine gastropod mollusc in the family Eubranchidae.

name: Minute Aeolis
shortDescription: Eubranchus exiguus, commonly referred to as the Minute Aeolis, is a small sea slug, an aeolid nudibranch in the family Eubranchidae, found in the Northern European Seas and the Cold Temperate Northwest Atlantic.
Eubranchus farrani is a species of sea slug or nudibranch in the family Eubranchidae, recorded from the Northern European Seas.

name: Three-coloured Aeolis
shortDescription: Eubranchus tricolor, commonly known as the Three-coloured Aeolis, is a species of sea slug belonging to the family Eubranchidae. This nudibranch is found in the Northern European Seas.

name: Galapagos Slate Pencil Urchin
shortDescription: Eucidaris galapagensis, known as the Galapagos slate pencil urchin, is a species in the family Cidaridae found in the Galapagos. It typically inhabits rocky, benthic environments and is primarily herbivorous, grazing on corals and algae.

name: Slate Pencil Urchin
shortDescription: Eucidaris thouarsii, known as the slate pencil urchin, is a species of cidaroid sea urchins found in the Tropical East Pacific, Warm Temperate Northeast Pacific, and Galapagos regions.

name: Pencil Sea Urchin
shortDescription: A chunky sea urchin with thick, blunt spines that often collects debris for camouflage. Common on Caribbean reefs, it hides in crevices during the day.
divingRegions: Brazil Coast, Caribbean, US East Coast, Argentina/Uruguay
photographyTips: Use macro lens to capture spine detail and texture. Approach slowly as they may retreat into crevices. Side lighting enhances spine structure and coloration.

name: Tasselled Wobbegong
shortDescription: The most elaborately camouflaged shark — fringed with branching tassels around the head. A must-see species in Raja Ampat and Papua New Guinea.
longDescription: The most elaborately camouflaged shark — fringed with branching tassels around the head. A must-see species in Raja Ampat and Papua New Guinea.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Coral Triangle, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, Southern Australia
photographyTips: The tassels are the shot — shoot from eye level to capture the full fringe in profile

name: Australian Droplet Tunicate
shortDescription: Eudistoma elongatum, commonly called the Australian droplet tunicate, is a species within the family Polyctoridae. Specific details regarding its range and characteristics are not available in current sources.

name: Giant Feather Duster Worm
shortDescription: Eudistylia polymorpha, commonly called the Giant Feather Duster Worm, is a marine polychaete worm in the family Sabellidae. It is characterized by a crown of tentacles that extends when submerged in water.

name: Northern Feather Duster Worm
shortDescription: Eudistylia vancouveri, referred to as the Northern Feather Duster Worm, is a species of marine polychaete worm in the family Sabellidae. It is found in the Cold Temperate Northeast Pacific region.

name: Fiordland penguin
shortDescription: Rare, crested penguin endemic to New Zealand's Fiordland coast. Breeds in dense rainforest near the sea.
longDescription: Shallow waters to 30 meters (penguins dive deeper but diver encounters typically in shallower water)
divingRegions: New Zealand
bestSeason: October to February during breeding season when most active in coastal waters
photographyTips: Move slowly and avoid sudden movements; use natural light when possible; focus on capturing their underwater swimming behavior; maintain respectful distance to avoid disturbing these vulnerable birds

name: Little Blue Penguin

imageCredit.creator: James St. John
imageCredit.disclaimerNotice: This image is provided as-is. The original creator and Flickr bear no liability for its use.
imageCredit.photoTitle: Eudyptula minor (little penguins) (Penneshaw, Kangaroo Island, South Australia)

shortDescription: The world's smallest penguin, found along southern Australian and New Zealand coasts. Divers may encounter them porpoising through the water or waddling ashore at dusk.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Southern Australia
bestSeason: Year-round, with increased activity during breeding season (September-February in Australia, July-December in New Zealand)
photographyTips: Best photographed from surface or shallow depths when feeding, use fast shutter speeds to capture swimming motion, early morning or late afternoon provide best lighting near shore, maintain respectful distance to avoid disturbing feeding behavior

name: Purple Sea Fan
shortDescription: Fan-shaped gorgonian in deep purple to red coloration found on Eastern Pacific rocky reefs. A characteristic species of the Sea of Cortez underwater landscape.
divingRegions: California & Baja

name: Emerald Green Paddle Worm
shortDescription: Eulalia clavigera, commonly called the Emerald Green Paddle Worm, is a polychaete worm in the family Phyllodocidae. It is native to the Northern European Seas, Lusitanian region, and the Mediterranean Sea, and has been confused with Eulalia viridis in the past.

name: New Zealand Paddle Worm
shortDescription: Eulalia microphylla, known as the New Zealand Paddle Worm, is a polychaete worm from the family Phyllodocidae. It is found in southern and northern New Zealand as well as the Southeast Australian Shelf.

name: Steller's sea lion

imageCredit.creator: Arthur T. LaBar
imageCredit.disclaimerNotice: This image is provided as-is. The original creator and Flickr bear no liability for its use.

shortDescription: The largest sea lion species, found in the cold North Pacific. Divers in Alaska and British Columbia may encounter these massive, powerful animals near rocky haul-outs.
divingRegions: Pacific Northwest, Southern Japan, Eastern Tropical Pacific, Micronesia, California & Baja, Japan
bestSeason: Year-round, but best encounters during pupping season (May-August) when more active near colonies
photographyTips: Use wide-angle lenses to capture their size and acrobatic behavior. Maintain respectful distance and let them approach you. Fast shutter speeds needed for action shots. Early morning or late afternoon light provides best contrast against their dark coats.

name: Cauliflower Soft Coral
shortDescription: Eunephthya thyrsoidea, or cauliflower soft coral, is a colonial soft coral in the family Nephtheidae.

name: Bobbit Worm

imageCredit.creator: Kris-Mikael Krister
imageCredit.disclaimerNotice: This image is provided as-is. The original creator and Flickr bear no liability for its use.

shortDescription: Terrifying giant polychaete worm that ambushes prey from the sand with lightning-fast jaws. Can reach several meters in length.
longDescription: The Bobbit worm (Eunice aphroditois) is a large predatory marine polychaete. Lives mainly in the Atlantic Ocean (with the type locality in the Mediterranean), and is also found in the Indo-Pacific. Burrows up to 3 m into sand and rubble bottoms with just its head and antennae exposed; ambushes passing fish with lightning strikes from its scissor-like jaws. Diver-favourite subject in muck-diving destinations like Lembeh, Anilao, and Bali, where individuals up to 3 m have been observed.
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, Bay of Bengal, Eastern Australia, Mediterranean, Great Barrier Reef, Red Sea, Northern Australia, Caribbean, South Pacific Islands, US East Coast, Japan, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round in tropical waters, best visibility during calmer seasons
photographyTips: Use macro lens with powerful strobes, photograph during night dives when more active, focus on the distinctive jaws and iridescent body segments, exercise extreme caution as jaws can cause serious injury

name: Swollen Knob Candelabrum
shortDescription: Candelabra-shaped gorgonian with thick branches bearing prominent swollen bumps where polyps emerge. One of the most recognizable gorgonians on Caribbean reef slopes.
divingRegions: Caribbean

name: Tournefort's Sea Rod
shortDescription: Bushy gorgonian with multiple ascending branches and prominent shelf-like calices. Named after the French botanist, it is common on shallow Caribbean reefs.
divingRegions: Caribbean

name: Yellow Gorgonian
shortDescription: A delicate yellow-orange sea fan common in the Mediterranean, forming elegant branching colonies on shaded walls and overhangs. Beautiful when backlit.
divingRegions: Mediterranean
bestSeason: Year-round, but spring and early summer offer best visibility and polyp extension activity
photographyTips: Use backlighting to highlight the translucent structure, shoot from below looking up for dramatic silhouettes, use macro lens to capture polyp detail, and look for associated fauna like gobies or nudibranchs

name: Nippled Sea Fan
shortDescription: Eunicella microthela, or the nippled sea fan, is a species of gorgonian sea fan in the family Eunicellidae, found in the Agulhas and Benguela regions.

name: White Gorgonian
shortDescription: A white Mediterranean gorgonian that hosts photosynthetic symbionts — unusual for a temperate gorgonian.
longDescription: A white Mediterranean gorgonian that hosts photosynthetic symbionts — unusual for a temperate gorgonian.
divingRegions: Mediterranean
photographyTips: Macro for polyp detail; wide for colony context

name: Sinuous Sea Fan
shortDescription: Eunicella tricoronata, known as the sinuous sea fan, is a gorgonian sea fan in the family Eunicellidae.

name: White Gorgonian
shortDescription: An elegant white or pink sea fan that forms branching colonies on temperate Atlantic and Mediterranean reefs. Creates beautiful underwater scenery when backlit.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean, North Sea & Baltic
bestSeason: Year-round, though spring and summer offer better visibility and calmer conditions
photographyTips: Use backlighting to highlight the delicate branching structure, shoot with blue water background for contrast, macro lens for polyp detail when extended, wide angle for colony formations and reef scenes

name: Stiff-footed Sea Cucumber
shortDescription: Eupentacta quinquesemita, or the stiff-footed sea cucumber, is a species characterized by its elongated body and leathery skin, occurring along rocky coasts in the cold and warm temperate regions of the Northeast and Northwest Pacific.

name: Pacific Krill
shortDescription: Euphausia pacifica, known as Pacific Krill, is a euphausiid found in the northern Pacific Ocean, ranging from the Cold and Warm Temperate Northwest and Northeast Pacific. This species is a significant food source for various fish and is subject to regulated fishing in Japanese waters.
longDescription: The dominant krill species in the North Pacific.
divingRegions: Worldwide
photographyTips: Macro essential — most crustaceans are under 10cm

name: Antarctic Krill

imageCredit.artist: Krill666.jpg: Uwe Kils I am willing to give the image in 1700 resolution to Wikipedia Uwe Kils

shortDescription: Euphausia superba, commonly known as Antarctic krill, is a species of krill found in the Southern Ocean. This small, swimming crustacean can grow up to 6 centimeters in length and is known to live in large swarms. It is one of the most abundant animal species globally, with significant biomass, but is currently suffering from overfishing.
divingRegions: Antarctic

shortDescription: Euphrosine aurantiaca is a species of bristle worm classified in the family Euphrosinidae.

name: Hammer Coral
shortDescription: A large-polyped coral with hammer or anchor-shaped tentacle tips. Extends spectacular tentacles day and night.
longDescription: A large-polyped coral with hammer or anchor-shaped tentacle tips. Extends spectacular tentacles day and night.
divingRegions: Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, Southern Japan, Sunda Shelf, Micronesia, Japan, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Macro for detail; wide for context

name_i18n.zh-Hant: 錨形紋葉珊瑚（腎形紋葉珊瑚）

name: Torch Coral
shortDescription: A coral with long, flowing tentacles tipped with glowing green or white — resembling torches. Spectacular at night under UV light.
longDescription: A coral with long, flowing tentacles tipped with glowing green or white — resembling torches. Spectacular at night under UV light.
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, Maldives & Chagos, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, Southern Japan, Sunda Shelf, South Pacific Islands, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Macro for detail; wide for context

name: Green Tree Coral
shortDescription: A branching coral with grape-like bubble tips on its tentacles, found on Indo-Pacific reefs. Expands beautifully at night and hosts various commensal shrimp.
divingRegions: Arabian Sea, Western Indian Ocean

name_i18n.ja: ツツコエダナガレハナサンゴ

name: Venus' Flower Basket
shortDescription: A spectacular deep-water glass sponge with an intricate silica lattice skeleton. Pairs of shrimp become trapped inside — living their entire lives within the sponge.
longDescription: Venus' Flower Basket is one of the ocean's most extraordinary organisms. Its skeleton is a masterpiece of biological engineering — an intricate lattice of silica (glass) fibers arranged in a pattern that fiber-optic engineers study for inspiration. A pair of shrimp enter the sponge as larvae, feed on particles the sponge captures, grow too large to leave, and live their entire lives imprisoned together. In Japan, dried specimens are given as wedding gifts symbolizing lifelong partnership.
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, New Zealand, Western Australia, Sunda Shelf, Coral Triangle
photographyTips: Macro for polyp detail; wide for colony context

name: Spaghetti Worm
shortDescription: A tube worm that extends dozens of long, spaghetti-like feeding tentacles across the reef surface.
longDescription: A tube worm that extends dozens of long, spaghetti-like feeding tentacles across the reef surface.
divingRegions: Caribbean, Eastern Atlantic, Eastern Australia, Mediterranean, Southern Australia, North Sea & Baltic, North Atlantic, Black Sea
photographyTips: Macro for small subjects; wide angle for larger ones

name: Berry's Bobtail Squid
shortDescription: A tiny, round bobtail squid found on sandy bottoms near Indo-Pacific reefs. Buries in sand during the day.
longDescription: A tiny, round bobtail squid found on sandy bottoms near Indo-Pacific reefs. Buries in sand during the day.
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, South China Sea, Japan, India & Sri Lanka
photographyTips: Macro essential

name: Hawaiian Bobtail Squid
shortDescription: Tiny bobtail squid famous for its symbiosis with bioluminescent bacteria in a light organ. A nocturnal sand dweller that buries itself by day and emerges at night.
divingRegions: Hawaii

name: Southern Dumpling Squid

imageCredit.photoTitle: Euprymna tasmanica, covered in a coat of sand

shortDescription: A tiny round bobtail squid that buries itself in sand during the day and emerges at night. Its adorable appearance makes it a night dive highlight in southern Australia.
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, Bay of Bengal, Maldives & Chagos, India & Sri Lanka, Western Indian Ocean

name: Flag-Bearing Comb Jelly
shortDescription: Deep-water lobate ctenophore with distinctive trailing filaments resembling flags. Produces ink-like bioluminescent secretion as a defense mechanism.
divingRegions: Caribbean

name: Longtail Catfish
shortDescription: Euristhmus lepturus is a species of catfish in the family Plotosidae, recorded from the East Central Australian Shelf, Sahul Shelf, and Northeast Australian Shelf.

name: Pretty Isopod
shortDescription: Eurydice pulchra is a species of isopod crustacean in the family Cirolanidae, recorded from the Mediterranean Sea. It is characterized by large eyes, long antennae, and a grey to brown coloration with black spots.
longDescription: A swimming isopod that burrows in sand between tide cycles.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, North Sea & Baltic, North Atlantic
photographyTips: Macro essential — most crustaceans are under 10cm

name: Striped Polyclad Worm
shortDescription: Eurylepta californica is a species of polyclad worm within the family Euryleptidae.

name: Triangle Crab
shortDescription: Eurynolambrus australis, commonly referred to as the triangle crab, is a small crab species belonging to the family Majidae. It is found throughout Southern and Northern New Zealand, and is the sole representative of its genus.

name: Dragon Sea Moth

imageCredit.creator: Rickard Zerpe
imageCredit.disclaimerNotice: This image is provided as-is. The original creator and Flickr bear no liability for its use.

shortDescription: A tiny, bizarre armored fish that walks on modified pelvic fins along sandy bottoms. Its dragonfly-like wing-shaped pectoral fins make it one of the most unusual muck dive finds.
divingRegions: South Africa, Andaman Sea, Maldives & Chagos, Eastern Australia, Lord Howe & Norfolk, Marquesas, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, Southern Japan, Micronesia, South Pacific Islands, Japan, India & Sri Lanka, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round, but more active during warmer months
photographyTips: Use macro lens with gentle lighting, approach slowly as they're easily startled, focus on the distinctive wing-like fins, shoot from low angle to capture their unique profile, and be patient as they often remain motionless for extended periods

name: Orange Fire Worm
shortDescription: Eurythoe complanata, commonly referred to as the Orange Fire Worm, is a polychaete from the family Amphinomidae. It is distributed across the Northeast Australian Shelf, Tropical Northwestern Atlantic, Warm Temperate Northeast Pacific, Tropical Southwestern Atlantic, and the Western Coral Triangle.

name: Moon-headed Sidegill Slug
shortDescription: Euselenops luniceps is a type of sea slug in the family Pleurobranchaeidae. This species is located in the Northeast Australian Shelf, East Central Australian Shelf, South China Sea, Sahul Shelf, and Northwest Australian Shelf.

name: Smooth Flower Coral
shortDescription: Eusmilia fastigiata, or smooth flower coral, is a stony coral species in the family Meandrinidae. It is found on reefs in the Tropical Northwestern Atlantic, particularly in the Caribbean Sea.

name: Winghead Shark
shortDescription: The most extreme hammerhead — head width is nearly half its body length. Found in shallow Indo-Pacific waters.
longDescription: The most extreme hammerhead — head width is nearly half its body length. Found in shallow Indo-Pacific waters.
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, Bay of Bengal, Great Barrier Reef, Northern Australia, Sunda Shelf, India & Sri Lanka
photographyTips: The enormous head width is the shot — shoot from the front to capture the full wing-like span

name: Kawakawa
shortDescription: A small, fast tuna found in Indo-Pacific coastal waters. Divers sometimes see schools streaking past at high speed, especially near reef edges and drop-offs.
divingRegions: South Africa, Maldives & Chagos, Polynesia, Eastern Australia, Great Barrier Reef, Northern Australia, Southern Australia, Eastern Tropical Pacific, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round in tropical waters, peak abundance varies by region during migration periods
photographyTips: Use fast shutter speeds to freeze motion, wide-angle lens for schools, anticipate movement patterns, and position near cleaning stations or feeding areas for better opportunities

name: Little Tunny
shortDescription: Euthynnus alletteratus, or little tunny, is a species of tuna found in the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea, recognized for its 'worm-like' back markings and dark spots between its fins. It is a highly migratory pelagic fish.

name: Grey Gurnard

imageCredit.artist: (c) Libby Keatley, some rights reserved (CC BY)
imageCredit.photoTitle: Grey Gurnard, Ards, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom imported from iNaturalist photo 436873353

shortDescription: A bottom-dwelling fish with fan-like pectoral fins and three finger-like rays used for walking on the seabed. Found on sandy and muddy European bottoms.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic

name: Mottled Star
shortDescription: A large, long-armed Pacific sea star with mottled orange-and-brown coloring. Common in kelp forests.
longDescription: A large, long-armed Pacific sea star with mottled orange-and-brown coloring. Common in kelp forests.
divingRegions: Pacific Northwest, California & Baja
photographyTips: Get low and shoot from eye level

name: Kina
shortDescription: New Zealand's most common sea urchin with a green-brown test and long spines. Dense populations create urchin barrens on NZ reefs, and it is culturally significant to Maori as kina.
longDescription: Intertidal to 50 meters
divingRegions: New Zealand
bestSeason: Year-round, most active in warmer months
photographyTips: Use macro lens to capture spine detail and texture. Natural lighting works well in shallow water. Be careful not to touch or damage the specimen.

name: Blackbelly Dwarf Goby
shortDescription: A tiny, semi-translucent goby found on Indo-Pacific coral reefs. One of many diminutive Eviota species that are easy to overlook among coral rubble.
divingRegions: Coral Triangle, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef
photographyTips: Super-macro essential; patience required to find and focus on this nearly invisible species.

name: Twobar Pygmy Goby
shortDescription: Eviota bifasciata, known as the Twobar Pygmy Goby, is a member of the Gobiidae family found in the Eastern Coral Triangle, Northeast Australian Shelf, South Kuroshio, Sunda Shelf, and the Tropical Northwestern Pacific.
longDescription: One of the world's smallest vertebrates — just 2cm. Found on rubble slopes.
divingRegions: Coral Triangle, Great Barrier Reef, Southern Japan, Sunda Shelf, Micronesia
photographyTips: Macro essential

name: Lachdebre's Goby
shortDescription: Eviota lachdeberei is a species of goby in the Gobiidae family, recorded from the Eastern Coral Triangle, Northeast Australian Shelf, Northwest Australian Shelf, South Kuroshio, and Sunda Shelf.
longDescription: A recently described pygmy goby from the Coral Triangle.
divingRegions: Coral Triangle, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Southern Japan, Sunda Shelf, Micronesia
photographyTips: Approach carefully

name: Headspot Goby
shortDescription: Headspot Goby (Eviota melasma) is a small marine fish from the family Gobiidae, recorded in the Eastern Coral Triangle and surrounding regions.
longDescription: A tiny pygmy goby with a distinctive dark head spot
divingRegions: Coral Triangle, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Southern Japan, Sunda Shelf, South Pacific Islands
photographyTips: Approach carefully

name: Pellucida Pygmy Goby

imageCredit.artist: Michiels, Nico K., Nils Anthes, Nathan S. Hart, Jürgen Herler, Alfred J. Meixner, Frank Schleifenbaum, Gregor Schulte, Ulrike E. Siebeck, Dennis Sprenger, and Matthias F. Wucherer (2008)

shortDescription: A minuscule, nearly transparent goby found perching on coral branches in the Indo-Pacific. Among the smallest vertebrates — a true macro challenge.
longDescription: 3-20 meters on coral rubble and dead coral
divingRegions: Coral Triangle, Great Barrier Reef, Southern Japan, Sunda Shelf, Micronesia, South Pacific Islands
photographyTips: Super-macro with diopter essential; the transparent body benefits from backlighting to reveal internal structures.

name: Prasites Goby
shortDescription: Eviota prasites is a species of goby in the family Gobiidae, found in Central Polynesia, Eastern Coral Triangle, Marshall, Gilbert and Ellis Islands, and Northeast and Northwest Australian Shelves. This species is known to inhabit depths ranging from 1 to 40 meters.
longDescription: A vivid red-and-white pygmy goby found on rubble
divingRegions: Polynesia, Coral Triangle, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, South China Sea, Southern Japan, South Pacific Islands
photographyTips: Approach carefully

name: Queensland Pygmy Goby
shortDescription: Eviota queenslandica is a goby belonging to the family Gobiidae, found in the Andaman, Eastern Coral Triangle, Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands, Northeast Australian Shelf, and Northwest Australian Shelf.
longDescription: A tiny Australian pygmy goby found on reef rubble.
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, Coral Triangle, Lord Howe & Norfolk, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, Southern Japan, Sunda Shelf, Micronesia, South Pacific Islands
photographyTips: Approach carefully

name: Sebree's Pygmy Goby
shortDescription: Eviota sebreei, known as Sebree's pygmy goby or the striped dwarfgoby, is a species of goby in the family Gobiidae. It inhabits the tropical Northwestern Pacific, the Western Indian Ocean, and waters around Northeast Australia and the Andaman Islands.

name: Adorned Dwarf Goby
shortDescription: One of the shortest-lived vertebrates, surviving only about 59 days. A tiny coral reef goby found in the western Pacific — remarkable for its extreme life history.
longDescription: 3-15 meters among coral colonies
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, Maldives & Chagos, Polynesia, Coral Triangle, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, Micronesia, South Pacific Islands, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Extreme challenge; requires patience, keen eyes, and super-macro equipment to document this record-holding species.

name: Terry's Pygmygoby
shortDescription: Eviota teresae is a goby recorded from the Tropical Southwestern Pacific and Central Polynesia.

name: Zebra Goby
shortDescription: Eviota zebrina, known as the zebra goby, is a goby species found in the Andaman, Central Indian Ocean Islands, Northeast Australian Shelf, Northwest Australian Shelf, and Sahul Shelf. It typically inhabits depths of 1 to 40 meters and is characterized by its striped appearance.
longDescription: A tiny striped pygmy goby found in caves
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, Maldives & Chagos, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, Sunda Shelf, South Pacific Islands, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Approach carefully

name: Pale Anemone
shortDescription: Exaiptasia diaphana, commonly referred to as the pale anemone, is a species belonging to the family Aiptasiidae. It inhabits various regions including the Tropical Northwestern Atlantic and Warm Temperate Northwest Pacific.

name: Leopard Blenny
shortDescription: A unique blenny that feeds exclusively on coral polyps — one of the few blennies with this diet. Spotted pattern resembles a miniature leopard.
longDescription: A unique blenny that feeds exclusively on coral polyps — one of the few blennies with this diet. Spotted pattern resembles a miniature leopard.

name: Tropical Two-Wing Flyingfish
shortDescription: Classic two-winged flyingfish seen skimming the surface during boat rides to dive sites. Occasionally observed underwater in blue water.
divingRegions: Polynesia, North Atlantic, Eastern Australia, Galápagos, Hawaii, Mediterranean, Great Barrier Reef, South China Sea, Southern Japan, Eastern Tropical Pacific, Caribbean, Brazil Coast, South Pacific Islands, US East Coast, West Africa, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean

name: Exyrias Akihito Goby
shortDescription: A small sand-dwelling goby named in honor of Emperor Akihito of Japan, a noted ichthyologist. Found on sandy patches near reefs in the western Pacific.
longDescription: Exyrias akihito (Akihito's prawn-goby) is an Indo-West Pacific goby found in coastal sand and rubble habitats from the Indian Ocean east through the Coral Triangle to the western Pacific. Like other prawn-gobies it often shares a burrow with an alpheid shrimp.

name: Auriculate Facelina
shortDescription: Purple-tipped cerata on a translucent body with orange highlights. A beautiful Mediterranean aeolid frequently spotted on shallow rocky reefs.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic

name: Boston Facelina
shortDescription: Facelina bostoniensis, known as the Boston Facelina, is a species of aeolid nudibranch that inhabits the Northern European Seas and the Cold Temperate Northwest Atlantic.
Facelina rubrovittata is a species of sea slug, classified as an aeolid nudibranch in the family Facelinidae.

name: Honeycomb Coral

imageCredit.photoTitle: Helcogramma striata (Neon triplefin) on Diploastrea heliopora (Hard coral)

shortDescription: A common reef coral with round closely packed corallites giving a honeycomb pattern. A hardy species found across varied reef habitats.
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, Maldives & Chagos, Polynesia, Eastern Australia, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Red Sea, Northern Australia, Southern Japan, Sunda Shelf, Micronesia, Japan, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean

name: Rusty Crayfish
shortDescription:
The rusty crayfish (Faxonius rusticus, formerly Orconectes rusticus) is a large freshwater crayfish native to the Ohio River basin in North America. Adults reach 10-13 cm in body length and display a brown to greenish-brown body with distinctive rusty-red patches on each side of the carapace, which give the species its common name. The claws are greyish-green with dark black bands at the tips.

They inhabit lakes, rivers, and streams with rocky or gravelly bottoms at depths of 0-10 meters, preferring areas with cover such as rocks, logs, and aquatic vegetation. They are aggressive omnivores feeding on aquatic plants, invertebrates, fish eggs, and detritus. As an invasive species outside their native range, they can significantly alter aquatic ecosystems by reducing aquatic vegetation and displacing native crayfish. Divers encounter them in clear freshwater sites throughout eastern North America, where their bold behavior and distinctive markings make them easy to identify and observe.
divingRegions: North American Inland
bestSeason: Year-round, most active spring through autumn
photographyTips: Use a macro lens in clear freshwater; they are less shy than many crayfish and will often hold their ground with raised claws for dramatic portraits.

name: Virile Crayfish
shortDescription:
The virile crayfish (Faxonius virilis, formerly Orconectes virilis) is a medium-sized freshwater crayfish native to North America. Adults reach 8-13 cm in body length and display a brownish-green body with distinctive blue-tipped claws marked with orange or red spots at the joints. The carapace has a pair of dark saddle marks.

They inhabit clear rivers, lakes, ponds, and reservoirs with rocky or gravelly substrates at depths of 0-10 meters, constructing burrows under rocks and logs. They are omnivorous, feeding on aquatic plants, insects, snails, fish eggs, and detritus. They are important members of freshwater ecosystems, serving as both predators of smaller invertebrates and prey for fish, wading birds, and mammals.

Males develop enlarged claws during the breeding season. Divers encounter them in clear freshwater sites throughout central and northern North America, where they can be observed foraging on the bottom and defending their shelters with raised-claw displays.
divingRegions: European Inland, North American Inland
bestSeason: Year-round, most active spring through autumn
photographyTips: Use a macro lens in clear freshwater; approach slowly and look under rocks where they shelter, capturing the distinctive blue claw tips.

name: Felimare Tricolor Nudibranch
shortDescription:
Felimare tricolor is a beautifully colored dorid nudibranch found in the Mediterranean Sea and eastern Atlantic. Adults reach 3-5 cm and display a deep blue to indigo body with three prominent bright yellow longitudinal lines running along the back and flanks, and a yellow border around the mantle edge. The rhinophores and gill plume are typically orange-tipped.

They inhabit rocky reefs and boulder fields at depths of 5-40 meters, feeding on sponges from which they sequester chemical compounds for their own defense. Their striking three-color pattern of blue, yellow, and orange gives them their name and makes them one of the most visually striking nudibranchs in European waters. They are hermaphroditic and often observed mating in pairs or chains. Formerly classified as Hypselodoris tricolor, this species was reclassified to the genus Felimare. They are a highlight of Mediterranean macro diving and are enthusiastically sought by underwater photographers.

name: Blue-Spotted Cornetfish
shortDescription:
The blue-spotted cornetfish (Fistularia commersonii) is a remarkably elongated fish reaching up to 1.6 meters in length, though much of this is due to its extremely long, tubular snout and a whip-like tail filament that extends beyond the caudal fin. Its body is slender and slightly compressed, colored greenish to brownish on the back with scattered blue spots and lines, and silvery below. This species is a stealthy predator that feeds on small fish and shrimps, sucking them into its tubular mouth with a rapid expansion of its jaw. A clever hunting strategy involves shadowing larger, non-threatening fish such as parrotfish or groupers, using them as mobile blinds to approach unsuspecting prey.

Originally an Indo-Pacific species, it invaded the Mediterranean Sea via the Suez Canal and has become one of the most successful Lessepsian migrants, spreading rapidly across the Mediterranean since the early 2000s. Divers commonly see them hovering motionlessly near reef edges or gliding slowly over coral formations, often in small groups.
divingRegions: Polynesia, Eastern Australia, Galápagos, Hawaii, Lord Howe & Norfolk, Micronesia, Mediterranean, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, Eastern Tropical Pacific, South Pacific Islands, California & Baja, Japan, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Wide-angle lens captures the full body length; try to include shadow-hunting behavior with other fish. Their stillness makes them relatively easy subjects.

name: Yucatan Killifish
shortDescription:
The Yucatan killifish (Floridichthys polyommus), also known as the ocellated killifish, is a small freshwater fish reaching up to 10 cm. It has a silvery body decorated with numerous dark ocelli (eye-spots) along the flanks. Endemic to the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico, it inhabits coastal lagoons, cenote entrances, and brackish waters at depths of 0 to 3 meters. This hardy species tolerates a wide range of salinities and temperatures.

It feeds on algae, detritus, and small invertebrates. Schools of these attractive killifish are commonly encountered by divers entering cenotes along the Caribbean coast of the Yucatan, where they gather in the light-filled entrance zones.

photographyTips: Use macro for the ocellated spot pattern; schools in cenote entrances with natural light beams create atmospheric images.

name: Yellow Longnose Butterflyfish
shortDescription:
The yellow longnose butterflyfish (Forcipiger flavissimus) is a small, elegant reef fish reaching up to 22 cm. It has a bright yellow body, a long needle-like snout resembling forceps used for picking food from tight crevices, and a black upper head with white lower face. Found across the tropical Indo-Pacific from East Africa to Hawaii, the Galapagos, and the eastern Pacific, it inhabits coral reefs, rocky areas, and reef slopes at depths of 2 to 114 meters.

This species is territorial, patrolling coral patches with a monogamous partner. It feeds on small invertebrates, hydroids, and fish eggs extracted from coral crevices using its specialized snout. Its distinctive silhouette and brilliant coloration make it instantly recognizable and a popular subject for underwater photography.

The Seminole killifish (Fundulus seminolis) is a freshwater killifish in the family Fundulidae, endemic to the US state of Florida. Adults reach about 13 cm with an elongated body showing olive-green to dark green dorsal coloration, silvery flanks with dark vertical bars, and yellowish fins. Males become more intensely colored during breeding season.

This species inhabits clear, vegetated springs, rivers, lakes, and marshes at depths of 0-3 meters throughout peninsular Florida. They feed on insects, small crustaceans, and aquatic invertebrates near the surface and among vegetation. Seminole killifish are often encountered during freshwater dives in Florida's spring systems, where they swim in loose groups near aquatic vegetation. Their attractive coloration and endemic status make them an interesting species for underwater naturalists exploring Florida's unique freshwater ecosystems.

name: Pacific Cod
shortDescription:
The Pacific cod (Gadus macrocephalus) is a large, commercially important fish reaching up to 119 cm and 22 kg. It has a brownish body with darker mottling, three dorsal fins, two anal fins, and a prominent chin barbel. Found across the North Pacific from Japan and the Sea of Okhotsk to the Bering Sea, Alaska, and California, it inhabits sandy and muddy bottoms over the continental shelf at depths of 0 to 500 meters, most commonly between 50 and 300 meters.

This species feeds on fish, crustaceans, worms, and cephalopods. It forms large aggregations, particularly during spawning season. Cold-water divers in the Pacific Northwest and Alaska occasionally encounter Pacific cod on deeper dives, where their large size and schooling behavior create impressive underwater spectacles.

bestSeason: Year-round; best encountered during winter spawning aggregations
photographyTips: Use wide-angle for schooling shots; cold water and depth require appropriate exposure settings.

name: Mountain Galaxias
shortDescription:
The mountain galaxias (Galaxias olidus) is a small freshwater fish in the family Galaxiidae. Adults reach about 12 cm with a small head, large mouth, and short-based fleshy fins. They lack scales, showing a smooth skin with yellowish-green to brown coloration above, olive to silvery below, with speckles, blotches, and banding.

This species occurs on both sides of the Great Dividing Range from southern Queensland to eastern South Australia, inhabiting freshwater streams from the coast up to 1,800 m elevation at depths of 0-2 meters. Mountain galaxias are predatory, feeding on aquatic insects, small crustaceans, and terrestrial insects that fall into the water. Recent taxonomic revision has revealed that what was considered one species is actually a complex of at least 15 distinct species. They require cold, clear, well-oxygenated flowing water and their presence indicates high-quality mountain stream habitat.

Black feathery gills emerge when it is underwater for it to filter feed on plankton.
