name: Mosquitofish
shortDescription:
Gambusia affinis, the western mosquitofish, is a small freshwater livebearer in the family Poeciliidae. Adults are tiny, with females reaching about 7 cm and males only about 3.5 cm. They have an olive-grey body, a slightly upturned mouth adapted for surface feeding, and a rounded caudal fin.

Males possess a modified anal fin (gonopodium) for internal fertilization. This species is native to the southeastern United States and northern Mexico at depths of 0-2 meters in freshwater habitats, but has been introduced to over 60 countries worldwide for mosquito control. They inhabit virtually any warm freshwater habitat including ponds, ditches, streams, and marshes. Mosquitofish are voracious predators of mosquito larvae and other small insects at the water surface.

As livebearers, females can produce multiple broods without re-mating. While effective at mosquito control, they are considered one of the world's most invasive fish species, often outcompeting native fish.
divingRegions: North American Inland, New Zealand, East Asia Inland
photographyTips: Extremely small; requires super-macro capability in shallow, clear water with abundant vegetation.

name: Yucatan gambusia
shortDescription:
The Yucatan gambusia (Gambusia yucatana) is a small livebearing fish reaching up to 6 cm. Females are larger than males and have a silvery-green body, while males are smaller with a modified anal fin (gonopodium) used for internal fertilization. Endemic to the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico, Belize, and northern Guatemala, it inhabits cenotes, springs, coastal lagoons, and freshwater streams at depths of 0 to 3 meters. This hardy species is tolerant of variable water conditions and is often found in enormous schools in the shallow, sunlit zones of cenote entrances.

It feeds on mosquito larvae, algae, and small invertebrates. Cenote divers routinely swim through clouds of these small fish when entering and exiting cenotes, where their silvery bodies catch and reflect the dramatic light beams penetrating the water.
divingRegions: Yucatán Freshwater
photographyTips: Use wide-angle to capture schools in cenote light beams; the sun ray and fish combination creates iconic cenote imagery.

The opaleye (Girella nigricans) is a medium-sized sea chub reaching up to 66 cm. It has an olive-green body with one or two distinctive white or light blue spots below the dorsal fin, and characteristic brilliant opalescent blue-green eyes that give the species its common name. Found in the eastern Pacific from San Francisco to southern Baja California and the Galapagos, it inhabits rocky reefs, kelp forests, and tide pools at depths of 0 to 30 meters. This herbivorous species feeds primarily on red and green algae, with occasional consumption of small invertebrates.

It is commonly seen in schools on rocky reefs and kelp-lined channels. Its bright eyes are its most distinctive feature, appearing to glow with an inner light underwater, making it an instantly recognizable and charming resident of California's kelp forests.

name: Striped Large-Eye Bream
shortDescription:
The striped large-eye bream (Gnathodentex aureolineatus), also known as the goldspot emperor, is the sole member of its genus in the family Lethrinidae. Adults reach about 30 cm with a moderately deep body, large prominent eyes, and silvery coloration adorned with golden horizontal stripes and a distinctive gold spot on the upper caudal peduncle. This species inhabits coral reefs, reef passages, and channels at depths of 3-30 meters across the Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea and East Africa to Hawaii and French Polynesia.

They form dense, tightly packed schools during the day, often hovering near reef walls and in passages where currents bring plankton. They feed on zooplankton, small fish, and benthic invertebrates. Their large schools in reef channels create impressive underwater spectacles, and the golden markings stand out beautifully against their silvery bodies.
divingRegions: Polynesia, Coral Triangle, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef, Southern Japan, French Polynesia, South Pacific Islands, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round; best in current-swept reef passages
photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens to capture schooling formations in channels; the golden stripes and large eyes make for striking compositions.

name: Two-spotted Goby
shortDescription:
The two-spotted goby (Gobiusculus flavescens) is a small goby reaching about 6 cm found in the northeastern Atlantic from Norway to the Mediterranean. It is translucent pinkish-orange with two distinct dark spots at the base of the tail fin. Unlike most gobies, it is a midwater swimmer rather than a bottom-dweller, hovering among kelp fronds and seaweed in small groups.

It feeds on tiny planktonic crustaceans. Males develop brighter orange coloration during breeding season and guard egg clutches laid on the underside of rocks and shells. It is one of the most abundant small fish in northern European coastal waters and kelp forests.

name: Japanese Moray Eel
shortDescription:
The Japanese moray eel (Gymnothorax kidako) is a large moray reaching up to 90 cm in length, found primarily in the temperate and subtropical waters of the northwestern Pacific. It has a robust, muscular body with mottled brown to dark brownish-grey coloration marked with irregular lighter spots and patches. Like all morays, it lacks pectoral and pelvic fins and has a continuous dorsal fin running along its back.

It constantly opens and closes its mouth to pump water over its gills, a behavior that can appear threatening but is simply respiration. This species inhabits rocky reefs, boulder fields, and crevice-rich environments where it shelters during the day and hunts at night. It feeds on fish, octopus, and crustaceans, using its keen sense of smell to locate prey in the dark.

Divers commonly encounter it peering from holes and overhangs on Japanese reef sites, often accompanied by cleaner shrimp that pick parasites from its skin and mouth. It is generally not aggressive toward divers unless provoked or fed.
divingRegions: Southern Japan, Japan
bestSeason: Year-round; summer months offer best visibility and warmer water in temperate Japanese waters
photographyTips: Macro lens for portraits emerging from crevices; focus on the eyes and wait for mouth-open poses. Include cleaner shrimp for behavior shots.

Relatively rare across most of its range — except in Hawaii, where it's common. Inhabits shallow lagoons and coral-rich reefs to ~36 m, spending the day tucked into reef holes and emerging to ambush passing fish, which it locates by smell.

name: Goldentail Moray Eel
shortDescription:
The goldentail moray eel (Gymnothorax miliaris), also called the banana eel, is a small to medium-sized moray reaching up to 70 cm, though most individuals are around 40 cm. Its body is dark brown to purple-black covered densely with bright golden-yellow spots, and the tail tip is distinctively golden. Found throughout the western Atlantic from Florida and Bermuda to Brazil, including the Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico, it inhabits coral reefs, rocky areas, and rubble zones at depths of 1 to 60 meters.

It feeds on small fish, crustaceans, and octopuses, hunting primarily at night. This species is often more visible and photogenic than larger moray species, frequently peering out from small holes in the reef with its speckled face. Its compact size and stunning golden-spotted coloration make it a favorite subject for Caribbean macro photography.

photographyTips: Use macro for face portraits; look for them peering from small reef holes and use gentle lighting to bring out the golden spots.

name: Easter Island Moray Eel
shortDescription:
The Easter Island moray (Gymnothorax nasuta) is a moray eel reaching up to 60 cm. It has a brownish body with a distinctive pointed snout, adapted to the volcanic rock reef habitat of Easter Island. Found in the southeastern Pacific around Easter Island and Chile, it inhabits rocky reefs and volcanic boulder fields at depths of 3 to 30 meters.

This species shelters in the many crevices and holes provided by Easter Island's volcanic rock substrate, emerging at night to hunt small fish and invertebrates. As one of the endemic or near-endemic species of Easter Island's unique marine ecosystem, encountering it represents one of the special wildlife experiences available only at this remote Pacific island. Its rarity and restricted range make every sighting a notable event for visiting divers.

name: Paintspotted Moray Eel
shortDescription:
The peppered moray eel (Gymnothorax pictus) is a medium-sized moray reaching about 120 cm found across the Indo-Pacific from East Africa to the eastern Pacific. It has a white to cream body densely covered with small dark brown to black spots, giving it a 'peppered' appearance. The head is more heavily spotted, and the spots may merge into blotches in some individuals.

It inhabits shallow reef flats, lagoons, and tide pools, often in areas with mixed coral and rubble substrate. More commonly active during the day than many morays, it can be seen hunting small fish and crustaceans in shallow water. It is one of the more commonly encountered morays in shallow reef habitats.

name: Brown Moray Eel
shortDescription:
The brown moray eel (Gymnothorax unicolor) is a large moray species found in the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Adults reach 80-100 cm in length and display a uniformly dark chocolate-brown to reddish-brown body without distinctive markings, which distinguishes it from the more mottled Mediterranean moray. They inhabit rocky reefs, caves, and boulder fields at depths of 5-100 meters, spending the day sheltered in crevices with their head protruding.

They are nocturnal predators feeding on fish, cephalopods, and crustaceans. They are frequently seen with cleaner shrimp attending to them, an interaction that allows close observation. Their powerful jaws with rows of sharp teeth give them a formidable appearance, though they are typically non-aggressive toward divers. They are commonly encountered on dives around the Canary Islands, Azores, Madeira, and throughout the Mediterranean, where they are often the largest predatory fish visible on the reef.

photographyTips: Use a macro or mid-range lens at crevice openings; look for cleaning station interactions with shrimp for compelling behavioral shots.

name: Greenlip Abalone
shortDescription:
The greenlip abalone (Haliotis laevigata) is a large marine gastropod in the family Haliotidae, endemic to southern Australia. The shell reaches up to 18 cm with a smooth, oval shape and a row of respiratory holes along the outer edge. The exterior is typically encrusted with marine organisms, while the interior displays brilliant iridescent nacre (mother-of-pearl) in greens, blues, and pinks.

The animal has a distinctive green edge to its large, muscular foot. This species inhabits rocky reef areas at depths of 3-40 meters from Western Australia around to southeastern Australia. Greenlip abalone are herbivorous grazers feeding primarily on drift algae and kelp.

They cling tightly to rock surfaces using their powerful muscular foot. This species is commercially farmed and is one of Australia's most valuable aquaculture products. Their beautiful shells and ecological importance make them significant for both divers and the fishing industry.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Western Australia, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia
photographyTips: Use a macro lens to capture the iridescent shell interior; photograph them in situ on rocky surfaces for habitat context.

name: Tropical Striped Triplefin

It features vivid horizontal stripes of red, orange, and blue along its body with three separate dorsal fins characteristic of the triplefin family. Found across the central Indo-Pacific from the Maldives to the western Pacific, it inhabits coral rubble, dead coral, and rocky substrates at depths of 2 to 30 meters.

This species perches on exposed surfaces using its pelvic fins as props, making short darting movements to capture tiny zooplankton and invertebrates. Males become more brightly colored during courtship displays. Despite its diminutive size, its intense coloration makes it a highly sought-after subject for macro photographers who enjoy searching coral rubble for tiny treasures.

name: Indian Ocean Longfin Bannerfish
shortDescription:
The Indian Ocean longfin bannerfish (Heniochus pleurotaenia), also known as the phantom bannerfish, is a beautiful butterflyfish found in the Indian Ocean. Adults reach 17-20 cm and display bold black and white vertical banding across a laterally compressed body, with a characteristic elongated fourth dorsal spine forming a trailing white filament. They have a shorter snout compared to some other bannerfish species and subtle brown shading on the posterior body.

They inhabit coral reef slopes, walls, and channels at depths of 5-40 meters, often found in pairs or small groups near coral overhangs and drop-offs. They feed on zooplankton and small benthic invertebrates. Their elegant profile with the banner-like dorsal filament creates beautiful silhouettes when photographed against blue water. They are commonly encountered on dives in the Maldives, Seychelles, and East African coast, where they add grace and beauty to reef wall scenes.
divingRegions: Andaman Sea, Coral Triangle
photographyTips: Use a mid-range lens and capture the trailing dorsal filament in full; pairs photographed against blue water backgrounds create elegant compositions.

shortDescription:
The blood sea star (Henricia sanguinolenta) is a delicate starfish reaching up to 20 cm in diameter. It has five slender, tapering arms and a vivid blood-red to orange coloration with a smooth, fine-textured surface. Found in the North Atlantic and North Pacific from the Arctic to the temperate zones, it inhabits rocky substrates, cobble fields, and sponge-encrusted surfaces at depths of 0 to 2,500 meters, though most commonly found at 10 to 200 meters.

Unlike most sea stars, it does not evert its stomach to feed. Instead, it filter-feeds on suspended organic particles and bacteria using ciliated surfaces. It is a brooding species, with females protecting developing embryos under their bodies. Its striking blood-red coloration against cold-water rocky reefs makes it a photogenic and commonly encountered invertebrate for temperate and cold-water divers.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, California & Baja, US East Coast
bestSeason: Year-round; found on most cold-water rocky reef dives

shortDescription:
The thick-horned nudibranch (Hermissenda crassicornis), also known as the opalescent nudibranch, is a brightly coloured aeolid sea slug in the family Facelinidae. Adults reach about 5 cm long and have a translucent body marked with electric-blue lines, an orange head stripe, and clusters of orange-tipped cerata. The cerata store stinging nematocysts stolen from the hydroids and anemones the slug feeds on, providing chemical defense against predators.

It lives on rocky intertidal and subtidal habitats from Kodiak Island, Alaska, south through British Columbia and Washington into northern California, typically at depths of 0–35 m on rocks, pilings, kelp, and floating docks where hydroids grow. A voracious predator, it eats hydroids, bryozoans, small anemones, ascidians, fish eggs, and even other nudibranchs, and is well known in neuroscience for studies of associative learning.

photographyTips: Use a macro lens with diffused strobes to capture the translucent body and electric-blue lines without blowing highlights; look for them on hydroids, kelp, and floating dock undersides.

Heterandria bimaculata, the spottail killifish or twospot livebearer, is a small freshwater livebearer in the family Poeciliidae. Adults reach about 10 cm (females) and 5 cm (males) with an elongated body showing olive-brown to yellowish coloration. Two distinctive dark spots are present: one at the base of the dorsal fin and one at the caudal base.

Males have a modified anal fin (gonopodium) for internal fertilization. This species inhabits freshwater streams, rivers, and springs at depths of 0-3 meters in the highlands of Mexico and Central America, from San Luis Potosi to Honduras. They prefer flowing waters with rocky or gravelly substrates and moderate vegetation. Heterandria bimaculata feed on small insects, algae, and detritus.

As livebearers, females give birth to relatively small broods of live young. They are found at higher elevations than most poeciliids, inhabiting cooler mountain streams. Their two distinctive spots and highland habitat make them interesting subjects for freshwater naturalists.
divingRegions: Mexico & Central America Freshwater
bestSeason: Year-round; clearest water in dry season
photographyTips: Macro lens recommended in clear mountain streams; the two distinctive spots are key identification features to capture.

name: Least Killifish
shortDescription:
The least killifish (Heterandria formosa) is one of the smallest vertebrates in the world, belonging to the family Poeciliidae. Males reach only about 2 cm and females about 3 cm. Despite its name, it is not a true killifish but a livebearer related to guppies and mollies.

They have an olive-brown body with a distinctive dark horizontal stripe and a dark spot on the dorsal fin. This species inhabits densely vegetated shallow freshwater and brackish habitats at depths of 0-1 meter across the southeastern United States, from North Carolina through Florida to Louisiana. Despite their tiny size, they are voracious micro-predators feeding on small invertebrates, algae, and detritus.

Females give birth to live young through a unique process of superfetation, carrying embryos at multiple developmental stages simultaneously. Their remarkable miniature size makes them a fascinating find for observant freshwater divers.

name: Japanese Bullhead Shark
shortDescription:
The Japanese bullhead shark (Heterodontus japonicus) is a small, bottom-dwelling shark reaching up to 120 cm. It has a blunt head with prominent ridges above each eye, a brownish body with darker harness-like markings, and two dorsal fins each preceded by a spine. Found in the northwestern Pacific off Japan, Korea, and China, it inhabits rocky and coral reefs at depths of 6 to 37 meters. This nocturnal species rests in caves and crevices during the day, feeding at night on sea urchins, crabs, and mollusks.

It produces distinctive spiral-shaped egg cases that are often found wedged in rocks. Its docile nature and tendency to rest in accessible locations make it a popular and cooperative subject for divers in Japanese waters.

name: Leopard Whipray
shortDescription:
The leopard ray (Himantura leoparda) is a large whipray reaching disc widths of up to 140 cm, found in the Indo-West Pacific from South Africa and the Red Sea to northern Australia and the western Pacific. Its dorsal surface features a stunning pattern of large dark brown or black leopard-like spots and rosettes on a golden-brown to tan background, making it one of the most visually striking rays in tropical waters. The ventral surface is white.

It has a very long, whip-like tail that can exceed twice the body length, equipped with one or two venomous barbs. Found at depths of 1 to 70 meters, it favors sandy flats, seagrass beds, and lagoons adjacent to coral reefs, where it partially buries itself in sand to ambush prey. Its diet consists of small fishes, crustaceans, and mollusks, which it crushes with plate-like dental plates.

This species is often confused with other spotted whiprays, and its taxonomy has undergone recent revisions. Encounters with this beautiful ray are considered highlights of tropical reef diving.

name: Pacific Halibut
shortDescription:
The Pacific halibut (Hippoglossus stenolepis) is one of the largest flatfish in the world, reaching up to 267 cm and over 220 kg. It has a dark brown upper side that matches the ocean floor and a white underside, with both eyes positioned on the right side. Found in the North Pacific from Japan and the Bering Sea to California, it inhabits sandy and gravel bottoms at depths of 0 to 1,200 meters, though most commonly at 100 to 400 meters. This powerful predator feeds on fish, crabs, clams, and octopus.

Females grow much larger than males and can live for over 55 years. Encountering a large halibut on a dive is an impressive and somewhat startling experience, as these massive fish can appear suddenly from the substrate when disturbed, their enormous diamond-shaped body creating an unforgettable sight.

name: Clarion Angelfish
shortDescription:
The clarion angelfish (Holacanthus clarionensis) is a stunningly beautiful marine angelfish in the family Pomacanthidae, reaching up to 25 cm in length. Adults display a brilliant bright orange body with fine blue markings on the face, bright blue fin margins, and an electric blue ring around the eye. Juveniles are darker with blue vertical bars that fade as they mature.

This species is primarily endemic to the Revillagigedo Islands off the Pacific coast of Mexico, with occasional sightings at Clipperton Island and along Baja California. They inhabit rocky reefs and boulder-strewn areas at depths of 5-30 meters. Clarion angelfish feed on sponges, tunicates, and algae.

They are curious and often approach divers, particularly around the remote Revillagigedo archipelago. Their extreme rarity and striking beauty make them one of the most prized sightings among diving enthusiasts worldwide.

name: Atlantic Black Sea Cucumber
shortDescription: Holothuria forskali, the black sea cucumber or cotton-spinner is a species of sea cucumber in the family Holothuriidae. It is found at shallow depths in the eastern Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. It was placed in the subgenus Panningothuria by Rowe in 1969 and is the type taxon of the subgenus. Sea cucumbers are marine invertebrates and are closely related to the sea urchins and starfish. All these groups tend to be radially symmetric and have a water vascular system that operates by hydrostatic pressure, enabling them to move around by use of many suckers known as tube feet. Sea cucumbers are usually leathery, gherkin-shaped animals with a cluster of short tentacles at one end.

name: Blue Dorid
shortDescription:
Hypselodoris festiva is a strikingly beautiful nudibranch reaching about 5 cm in length, found primarily in the western Pacific from Japan to the Philippines. Its mantle is a vivid blue to purple-blue, decorated with yellow to orange-gold lines and spots that create an intricate pattern unique to each individual. The mantle margin is often edged with a thin yellow-orange line, and the rhinophores and gills are deep purple to blue.

This species belongs to the chromodorid family, whose members are renowned for their spectacular colors, which serve as aposematic warning signals to predators. The bright coloration advertises the presence of distasteful chemical compounds derived from the sponges on which it feeds. Hypselodoris festiva is typically found on rocky reefs and coral rubble where its preferred sponge prey grows, at depths from the shallows to about 30 meters.

It is especially popular among underwater photographers in Japan, where it is commonly encountered at diving hotspots like Izu, Kushimoto, and Okinawa. Like all nudibranchs, it is a hermaphrodite that lays spiral-shaped egg ribbons on the substrate.
divingRegions: Southern Japan, Japan
bestSeason: Year-round; spring and summer in temperate Japanese waters for peak diversity
photographyTips: Macro lens with a diopter for maximum detail; shoot at the slug's level for eye-catching compositions. Dual strobes prevent harsh shadows and bring out blue and orange tones.

name: Smallmouth Buffalo
shortDescription:
The smallmouth buffalo (Ictiobus bubalus) is a large freshwater fish reaching up to 90 cm and 36 kg. It has a deep, laterally compressed body with an olive to dark grey coloration and a characteristic small, subterminal, sucker-like mouth. Found in major river systems of central North America, particularly the Mississippi River basin, it inhabits rivers, lakes, and reservoirs at depths of 1 to 20 meters. Recent research has revealed that this species can live over 100 years, making it one of the longest-lived freshwater fish in North America.

It feeds by filtering zooplankton and detritus from the water or substrate. Despite its large size and abundance, it is often overlooked by divers who focus on more colorful species. Encountering a large, century-old smallmouth buffalo underwater is a humbling experience that connects divers with living history.

name: Indo-Pacific sailfish
shortDescription:
The Indo-Pacific sailfish (Istiophorus platypterus) is a billfish reaching up to 3.4 m, famous for its enormous retractable dorsal fin that resembles a sail. The fastest fish in the ocean, it can reach speeds over 110 km/h. Its body is dark blue above fading to silver-white below, with about 20 vertical bars of pale blue spots. The sail is cobalt blue with dark spots.

It hunts cooperatively, using its sail to herd schools of baitfish like sardines into tight balls before slashing through them with its bill. Divers occasionally encounter them during organized sailfish encounters off Mexico, Mozambique, and other locations. Witnessing a sailfish hunt is considered one of the ultimate marine wildlife experiences.
divingRegions: South Africa, Andaman Sea, Maldives & Chagos, Eastern Australia, Coral Triangle, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Red Sea, Arabian Sea, Southern Japan, Eastern Tropical Pacific, Caribbean, South Pacific Islands, California & Baja, US East Coast, India & Sri Lanka, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: December-March for organized encounters off Mexico and Mozambique; year-round in tropical areas, summer months in temperate zones when following baitfish migrations
photographyTips: Wide-angle essential; fast shutter speed to freeze action; snorkel encounters allow surface lighting; anticipate the bait ball direction for best positioning.

name: Jason Mirabilis Nudibranch
shortDescription:
Jason mirabilis, commonly known as Jason's nudibranch, is a large and strikingly beautiful aeolid nudibranch endemic to New Zealand. Adults reach 5-10 cm and display an elongated body covered with numerous long, flowing cerata (finger-like appendages) that can be orange, brown, purple, or red with white tips, giving the animal a dramatic flowing appearance. The body is translucent white to pale orange.

They inhabit rocky reefs and kelp forests at depths of 5-30 meters, feeding on hydroids and other cnidarians. Like other aeolid nudibranchs, they can sequester stinging nematocysts from their prey and store them in the tips of their cerata for defense. They were first described by M.C. Miller in 1974. Their large size, dramatic flowing cerata, and New Zealand endemism make them one of the most prized nudibranch sightings for underwater photographers visiting NZ waters, particularly around the Poor Knights Islands.

name: Striped Marlin

shortDescription:
The striped marlin (Kajikia audax) is a large, fast-swimming billfish found in the Indo-Pacific. Adults reach 2.5-4 meters in length and weigh up to 190 kg. They display a dark blue dorsal surface, silver flanks, and their namesake vivid vertical stripes that can flash neon blue and purple during hunting excitement, created by rapid chromatophore changes.

Their tall, pointed dorsal fin and long, spear-like bill are used to slash through schools of baitfish. They inhabit open ocean waters near continental shelves and around oceanic islands at depths of 0-200 meters. Divers encounter them during seasonal baitball events, particularly off Baja California (Mexico), where they cooperatively herd sardines into tight balls before slashing through them with their bills. These encounters are among the most thrilling in recreational diving, as the marlin display their full range of color-changing abilities while hunting at high speed just meters from divers.

bestSeason: October to February off Baja California; varies by location
photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens with fast shutter speed; these are snorkeling rather than scuba encounters, and the rapidly changing neon stripes are best captured in video.

name: Lembeh Sea Dragon
shortDescription:
The Lembeh sea dragon (Kyonemichthys rumengani), also called the pygmy pipehorse or thread pipefish, is an extraordinarily tiny syngnathid reaching only 3 cm. Its body is extremely thin and thread-like, with a filamentous appearance that helps it mimic strands of algae or hydroids. Found in the Lembeh Strait of Sulawesi, Indonesia, and possibly other parts of the Coral Triangle, it inhabits sandy and rubble substrates near hydroids and algae patches at depths of 5 to 20 meters. First described scientifically in 2007, this species was named after the dive guide who discovered it.

It feeds on tiny zooplankton, hovering nearly invisibly among hydroids. Finding this minuscule creature requires exceptional spotting skills, and encountering one is considered the pinnacle achievement for muck diving enthusiasts visiting the Lembeh Strait.
divingRegions: Coral Triangle
bestSeason: Year-round; Lembeh offers excellent muck diving conditions all year
photographyTips: Use super-macro lens or diopter; extreme patience required as the subject is nearly invisible without a trained eye.

name: Brook Silverside
shortDescription:
The brook silverside (Labidesthes sicculus) is a slender freshwater fish in the family Atherinopsidae. Adults reach about 6-10 cm with an extremely slender, translucent body showing a prominent silver lateral stripe. The head features a distinctive elongated, upward-pointing snout adapted for surface feeding.

This species inhabits clear, calm waters of lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams at depths of 0-3 meters across eastern North America, from the Great Lakes to the Gulf Coast. Brook silversides are surface-oriented fish, forming shimmering schools near the water surface where they feed primarily on small insects, both aquatic and terrestrial. They have a short lifespan of only about one year.

Their translucent bodies and surface-dwelling habits create beautiful light effects when seen from below. Despite their small size, they are ecologically important as both predators of small invertebrates and prey for larger fish and wading birds.
divingRegions: North American Inland
photographyTips: Photograph from below looking up toward the surface for dramatic silversides-against-light effects; their translucent bodies create beautiful images.

name: Thornback Cowfish
shortDescription:
The thornback cowfish (Lactoria diaphana) is a distinctive member of the boxfish family found across the Indo-Pacific region. Growing to about 25 cm, it has a rigid, boxy body encased in a carapace of fused bony plates, with two forward-pointing horns above the eyes and prominent spines along the back, giving it its common name. The body is typically pale with scattered dark spots or blotches. This slow-moving fish inhabits sandy and rubble areas near reefs, seagrass beds, and sheltered lagoons at moderate depths.

It feeds on benthic invertebrates, algae, and small organisms found in the sediment. When threatened, cowfish can release a toxic mucus called ostracitoxin from their skin, which discourages predators. Their deliberate, hovering swimming style and curious nature make them approachable subjects for underwater photographers. Thornback cowfish are solitary or found in pairs, and their unusual silhouette makes them instantly recognizable even from a distance on the reef.

bestSeason: Year-round; commonly encountered during day dives on sandy reef slopes
photographyTips: Use macro or mid-range lens to capture the detailed bony plates and horn projections; photograph from eye level for a face-on portrait showing the horns; move slowly to avoid startling the fish

name: Salmon Shark
shortDescription: The salmon shark is the North Pacific's cold-water counterpart to the great white — a stocky mackerel shark with the same conical snout and heavy, torpedo-shaped body, though it rarely exceeds 2.6 m and about 220 kg. Adults are dark grey to nearly black above with a white belly broken by dusky blotches; juveniles are plain underneath. Like its relatives it is regionally endothermic: paired counter-current heat exchangers, the retia mirabilia, trap metabolic heat and hold the core near 16-19°C in water around 8°C, which is what lets it hunt fast and accurately in sub-Arctic seas. Its range runs from the Sea of Japan across the North Pacific to Alaskan waters above 65°N. It spends most of its time in the sunlit surface layer but has been tracked as deep as 668 m. Salmon give the shark its name, though it also takes squid, herring, walleye pollock, sablefish and the occasional seabird. Females bear two to six live pups after roughly nine months and mature at eight to ten years; males mature at about five. Divers meet salmon sharks only by chance, typically in cold open water near the summer salmon runs, and no attack on a person has ever been confirmed. The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern.

name: Blue-Lipped Sea Krait
shortDescription:
The large-tailed sea snake (Laticauda laticaudata), also known as the blue-lipped sea krait, is a venomous sea snake in the family Elapidae. Adults reach 100-150 cm in length with a cylindrical body displaying bold dark blue-black and pale blue-white banding. The tail is laterally flattened and paddle-shaped for swimming. Distinguished from other sea kraits by its blue-gray upper lip coloration.

This species is semi-aquatic, hunting fish and eels in coral reefs at depths of 0-80 meters while returning to land to rest, digest prey, and breed. Found throughout the Indian and western Pacific Oceans from India to Fiji. Despite possessing potent neurotoxic venom, blue-lipped sea kraits are remarkably docile and rarely bite divers.

They are commonly encountered resting on reef ledges or swimming gracefully through the water column. Their striking banding pattern and calm demeanor make them a fascinating, if initially nerve-wracking, diving encounter.

name: Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle

imageCredit.artist: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Southeast Region

shortDescription:
Kemp's ridley sea turtle (Lepidochelys kempii) is the smallest and most critically endangered sea turtle in the world, with adults reaching only 60-70 cm in carapace length and weighing about 45 kg. Its nearly circular carapace is olive-grey to greenish, and the plastron (belly) is yellowish-white. This species is famous for its synchronized nesting behavior called an arribada, where thousands of females come ashore simultaneously on a single beach to lay eggs. The primary nesting site is Rancho Nuevo on the Gulf coast of Tamaulipas, Mexico.

Kemp's ridley turtles feed primarily on crabs, particularly blue crabs, as well as jellyfish, sea urchins, and mollusks. They prefer shallow coastal waters with sandy or muddy bottoms. Once numbering in hundreds of thousands, the population crashed to fewer than 1,000 nesting females by the 1980s due to egg harvesting and incidental capture in fishing nets. Intensive conservation efforts have helped the population slowly recover. Divers may encounter them in the Gulf of Mexico and western Atlantic, where they forage in coastal waters.

name: Dollar Sunfish
shortDescription:
The dollar sunfish (Lepomis marginatus) is a small freshwater fish in the family Centrarchidae. Adults reach about 12 cm with a deep, laterally compressed body displaying olive-green to brownish coloration with rows of iridescent blue-green to turquoise spots on the sides. The opercular flap has a distinctive light-colored margin.

Males become intensely colorful during breeding season with vivid blue, green, and orange tones. This species inhabits slow-moving streams, swamps, springs, and vegetated lake margins at depths of 0-3 meters across the southeastern United States, from the Carolinas to Texas. Dollar sunfish prefer areas with abundant vegetation and woody debris.

They feed on small insects, crustaceans, and snails. Males construct and guard nests in sandy or gravelly substrates. Their small size and brilliant breeding colors make them popular subjects for freshwater underwater photography.

bestSeason: Spring and summer (April-August) for breeding colors
photographyTips: Use a macro lens in clear spring-fed streams; males in breeding coloration are most photogenic near their nests.

name: Yellowtail Emperor
shortDescription:
The yellowtail emperor (Lethrinus atkinsoni) is a medium to large reef fish belonging to the family Lethrinidae. Adults typically reach 30-45 cm in length, with a maximum of about 60 cm. They display a silvery-blue body with a distinctive yellow tail and yellowish pectoral fins.

The head is robust with a slightly elongated snout and large eyes. Yellowtail emperors inhabit coral reefs, lagoons, and sandy areas at depths of 2-30 meters throughout the western Pacific, from southern Japan to northern Australia and eastward across Micronesia. They are often found singly or in small groups foraging over sandy substrates near reef edges.

Their diet consists primarily of benthic invertebrates including crustaceans, mollusks, sea urchins, and polychaete worms, which they crush with their strong pharyngeal teeth. Juveniles tend to inhabit seagrass beds and sheltered lagoons. This species is important in both commercial and recreational fisheries across its range.

name: Sunbleak
shortDescription:
The sunbleak (Leucaspius delineatus) is a small cyprinid fish found in freshwater habitats across Europe. Adults reach 6-9 cm in length and display a slender, laterally compressed silvery body with a distinctive bright blue-silver lateral stripe that gives the species a reflective, sun-catching appearance. They form large schools in still and slow-moving waters including ponds, lakes, ditches, and flooded quarries at depths of 0-5 meters.

They feed on small invertebrates, insect larvae, and algae near the water surface. Males develop small tubercles on the head during breeding season and guard egg ribbons laid on aquatic plants. Their schooling behavior creates shimmering displays in sunlit freshwater environments.

While small, they add life and motion to freshwater dive sites across Europe, and their reflective scales create attractive light effects in underwater photography. They are a common sight in popular freshwater diving locations throughout central and northern Europe.
divingRegions: European Inland
bestSeason: Year-round, most active spring through autumn
photographyTips: Use a macro or mid-range lens; schools near the surface in sunlit water create beautiful light-play effects on their reflective scales.

name: Common Dace
shortDescription:
The common dace (Leuciscus leuciscus) is a slender, streamlined freshwater fish reaching about 25-30 cm in length, found in rivers and streams across Europe from the British Isles and France to western Siberia. It has a bright silvery body with yellowish-green fins and a slightly forked tail, with a small, subterminal mouth adapted for surface and mid-water feeding. Dace prefer clean, well-oxygenated rivers and streams with moderate to fast current, particularly in the upper and middle reaches.

They form loose schools, often seen in large numbers hovering in the current over gravel and sand substrates. Their diet consists of aquatic and terrestrial insects, larvae, small crustaceans, and plant matter. They are one of the first fish to rise to surface insects, creating characteristic small rings on the water. Freshwater divers in clear English chalk streams and European rivers regularly encounter schools of dace, which shimmer attractively in the current. They spawn in spring over gravelly shallows, with males developing small tubercles on the head and body during the breeding season.

bestSeason: Spring through autumn for active behavior; clearest water often in summer

name: Yellowtail Flounder
shortDescription:
The yellowtail flounder (Limanda ferruginea) is a right-eyed flatfish found in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean. Adults reach 35-55 cm and display a flat, oval body with both eyes on the right side. The upper (eyed) side is olive to reddish-brown with irregular rusty spots, while the blind side is white with a distinctive yellow caudal (tail) fin that gives the species its name.

They inhabit sandy and muddy bottoms on the continental shelf at depths of 10-100 meters, typically between 20-60 meters. They lie flat on the substrate, partially buried in sediment, using their remarkable camouflage to ambush small invertebrates, worms, and crustaceans. Their ability to change color to match the surrounding substrate demonstrates sophisticated neural control of skin pigment cells. Divers encounter them on sandy bottom dives in the northwest Atlantic, where spotting a well-camouflaged flounder is a satisfying test of observational skills.

photographyTips: Use a macro or mid-range lens; scan sandy areas carefully and photograph from directly above to show their camouflage pattern and unique eye placement.

The species was driven to functional extinction by pollution, ship traffic, dam construction, and illegal fishing in the Yangtze River. It represents the first documented extinction of a large mammal caused directly by human activity in modern times. Its loss is a stark warning about the vulnerability of river dolphins worldwide.

name: Puget Sound King Crab
shortDescription:
The Puget Sound king crab (Lopholithodes mandtii) is a large, strikingly colorful lithodid crab found in the Pacific Northwest of North America. Adults reach a carapace width of 20-30 cm and display a rough, heavily armored body with vivid coloration ranging from bright orange and red to purple and brown, often with contrasting bands on the legs. Their box-like carapace has prominent bumps and ridges.

They inhabit rocky reefs, boulder fields, and kelp forests at depths of 10-140 meters, though most commonly encountered between 20-60 meters. They are omnivorous scavengers and predators feeding on sea urchins, barnacles, and other invertebrates. Despite their name, they are only distantly related to commercial king crabs.

They are solitary and can tuck their legs beneath their shell to resemble a rock when disturbed. Their spectacular coloration and impressive size make them one of the most exciting crustacean encounters for divers in the Pacific Northwest.
divingRegions: Pacific Northwest, California & Baja
photographyTips: Use a wide-angle or mid-range lens to capture the full armored body and vivid colors; strobes are essential at depth to restore the orange and purple coloration.

name: Red Bass
shortDescription:
The red bass (Lutjanus bohar), also known as the two-spot red snapper, is a large, robust snapper reaching up to 90 cm in length and 12 kg in weight. Adults display a deep crimson to dark red body with two silvery-white spots on the upper flank that fade in larger specimens. The body is deep and powerful, with a large head and a slightly forked tail.

Juveniles are lighter colored, often pinkish with more prominent white spots. This species is found throughout the Indo-Pacific on coral reefs, particularly around reef passes, channels, and steep drop-offs where currents concentrate prey. It forms large schools that can contain dozens of individuals, especially during spawning aggregations. Red bass are active predators feeding on fish, cephalopods, and crustaceans, hunting both day and night.

They are known for their bold, unafraid approach to divers. Notably, larger specimens may accumulate ciguatera toxin in their flesh, making them potentially dangerous to eat in certain regions despite being a popular food fish.
divingRegions: Polynesia, Micronesia, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, South Pacific Islands, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round; spawning aggregations during full moon periods offer the most impressive schooling displays
photographyTips: Wide-angle lens for school photography around reef passes; they often approach closely, allowing frame-filling shots with minimal effort.

name: Stripey Snapper
shortDescription:
The stripey snapper (Lutjanus carponotatus), also known as the Spanish flag snapper, is a species of snapper in the family Lutjanidae. Adults reach up to 40 cm with a distinctive body pattern of golden-yellow horizontal stripes on a silvery to olive background. This species inhabits coral reefs, rocky reefs, and coastal waters at depths of 1-40 meters across the western Pacific, from southern Japan to northern Australia.

They are commonly found in schools around reef structures, bommies, and drop-offs. Stripey snappers feed on small fish, crustaceans, and cephalopods. They are one of the most commonly encountered snappers on Great Barrier Reef dives and are often seen in mixed schools with other snapper species. Their reliable presence and photogenic golden stripes make them a regular highlight of tropical Australian diving.

name: Pacific Red Snapper
shortDescription:
The Pacific red snapper (Lutjanus peru) is a large, reef-associated fish found in the eastern Pacific Ocean. Adults reach 70-95 cm in length and display a deep red to pinkish-red body that is deeper and more robust than many other snapper species. They inhabit rocky reefs, coral formations, and adjacent sandy areas at depths of 5-80 meters. As opportunistic predators, they feed on fish, crustaceans, and cephalopods.

They are often found solitary or in small groups near rocky outcrops and ledges during the day. Juveniles may occur in shallower waters including mangrove areas. Their large size and striking red coloration make them an impressive sight on eastern Pacific dives, particularly around the Sea of Cortez, Costa Rica, and the Galapagos Islands. They are an important commercial and recreational fish species throughout their range and are commonly encountered by divers exploring deep reef walls and rocky pinnacles.

name: Freshwater Snail
shortDescription:
The great pond snail (Lymnaea stagnalis) is one of the largest freshwater snails in Europe, with a distinctive elongated, right-handed spiral shell reaching up to 6 cm in length. The shell is thin, translucent, and light brown to yellowish, tapering to a pointed apex. The soft body is greyish to olive-green with small yellowish spots.

This species inhabits still or slow-moving freshwater bodies including ponds, lakes, ditches, and calm river sections throughout Europe, northern Asia, and parts of North America where it has been introduced. It is a pulmonate snail, meaning it breathes air and must periodically visit the surface to replenish its air supply, creating a silvery bubble visible under its mantle. It feeds primarily on algae, decaying plant matter, and biofilm scraped from surfaces using its radula.

As a hermaphrodite, each individual possesses both male and female reproductive organs and can either self-fertilize or mate reciprocally with another snail. Freshwater divers often spot them gliding along submerged logs, rocks, and aquatic plants.

name: Blue-banded Goby

imageCredit.artist: The original uploader was Aquaimages at English Wikipedia.

shortDescription:
The blue-banded goby (Lythrypnus dalli), also known as Catalina goby, is a strikingly colorful small fish native to the eastern Pacific from Morro Bay, California, to the Gulf of California. Adults reach only 2.5 cm in length, making them one of the smallest vertebrates in their range. Their vivid appearance features a bright red-orange body adorned with iridescent blue vertical bands, typically numbering four to nine. These tiny gobies inhabit rocky reefs, boulder fields, and crevice-rich areas where they perch on rock surfaces using their fused pelvic fins as suction discs.

They are sequential hermaphrodites, typically female-first, with dominant individuals transitioning to male when the social hierarchy demands. Blue-banded gobies are territorial and defend small areas of rock face. They feed on tiny planktonic organisms and small invertebrates.

Despite their diminutive size, their brilliant coloration makes them highly sought-after subjects for underwater macro photography. They are found at depths ranging from 2 to 80 meters, though most commonly between 5 and 25 meters on rocky substrates.

It has a semi-transparent body with blue-grey coloring and distinctive long, toothed rostrum. Native to the Indo-Pacific region from Pakistan to northern Australia, it inhabits freshwater rivers, lakes, and estuarine waters at depths of 0 to 20 meters.

Males exhibit dramatic claw development with dominance hierarchies based on claw size. This species is commercially important in aquaculture throughout Southeast Asia. Divers exploring freshwater springs, rivers, and cenotes in Southeast Asia regularly encounter these impressive prawns, whose large blue claws and territorial displays make them engaging subjects for underwater photography.

name: Long-Arm Octopus
shortDescription:
The long-arm octopus (Macrotritopus defilippi), also known as the Atlantic longarm octopus, is a small, sand-dwelling cephalopod found in the tropical western Atlantic. Adults reach a mantle length of 5-8 cm with disproportionately long, slender arms extending to 30 cm or more. They display a pale sandy coloration with the ability to change color and texture to match the substrate perfectly.

They inhabit sandy and rubble bottoms at depths of 5-40 meters and are remarkable for their ability to mimic flatfish, flattening their body, tucking their arms, and swimming in a rapid, undulating motion along the sea floor that closely resembles a flounder. They can also burrow completely into sand in seconds, disappearing from view. They are nocturnal hunters feeding on small crustaceans and worms. Their exceptional camouflage and flounder-mimicry behavior make every encounter a memorable experience for divers exploring Caribbean sandy habitats, particularly during night dives.

name: Freshwater Mussel
shortDescription:
The freshwater pearl mussel (Margaritifera margaritifera) is a large bivalve reaching up to 15 cm in length, found in clean, fast-flowing rivers and streams across the Northern Hemisphere. Its shell is dark brown to black, elongated and kidney-shaped, often eroded and pitted in older specimens. It is one of the longest-lived animals known, with individuals documented at over 250 years old. These mussels are filter feeders, drawing water through their siphons and extracting algae, bacteria, and organic particles, with each adult filtering up to 50 liters of water per day.

This filtration plays a vital role in maintaining water quality. Their reproductive cycle is remarkable: females brood larvae (glochidia) in their gills before releasing them into the water, where they must attach to the gills of juvenile salmon or trout to complete their development. After several months, the young mussels drop off and bury themselves in clean gravel substrate. Once common, the species is now critically endangered across most of its range due to pollution, habitat degradation, and declining host fish populations.

bestSeason: Summer (June-September) when water levels allow safe river diving; breeding season for observing glochidia release

name: Northern Krill

imageCredit.artist: No machine-readable author provided. Saperaud~commonswiki assumed (based on copyright claims).

shortDescription:
The northern krill (Meganyctiphanes norvegica) is the largest and most abundant euphausiid crustacean in the North Atlantic. Adults reach 3-4 cm in length and display a translucent pinkish body with darker compound eyes and prominent antennae. They are capable of bioluminescence, producing blue-green light from specialized photophores on the underside of their body, likely for communication and counter-illumination camouflage.

They form dense swarms of millions of individuals in the water column at depths of 0-400 meters, undertaking daily vertical migrations — ascending to surface waters at night to feed on phytoplankton and descending to deeper waters during the day. They are a keystone species in North Atlantic ecosystems, serving as the primary food source for baleen whales, many fish species, and seabirds. Divers occasionally encounter dense krill swarms on night dives, where their bioluminescent displays create magical underwater light shows.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean, North Sea & Baltic, US East Coast
bestSeason: Year-round, surface swarms more common in spring and autumn
photographyTips: Best captured during dense surface swarms on night dives; use macro for individual specimens or wide-angle for the swarm effect, with minimal strobe to preserve bioluminescence.

name: Black Durgon
shortDescription:
The black durgon (Melichthys niger) is a medium-sized triggerfish reaching about 35 cm found circumtropically in the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans. It is one of the most uniformly colored triggerfish, with an entirely dark brown to black body accented by thin pale blue to white lines at the bases of the dorsal and anal fins. It aggregates in midwater above outer reef slopes and drop-offs, feeding on algae, planktonic organisms, and floating debris.

Unlike many aggressive triggerfish, the black durgon is generally shy and non-threatening to divers. It is particularly common in the Caribbean, Hawaii, and isolated oceanic islands.

photographyTips: Dark body requires careful exposure; blue fin lines show best with strobe light; photograph against blue water for best contrast; schools make good wide-angle subjects.

name: Stone Crab

imageCredit.artist: Andrea Westmoreland from DeLand, United States

shortDescription:
The stone crab (Menippe mercenaria), also known as the Florida stone crab, is a robust crab found in the western Atlantic from Connecticut to Belize, most abundant in Florida waters. It has a heavy, dark brownish-red oval carapace reaching about 14 cm and massive, unequal claws with black-tipped fingers powerful enough to crush oyster and clam shells. It inhabits rocky shorelines, jetties, seagrass beds, and oyster reefs from the intertidal to about 60 m.

The species is commercially important as only its claws are harvested; the crab is returned alive to regenerate new claws. Divers may encounter them in rocky crevices or burrowed in muddy substrate.
longDescription: Intertidal to 60 m

photographyTips: Macro for claw detail; look in rocky crevices and under ledges; the massive black-tipped claws are the most distinctive feature to capture.

shortDescription: A beaked whale with the most bizarre teeth of any mammal — two strap-like teeth in the lower jaw curl up and over the upper jaw, eventually preventing the mouth from opening more than a few centimeters. Males can only eat squid small enough to be sucked in.
longDescription: The Strap-Toothed Beaked Whale possesses the most extraordinary teeth of any mammal. Two flattened, strap-like teeth grow from the lower jaw, curving upward and over the upper jaw like a muzzle. In older males, these teeth completely prevent the mouth from opening more than a few centimeters — the whale must suck in squid through the narrow gap. Despite this seemingly debilitating feature, these whales grow to over 6 meters and appear well-nourished.

name: Giant Plumose Anemone
shortDescription:
The giant plumose anemone (Metridium farcimen) is one of the largest sea anemones in the world, reaching up to 1 meter tall with a column diameter of 25 cm. It has a smooth, white to orange cylindrical column topped with a crown of hundreds of fine, feathery tentacles creating a plume-like appearance. Found along the Pacific coast of North America from Alaska to southern California and in the western Pacific, it inhabits rocky reefs, pier pilings, and hard substrates at depths of 0 to 40 meters.

This species forms dense aggregations called anemone gardens, creating spectacular underwater landscapes. It is a filter feeder, using its numerous fine tentacles to capture zooplankton and suspended organic particles from the water column. Dense colonies on pier pilings and reef walls create some of the most dramatic and photogenic scenes in Pacific Northwest diving.
divingRegions: California & Baja
photographyTips: Use wide-angle for anemone garden scenes; sidelight brings out the translucent quality of the tentacles.

name: Northern Elephant Seal

imageCredit.creator: Mike Baird
imageCredit.photoTitle: Mating scene with elevated Alpha Male, Elephant Seals of Piedras Blancas

shortDescription:
The northern elephant seal (Mirounga angustirostris) is the largest pinniped in the Northern Hemisphere. Adult males reach 4-5 meters in length and weigh up to 2,300 kg, sporting the species' characteristic large, inflatable proboscis (nose) used to produce loud roaring vocalizations during breeding season. Females are significantly smaller at 2.5-3 meters and 400-900 kg.

They have a dark grey to brown coloration with thick blubber for insulation. They breed and molt on beaches along the Pacific coast of North America from Baja California to Alaska, but spend the majority of their lives at sea, diving to extraordinary depths of up to 1,500 meters for up to 2 hours to feed on squid, ratfish, and small sharks. Divers occasionally encounter juveniles and sub-adults in nearshore waters, particularly around the Channel Islands and along the California coast, where these curious and playful animals may approach divers with surprising grace despite their bulk.
divingRegions: California & Baja
bestSeason: Best underwater encounters spring through autumn, away from breeding/molting season
photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens; maintain respectful distance and let them approach you, which they often do out of curiosity — avoid blocking their path to shore.

name: Southern Elephant Seal
shortDescription:
The southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina) is the largest pinniped and largest marine carnivore, with bulls reaching 4.2 to 5.8 meters and 1,500 to 3,700 kg. Males develop a large inflatable proboscis used to produce thunderous roars during breeding season. This species shows the greatest sexual dimorphism of any mammal, with males five to six times heavier than females.

Found across the Southern Hemisphere from sub-Antarctic islands to Antarctica, they haul out on beaches in large colonies during breeding and molting seasons. They are extraordinary divers, capable of reaching depths over 1,000 meters and holding their breath for up to two hours while hunting squid, octopus, and fish. Divers in sub-Antarctic waters may encounter curious juveniles underwater, while topside encounters at breeding colonies are unforgettable wildlife experiences.
divingRegions: Patagonia, Argentina/Uruguay
bestSeason: October–November for breeding season; January–March for molting
photographyTips: Wide-angle essential for these massive animals; underwater encounters with juveniles require patience and non-threatening positioning.

name: Bump-head Sunfish
shortDescription: The bump-head sunfish is one of the two giant ocean sunfishes of the southern hemisphere and the heaviest bony fish ever weighed, at well over two tonnes and up to about three metres long. Adults are deep-bodied and abruptly truncated behind, so the animal reads as a swimming head, with a bony bump on the snout and another above the eyes in large individuals. It ranges through open ocean but rises from cool deep water to visit cleaning stations on coastal reefs, where bannerfish and other cleaner species strip parasites from its skin — the behaviour that makes it reliably divable at Nusa Penida in Bali and around southern Australia and New Zealand. It feeds mainly on gelatinous plankton such as jellyfish and salps.

shortDescription:
The fan-bellied leatherjacket (Monacanthus chinensis) is a species of filefish in the family Monacanthidae. Adults reach about 38 cm with a laterally compressed body, a prominent first dorsal spine, and a distinctive expandable fan-like ventral flap. Coloration is variable, ranging from mottled brown and green to olive with darker blotches, providing excellent camouflage among seagrass.

This species inhabits seagrass beds, soft sediment areas, and coastal reefs at depths of 1-50 meters throughout the western Pacific and eastern Indian Ocean. Fan-bellied leatherjackets feed on a variety of organisms including small invertebrates, algae, and seagrass. They use their specialized expandable belly fan in social displays and to appear larger to predators. Their excellent camouflage abilities make them challenging to spot among vegetation, rewarding divers with keen observation skills.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, South China Sea, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia, Sunda Shelf, Coral Triangle
photographyTips: Look carefully among seagrass where they hide; a macro lens captures the textured skin and fan display when they feel threatened.

It may function as a sensory organ, detecting changes in water temperature, salinity, and pressure. Narwhals dive to over 1,500 meters under Arctic ice and are rarely encountered by divers.

name: Argus Moray
shortDescription: Muraena argus, commonly known as the white-spotted moray, or the Argus moray, is a moray eel found in coral reefs from Mexico to Peru and around the Galápagos Islands. Males can reach a maximum total length of 120 centimetres (47 in), but more commonly reach a TL of 60 centimetres (24 in). Due to its wide distribution, lack of known threats, and lack of observed population decline, the IUCN redlist currently lists M. argus as Least Concern.

name: Jewel Moray Eel
shortDescription:
The jewel moray eel (Muraena lentiginosa) is a strikingly patterned moray found in the eastern Pacific Ocean. Adults reach 50-60 cm and display a dark chocolate-brown body densely covered with small, bright yellow-gold spots and circles, resembling scattered jewels that give the species its common name. They inhabit rocky reefs, crevices, and tidepools at depths of 1-25 meters, often in areas with moderate wave action.

They are nocturnal predators feeding on small fish and crustaceans, with the typical moray habit of resting in crevices during the day with only their head protruding. Their stunning pattern makes them one of the most photogenic moray species in the world and a highlight of diving in the Sea of Cortez, Galapagos, and along the coast of Central America. Unlike some larger moray species, their relatively small size and shy nature make them approachable for close-up photography.
divingRegions: Galápagos, Eastern Tropical Pacific, California & Baja
photographyTips: Use a macro lens for close-up portraits in reef crevices; strobe lighting brings out the golden spot pattern that appears dark without artificial light.

name: Scamp Grouper

The scamp grouper (Mycteroperca phenax) is a medium to large grouper reaching up to 107 cm and 13 kg. It has a brown to grey body heavily covered with darker brown spots that form clusters and lines, and elongated rays on the caudal fin giving it a distinctive broomtail appearance. Found in the western Atlantic from Massachusetts to the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico, it inhabits rocky reefs, ledges, and hard-bottom areas at depths of 10 to 100 meters. This protogynous hermaphrodite feeds on fish, squid, and crustaceans.

During spawning season, large aggregations form at traditional sites, making them vulnerable to fishing pressure. Its cat-like face and bold spotted pattern make it an attractive subject for underwater photographers exploring deeper reef structures in the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean.
divingRegions: Caribbean, US East Coast
bestSeason: Year-round; spawning aggregations from February to May

name: Bigscale Soldierfish
shortDescription:
The bigscale soldierfish (Myripristis berndti), also known as Berndts soldierfish or blotcheye soldierfish, is a medium-sized nocturnal reef fish reaching about 30 cm in length. It has a laterally compressed body with very large, light-sensitive eyes adapted for night vision, a bright red to pink-red body with silvery overtones, and distinctively large scales. The dorsal fin has a white leading edge, and a dark opercular bar marks the gill cover.

During the day, soldierfish shelter in caves, under ledges, and in deep crevices, often forming dense aggregations of dozens of individuals that face outward from their shelter. At dusk, they emerge to feed on zooplankton, larval fish, and small crustaceans in the water column above the reef. Their large eyes are highly reflective, creating dramatic red-eye effects in dive lights and camera strobes.

This species is found throughout the Indo-Pacific, from East Africa and the Red Sea to Hawaii and the eastern Pacific, making it one of the most widely distributed soldierfish. The sight of a cave full of bright red soldierfish is a common highlight of tropical reef dives.

photographyTips: Macro lens for cave portraits with dialed-down strobes to avoid harsh red-eye; wide-angle for cave aggregation scenes. Red filters can help reduce the glare from their reflective eyes.

name: Gangetic Mystus
shortDescription:
The gangetic mystus (Mystus cavasius) is a freshwater catfish in the family Bagridae, native to the Indian subcontinent. Adults reach about 20-25 cm with an elongated body, four pairs of barbels around the mouth, and a distinctive adipose fin. Coloration is silvery with a brownish-olive back.

This species inhabits rivers, streams, ponds, and floodplain wetlands at depths of 0-5 meters throughout India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, and Myanmar, particularly in the Ganges and Brahmaputra river systems. Gangetic mystus are omnivorous bottom-feeders consuming insects, crustaceans, mollusks, and plant matter. They are primarily nocturnal and shelter in submerged vegetation during the day.

This species is economically important as a highly valued food fish across the Indian subcontinent with significant market demand. Their presence in clear sections of Indian rivers can be observed by divers exploring freshwater habitats in the region.

California mussels are found clustered together, often in very large aggregations, on rocks in the upper intertidal zone on the open coast, where they are exposed to the strong action of the surf.

name: Spotted Unicornfish
shortDescription:
The spotted unicornfish (Naso brevirostris) is a large surgeonfish found throughout the Indo-Pacific. Adults reach 40-60 cm and display a grey to olive body covered in dark spots, with a characteristic short, rounded horn projecting forward from the forehead in adults. They have two fixed, blade-like caudal peduncle spines on each side of the tail base.

They inhabit outer reef slopes, channels, and drop-offs at depths of 5-50 meters, forming large schools that cruise along reef walls. They feed on zooplankton and leafy brown algae. The horn develops gradually with age and is more prominent in males.

Their large size, schooling behavior, and unique unicorn-like horn make them eye-catching additions to reef wall scenes. They are commonly encountered on dives in the Red Sea, Maldives, and throughout Southeast Asia, where schools glide effortlessly along current-swept reef edges.

shortDescription:
The bluespine unicornfish (Naso unicornis) is a large surgeonfish reaching up to 70 cm. Adults develop a prominent horn-like projection on the forehead and have two fixed, bright blue keel-shaped spines on each side of the caudal peduncle. The body is olive-grey to brownish.

Found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea and East Africa to Hawaii and French Polynesia, it inhabits reef flats, lagoons, and outer reef slopes at depths of 1 to 80 meters. This herbivorous species feeds primarily on coarse leafy brown algae. It is often seen in large schools on reef flats and in channels. The distinctive horn and vivid blue tail spines, combined with its large size and schooling behavior, make it one of the most recognizable and photogenic surgeonfish species on tropical reefs.

name: Chocolate Mahseer
shortDescription:
The chocolate mahseer (Neolissochilus hexagonolepis) is a freshwater cyprinid in the family Cyprinidae. Adults can reach up to 120 cm and 11 kg with a deep, robust body covered with distinctive large hexagonal scales that give the species its scientific name. Coloration is chocolate-brown to olive above with golden to silvery flanks.

This species inhabits fast-flowing hill streams and rivers at depths of 0-10 meters across northeastern India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Indonesia, and China. Chocolate mahseer are omnivorous, feeding on algae, aquatic insects, and small invertebrates. They prefer well-oxygenated rivers with boulder-strewn substrates and moderate to fast current. Listed as Near Threatened due to overfishing, habitat degradation, and dam construction.

In northeastern India, they are an important food fish and are increasingly the focus of aquaculture development. Their large, distinctively shaped scales and chocolate coloration make them immediately recognizable.
divingRegions: SE Asia Freshwater, South Asia Inland
photographyTips: Photograph in clear mountain streams to capture the distinctive hexagonal scale pattern; natural light highlights the chocolate-brown coloration.

name: Brownspotted Wrasse
shortDescription:
The brownspotted wrasse (Notolabrus parilus) is a species of wrasse in the family Labridae, endemic to the southern coast of Australia from Shark Bay, Western Australia, to southern Victoria. Adults reach up to 25 cm in length. Males display a dark brown or greyish-brown body with an interrupted horizontal white band running the length of the body, along with gold or brown markings on scales.

Females and juveniles are lighter brown or greenish with white blotches and grey-brown barring. This species inhabits rocky reefs with abundant seaweed growth at depths of 1-20 meters. They are active, inquisitive fish frequently encountered by divers on temperate Australian reefs. Brownspotted wrasse are carnivorous, feeding on small invertebrates including crustaceans, mollusks, and worms found among reef structures and kelp.

They are protogynous hermaphrodites, meaning females can change sex to become males. Their curious nature and tendency to approach divers make them engaging subjects for underwater observation.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Western Australia, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia
bestSeason: Year-round; best in Australian summer (December-March) for visibility
photographyTips: These curious fish often approach divers closely; use a macro or mid-range lens to capture their intricate scale patterns and color variations.

name: Southern Arrow Squid
shortDescription:
The southern arrow squid (Nototodarus sloanii), also known as the New Zealand arrow squid, is a medium to large squid reaching up to 42 cm in mantle length. It has a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body with short, muscular fins and large eyes adapted for hunting in low-light conditions. Found in the southwestern Pacific, primarily around New Zealand from the shelf break to offshore waters, it inhabits pelagic environments at depths of 0 to 500 meters.

This species is commercially important in New Zealand and is targeted by a major fishery. It feeds on fish, crustaceans, and other squid, hunting cooperatively in schools. Night divers in New Zealand waters occasionally encounter these squid attracted to dive lights, where they display rapid chromatophore color changes. Their speed, agility, and intelligence make them captivating encounters for divers lucky enough to see them.
divingRegions: New Zealand
bestSeason: Summer months (December–March) for best diving conditions
photographyTips: Best captured during night dives near lights; use fast shutter speeds to freeze their rapid movements.

shortDescription: Octopus insularis is a medium-sized octopus species described in 2008, found off the coast of Brazil and potentially beyond. It is a specialized generalist predator, primarily consuming crustaceans, bivalves, and gastropods.

name: Southern Sand Octopus
shortDescription: A small, sand-dwelling octopus endemic to southern Australia that buries in soft substrate by day. Patient divers may spot its eyes peeking from the sand at night.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Western Australia, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia
bestSeason: Year-round, with increased activity during warmer months (October to April)
photographyTips: Move slowly to avoid startling, use red filters to enhance color contrast, focus on eyes for sharp portraits, capture color-changing sequences, and photograph at their level rather than from above

name: Mexican Four-eyed Octopus
shortDescription: Octopus maya, commonly known as the Mexican four-eyed octopus, is a shallow water cephalopod found in the tropical Western Atlantic Ocean. It is often associated with seagrass prairies and coral formations.

name: Pale Octopus
shortDescription: A pale, smooth-skinned octopus found on sandy and muddy bottoms in southern Australian waters. Active at night when it emerges from its den to hunt crustaceans.
longDescription: The pale octopus (Octopus pallidus) is endemic to temperate southern Australia, ranging from southern New South Wales around Tasmania to southern Western Australia. Lives on soft and rubble bottoms from shallow water to ~275 m. Commercially fished in Tasmania.
divingRegions: Western Australia

name: Red Octopus

imageCredit.artist: Original uploader was Taollan82 at en.wikipedia

shortDescription: A small, reddish Pacific octopus found in tide pools and rocky reefs along the North American west coast. Changes color rapidly and is a clever, curious creature.
longDescription: The East Pacific red octopus (Octopus rubescens) is the most common shallow-water octopus along the temperate North American Pacific coast, ranging from the Gulf of Alaska south to Baja California. Inhabits rocky reefs, pilings, and soft bottoms to ~300 m; smaller and far more abundant than the Giant Pacific Octopus that shares much of its range.
divingRegions: California & Baja

name: Hairy Octopus

name: Gloomy Octopus

name: Pejerrey
shortDescription:
The pejerrey (Odontesthes bonariensis), also known as the Argentinian silverside, is an elegant freshwater fish reaching up to 52 cm. It has a slender, elongated body with a silvery lateral band, a translucent greenish back, and a slightly protruding lower jaw. Native to subtropical and temperate South America from the Rio Negro basin to the Rio de la Plata basin in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and southern Brazil, it inhabits freshwater lakes, rivers, and estuaries at depths of 0 to 20 meters.

This species forms large, shimmering schools that can number in the thousands. It feeds primarily on zooplankton and small crustaceans. Considered Argentina's national freshwater fish and an important recreational target, encountering a massive school of pejerrey during a freshwater dive creates a spectacular silver curtain effect in the water column.
divingRegions: South American Inland, East Asia Inland, Patagonia, European Inland
bestSeason: Year-round; spring and autumn for best fishing and diving conditions
photographyTips: Use wide-angle for school shots; the reflective silvery scales create stunning light effects when photographed against the sun.

name: Fiery Nudibranch
shortDescription:
The fiery nudibranch (Okenia amoenula) is a small dorid nudibranch in the family Goniodorididae. Adults are tiny, typically reaching only 5-15 mm. They display a vivid orange to red-orange body covered with elongated papillae that give them a flame-like appearance.

The body is soft and flattened with projections around the mantle edge. This species inhabits rocky and sandy reef areas along the Pacific coast of North America, from British Columbia to Baja California, at depths of 5-30 meters. They feed primarily on bryozoans. Due to their extremely small size, they require careful searching and a keen eye to locate, making them a rewarding find for divers and macro photographers. Their intense coloration against the often muted reef background creates spectacular photographic opportunities.
divingRegions: Western Indian Ocean, South Africa
bestSeason: Year-round; more commonly found spring through summer
photographyTips: Requires a dedicated macro lens and keen eye due to tiny size; use a gentle snooted strobe to illuminate the intense red-orange coloration.

name: Tidepool Sculpin
shortDescription:
The tidepool sculpin (Oligocottus maculosus) is a small, hardy fish reaching up to 9 cm. It has a mottled brown to greenish body that changes color to match its surroundings, with large pectoral fins and a broad, flattened head. Found along the Pacific coast from the Bering Sea to southern California, it inhabits intertidal tide pools, shallow rocky areas, and kelp zones at depths of 0 to 10 meters. This remarkable species demonstrates strong site fidelity, returning to its home tide pool even when displaced up to 100 meters away.

It can survive brief periods out of water trapped in moist crevices during low tide. It feeds on small crustaceans, snails, and algae. Its exceptional camouflage and homing ability make it a fascinating subject for tide pool exploration and shore diving.
divingRegions: California & Baja
bestSeason: Year-round; best observed in tide pools during low tides
photographyTips: Use macro in tide pools; their camouflage makes finding them a challenge, but they hold very still once located.

name: Westslope Cutthroat Trout

imageCredit.artist: USGS - Northern Rocky Mountain Science Center (NOROCK)

shortDescription:
The westslope cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarkii lewisi) is a subspecies of cutthroat trout in the family Salmonidae. Adults typically reach 25-45 cm with a streamlined body displaying olive-green to yellowish-brown coloration above, silvery sides with prominent dark spots concentrated toward the tail, and distinctive red-orange slash marks under the lower jaw that give the species its name. This fish inhabits cold, clear mountain streams, rivers, and lakes at elevations up to 3,000 meters across the northern Rocky Mountains, from Montana and Idaho to British Columbia.

They require pristine, cold-water habitats with temperatures below 15C. Westslope cutthroat feed on aquatic insects, crustaceans, and smaller fish. Named from specimens collected during the Lewis and Clark Expedition, they face conservation challenges from hybridization with introduced rainbow trout and habitat degradation. Encountering them in clear mountain streams is a testament to healthy watershed conditions.
divingRegions: North American Inland
bestSeason: Summer (June-September) when mountain streams are accessible
photographyTips: Use an underwater housing in clear shallow streams; natural light showcases their spotted pattern beautifully against rocky substrates.
