name: Panamic Fanged Blenny
shortDescription:
The Panamic fanged blenny (Ophioblennius steindachneri) is a small, robust combtooth blenny found in the eastern Pacific. Adults reach 12-18 cm and display a dark olive to brownish-black body with a blunt head and prominent fang-like teeth in the lower jaw used for territorial defense rather than feeding. Juveniles may show a broad pale band.

They inhabit shallow rocky reefs, surge zones, and reef flats at depths of 1-20 meters, aggressively defending patches of filamentous algae that they cultivate and graze. They are highly territorial, charging at other fish and even approaching divers who encroach on their domain. Their chunky appearance, pronounced underbite, and bold personality give them a comical, bulldog-like character. They are commonly encountered on dives in the Sea of Cortez, along the Mexican Pacific coast, and at the Galapagos Islands, where their territorial displays add entertainment to shallow reef dives.
divingRegions: Galápagos, Eastern Tropical Pacific, California & Baja
photographyTips: Use a macro lens in shallow water; their territorial nature means they often hold position, allowing close-up portraits showing the distinctive fanged underbite.

name: Giant Jawfish
shortDescription:
The giant jawfish (Opistognathus rhomaleus) is the largest species in the jawfish family, found in the eastern Pacific Ocean. Adults reach 35-50 cm and display a mottled brown to grey body with a disproportionately large head and enormous mouth, which is used both for excavating burrows and for mouthbrooding eggs. They inhabit sandy and rubble areas adjacent to rocky reefs at depths of 5-50 meters, constructing vertical burrows lined with small rocks and shell fragments.

They typically hover vertically above their burrow entrance, feeding on passing zooplankton and retreating tail-first into the burrow at the first sign of danger. Males incubate fertilized eggs in their mouths for several days until hatching, during which time they cannot feed. Their comical appearance, head-bobbing behavior, and fascinating reproductive biology make them a favorite encounter for divers in the Sea of Cortez and along the Pacific coast of Central America.
divingRegions: Eastern Tropical Pacific, California & Baja
bestSeason: Year-round, mouthbrooding males most common spring through summer
photographyTips: Use a macro lens and approach their burrow slowly; patience is key as they retreat when startled but re-emerge after a few minutes of stillness.

name: Blue Tilapia
shortDescription:
The blue tilapia (Oreochromis aureus) is a freshwater cichlid in the family Cichlidae, native to North and West Africa and the Middle East. Adults reach up to 45 cm and 2 kg with a deep, laterally compressed body. Males during breeding develop intense metallic blue coloration on the head and body, while females and non-breeding fish are grey to silvery with a bluish tinge.

This species inhabits lakes, rivers, ponds, and springs at depths of 0-10 meters. As an introduced species in many regions including Florida, they are commonly encountered by freshwater divers in spring systems where clear water allows excellent observation. Blue tilapia are omnivorous, feeding on algae, aquatic plants, and small invertebrates.

Males construct circular nest craters in sandy substrates and aggressively defend them during breeding. Females are mouthbrooders, carrying eggs and fry in their mouths for protection.
divingRegions: Florida Inland, North American Inland, Mexico & Central America Freshwater
bestSeason: Year-round; breeding colors most vivid in spring and summer
photographyTips: Florida springs offer crystal-clear water for photography; use natural light to capture the metallic blue breeding coloration of males.

name: Señorita Wrasse
shortDescription:
The senorita (Oxyjulis californica) is a small, cigar-shaped wrasse reaching about 25 cm, endemic to the eastern Pacific from central California to Baja California. It is brownish to bronze with a pale belly and a distinctive dark spot at the base of the tail. As the primary cleaner fish in California kelp forests, it establishes cleaning stations where larger fish visit to have parasites removed.

It is extremely active, darting constantly among kelp fronds and reef structure. The species sleeps buried in sand at night, and is one of the most commonly encountered fish by divers in Southern California kelp forests.

photographyTips: Macro for cleaning behavior shots; fast-moving so use quick shutter speed; kelp forest settings provide natural framing; look for cleaning station interactions.

name: Orange-Spotted Filefish
shortDescription:
The orange-spotted filefish (Oxymonacanthus longirostris), also known as the harlequin filefish or longnose filefish, is a small, brilliantly colored filefish reaching about 12 cm in length. Its elongated body is covered in vibrant orange spots on a turquoise to green-blue background, creating one of the most eye-catching color combinations found on any reef fish. The snout is long and narrow, adapted for picking individual coral polyps from branching Acropora corals, its exclusive food source. This extreme dietary specialization means the species is entirely dependent on healthy Acropora coral for survival.

It is found throughout the Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea to Fiji, inhabiting shallow coral reefs with abundant Acropora growth. Orange-spotted filefish are typically seen in pairs, maintaining long-term pair bonds. They sleep by biting onto a coral branch with their small teeth, hanging motionless among the branches.

This species is considered highly vulnerable to coral bleaching events, as loss of Acropora directly eliminates its food supply. Finding a pair on a reef is a sign of excellent coral health.

bestSeason: Year-round; best on reefs with healthy Acropora growth
photographyTips: Macro lens for the stunning color pattern; they hold relatively still near coral, but the long snout requires careful focus placement. Capture them feeding on coral polyps for behavior shots.

name: Glass Shrimp
shortDescription:
The glass shrimp (Palaemonetes paludosus), also known as the ghost shrimp or eastern grass shrimp, is a small freshwater shrimp in the family Palaemonidae. Adults reach about 2.5 cm in length and are largely transparent, with internal organs visible through their glass-like exoskeleton. They have long, slender legs, prominent antennae, and small chelae.

This species inhabits freshwater and slightly brackish habitats including springs, streams, ponds, and vegetated lake margins at depths of 0-3 meters across the southeastern United States. Glass shrimp are omnivorous scavengers feeding on algae, detritus, and tiny invertebrates. They are commonly found among aquatic vegetation where their transparency provides excellent camouflage. In Florida's crystal-clear spring systems, they are a familiar sight for freshwater divers. Their remarkable transparency makes them living windows into invertebrate anatomy.
divingRegions: North American Inland, Florida Inland
photographyTips: Requires macro photography with careful focus; their transparency makes backlighting effective for revealing internal structures.

name: Spot Prawn
shortDescription:
The spot prawn (Pandalus platyceros) is the largest shrimp in the eastern Pacific, reaching up to 27 cm. It has a reddish-brown body with distinctive white spots on the first and fifth abdominal segments and white-striped antennae. Found along the Pacific coast from Alaska to San Diego, it inhabits rocky reefs, crevices, and boulder fields at depths of 5 to 487 meters. This protandric hermaphrodite begins life as male and transitions to female at about 2 to 3 years of age.

It feeds on plankton, small mollusks, and worms, and is commercially harvested as a premium seafood product. Pacific Northwest divers regularly encounter spot prawns on rocky reef wall dives, where their bright spots and long antennae create attractive macro subjects. Dense aggregations in crevices provide opportunities for dramatic images.
divingRegions: California & Baja
bestSeason: Year-round; spawning season from October to January provides dense aggregations
photographyTips: Use macro with snooted light to isolate individuals; their spots glow beautifully with side-lighting.

name: Caribbean Spiny Lobster

imageCredit.artist: SEFSC Pascagoula Laboratory; Collection of Brandi Noble, NOAA/NMFS/SEFSC

shortDescription: Large spiny lobster of the Caribbean known for mass migration marches across sandy flats. Found under coral ledges by day.
longDescription: The Caribbean spiny lobster (Panulirus argus) ranges throughout the tropical western Atlantic from North Carolina and Bermuda south through Florida, the Bahamas, the entire Caribbean, and along the South American coast to southern Brazil. Inhabits coral reefs, rocky outcrops, mangroves, and seagrass beds from the intertidal to about 90 m, sheltering in crevices and under ledges by day in social groups, then dispersing at night to forage on snails, crabs, and small fish. Lacks the heavy claws of clawed lobsters; defends itself with long spiny antennae and a stridulating organ at the antennal base. Famous for autumn mass migrations across reef flats in single-file queues. Supports the largest spiny-lobster fishery in the world.
divingRegions: Caribbean, Brazil Coast, US East Coast
bestSeason: Year-round, but more active and visible during night dives; spawning season April-August offers increased activity
photographyTips: Best photographed on night dives when active; use wide-angle lens to capture full body and antennae; approach slowly from the side; use strobes to bring out orange-red coloration; focus on the large compound eyes for striking portraits

longDescription: The California spiny lobster (Panulirus interruptus) is found along the Pacific coast of North America from Monterey Bay south through Baja California to the Gulf of California, with greatest abundance between Point Conception and Magdalena Bay. Inhabits rocky reefs and kelp forests from the intertidal to about 65 m, sheltering in crevices by day and emerging at night to forage on snails, mussels, urchins, and worms. Lacks the large claws of clawed lobsters; defends itself with long spiny antennae and a distinctive raspy sound produced by the antennal base. Reaches 60 cm and 7 kg; supports an iconic California sport and commercial fishery.

bestSeason: Year-round, but more active and visible during warmer months (summer-fall)
photographyTips: Approach slowly to avoid spooking them into crevices, use red light to observe natural behavior, photograph from slightly below to show antennae and eyes prominently, best shots often in cave entrances or ledges where they rest during day

name: Japanese Spiny Lobster
shortDescription:
The Japanese spiny lobster (Panulirus japonicus), called ise-ebi in Japanese, is a large crustacean reaching up to 30 cm in body length with extremely long antennae. It has a striking coloration with a dark blue-green to reddish-purple carapace adorned with yellow and white markings. Found in the northwestern Pacific from Japan to Taiwan and Korea, it inhabits rocky reefs, caves, and crevices at depths of 5 to 30 meters. This nocturnal species shelters in reef holes during the day, emerging at night to forage for mollusks, worms, and small invertebrates.

In Japanese culture, ise-ebi is a symbol of celebration and longevity, prominently featured in New Year festivities and wedding ceremonies. Night divers in Japanese waters often encounter these magnificent lobsters emerging from their daytime hideouts, their long antennae waving in the current.
divingRegions: Southern Japan, Korea Strait, Taiwan, East China Sea
bestSeason: Year-round; night dives required for active behavior; autumn through winter for peak season
photographyTips: Use macro with red focus lights for night photography; avoid direct flash on the antennae to prevent startling them.

name: Variable Blenny
shortDescription:
The variable blenny (Parablennius pilicornis) is a small combtooth blenny found in the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Adults reach 8-12 cm and display highly variable coloration ranging from brown and grey to olive and reddish, with darker mottling and bars, which gives the species its common name. They have distinctive branched supraorbital tentacles (cirri) above the eyes, a characteristic feature of many blenny species.

They inhabit rocky reefs, boulder fields, and artificial structures at depths of 1-30 meters, often occupying small holes and crevices from which they peer out with their expressive faces. They are omnivorous, feeding on algae, small invertebrates, and detritus. Males guard territories and care for eggs laid in crevices.

Their comical appearance and habit of popping out of holes to observe passing divers makes them endearing subjects. They are one of the most commonly encountered blennies across the Mediterranean and Macaronesian islands.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean
photographyTips: Use a macro lens and look for them peering from small holes; a slow approach and patience will reward you with charming portraits showing the head tentacles.

name: Banded Blenny
shortDescription: Paraclinus fasciatus, the banded blenny, is a species of labrisomid blenny native to the Atlantic Ocean including the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea from southern Florida to Venezuela. The banded blenny is a marine organism, meaning it lives in an aquatic environment. This species lives in the vicinity of coral reefs preferring sea grass beds in shallow waters down to 2 metres (6.6 ft). Although they are typically located in shallow waters, their colors camouflage them exceptionally well, leading to them rarely being seen or recognized. They have also been found within floating algae. They are part of the family perciform teleost fishes within the sub order Blenniodei. The suborder blenniodei currently comprises 6 families, 151 genera, and 883 species. The perciform fish lineage is distinguished by its small body size, as well as their coastal and benthic habitats. The banded blenny has a typical lifespan of one year.

It inhabits coral reefs, areas of eroded limestone, tide pools, and rocky areas with algal growth down to depths of around 10 metres (33 ft). This species inhabits sandy bottoms, rocky reefs, and kelp forests at depths of 1-60 meters from Santa Cruz, California, to Baja California, Mexico.

They are opportunistic predators feeding on small fish, squid, octopus, and crustaceans. During summer spawning aggregations, they gather in impressive numbers. They are commonly encountered by divers in Southern California waters. Their curious nature and tolerance of divers make them rewarding subjects for underwater observation.

name: Red King Crab
shortDescription:
The red king crab (Paralithodes camtschaticus) is a large species of king crab in the family Lithodidae, native to the North Pacific Ocean. Adults can reach a carapace width of 28 cm and a leg span exceeding 1.8 meters, weighing up to 12.7 kg. They have a broad, spiny carapace and five pairs of legs, with the first pair modified as large chelipeds. Coloration is dark reddish-brown to burgundy, turning bright red when cooked.

This species inhabits cold, deep waters at depths of 5-400 meters in the Bering Sea, North Pacific, and Sea of Japan, as well as the introduced population in the Barents Sea. Red king crabs are omnivorous bottom-dwellers feeding on mollusks, sea stars, worms, and algae. They support one of the world's most valuable commercial fisheries. Their enormous size and dramatic appearance make them an unforgettable sight for cold-water divers exploring North Pacific kelp forests and rocky substrates.

name: Pygmy Sweeper
shortDescription:
The pygmy sweeper (Parapriacanthus ransonneti), also known as the golden sweeper, is a small fish in the family Pempheridae. Adults reach about 10 cm with a deep, compressed, translucent golden body and large eyes adapted for low-light conditions. This species inhabits coral reefs, caves, and overhangs at depths of 3-40 meters across the Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea and East Africa to the western Pacific and Australia.

During the day, pygmy sweepers aggregate in dense schools numbering hundreds to thousands inside caves, under ledges, and in shipwrecks, creating glowing golden clouds that are one of diving's most atmospheric sights. At night, they disperse to feed on zooplankton. Their translucent bodies catch and reflect ambient light in caves, creating a luminous, otherworldly effect that is a highlight of many tropical dive sites.
divingRegions: Lord Howe & Norfolk, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Southern Japan, South Pacific Islands, Japan, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round; visible in caves and overhangs during daytime dives
photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens to capture the dense golden schools inside caves; gentle ambient light creates a more atmospheric image than harsh strobes.

name: Sandpaper Fish
shortDescription:
The sandpaper fish (Paratrachichthys trailli) is a slimehead in the family Trachichthyidae found in southern Australian and New Zealand waters. Adults reach about 15 cm with a deep, compressed body covered with extremely rough ctenoid scales that give the fish its sandpaper-like texture and common name. Coloration is reddish to pinkish with large eyes adapted for nocturnal activity.

This species inhabits rocky reefs, caves, and overhangs at depths of 20-500 meters, though more commonly encountered by divers in the 20-100 m range. Sandpaper fish shelter in small groups in caves and under ledges during the day, emerging at night to feed on small crustaceans and zooplankton. Their rough skin texture is immediately noticeable to any diver who spots them, and their reddish coloration and large eyes give them a distinctive appearance among temperate reef fish communities.

name: Pink Whipray
shortDescription:
The pink whipray (Pateobatis fai) is a large stingray found throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific. Adults reach a disc width of up to 1.8 meters and display a smooth, uniformly greyish to pinkish-brown dorsal surface with a pale underside and an extremely long, thin tail bearing a single venomous spine. The disc is roughly diamond-shaped with rounded wingtips.

They inhabit sandy areas adjacent to coral reefs, lagoon floors, and channels at depths of 1-200 meters, though most commonly encountered between 5-40 meters. They are benthic feeders, using electroreception and their disc to excavate invertebrate prey from the sand. They are often encountered resting on sandy patches between coral heads, where their pale coloring blends with the substrate. Their large size, elegant form, and graceful swimming motion make them impressive encounters on tropical dives, particularly in the Maldives and French Polynesia where they are regularly seen.
divingRegions: Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, Micronesia, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Use a wide-angle lens and approach slowly from the side; capture them in flight for the most dramatic images showing the full disc and long trailing tail.

shortDescription:
The leopard nudibranch (Peltodoris atromaculata), also known as the dotted sea slug, is a large dorid nudibranch reaching up to 12 cm. It has a pale cream to yellow body covered with distinctive dark brown to black spots in a pattern resembling a leopard or cow, earning it nicknames of leopard slug and Swiss cow. Found almost exclusively in the Mediterranean Sea, it inhabits rocky reefs, sponge-covered walls, and caves at depths of 5 to 50 meters.

This species feeds on the sponge Petrosia ficiformis, and its spotted pattern may provide camouflage against the mottled sponge surfaces. It is one of the largest and most commonly encountered nudibranchs in the Mediterranean, making it a reliable macro photography target. Its bold spot pattern and substantial size make it one of the most photogenic invertebrates on Mediterranean dives.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean
bestSeason: Year-round; most commonly seen from spring through autumn
photographyTips: Use macro to fill the frame with the spotted pattern; they move slowly on sponge surfaces, allowing careful composition.

name: Rough Bullseye
shortDescription:
The rough bullseye (Pempheris klunzingeri) is a small sweeper fish in the family Pempheridae, endemic to temperate waters of southern Australia. Adults grow to about 21 cm with a deep, compressed body covered with small ctenoid scales that are rough to the touch. They have large eyes adapted for nocturnal activity and a copper to reddish-bronze coloration.

This species inhabits inshore rocky reefs at depths of 1-20 meters, from eastern South Australia to central Western Australia. During the day, rough bullseyes congregate in large schools in caves, under ledges, and in crevices, creating dense aggregations that are spectacular to observe. At night, they disperse to feed on zooplankton in the water column. Their large eyes and schooling cave-dwelling behavior make them a fascinating sight for cave divers.

name: Western King Prawn
shortDescription:
The western king prawn (Penaeus latisulcatus) is a large marine prawn in the family Penaeidae. Adults reach up to 23 cm with a translucent to pinkish body, distinctive grooves on the carapace, and long antennae. This species inhabits sandy and muddy substrates in coastal waters, estuaries, and offshore areas at depths of 1-80 meters throughout the Indo-West Pacific. Western king prawns are nocturnal, burying in the substrate during the day and emerging at night to forage on organic matter, small invertebrates, and detritus.

They are one of Australia's most commercially important prawn species, supporting major fisheries. During night dives, they can be observed walking across sandy substrates with their long antennae extended, searching for food. Their relatively large size and active nighttime behavior make them entertaining to observe on night diving excursions.

name: Ross Coral
shortDescription:
Ross coral (Pentapora foliacea) is the largest bryozoan found in British waters, despite its misleading common name as it is not a true coral but a colony of tiny filter-feeding animals called zooids. Colonies can reach 30 cm or more in diameter and form distinctive wavy, leaf-like fronds resembling orange-brown lettuce or potato crisps. Each colony consists of millions of individual zooids, each less than 1 mm in size, that extend tiny tentacle crowns (lophophores) to filter plankton from the water.

Found attached to rocky substrates and wrecks at depths of 10-80 meters, they prefer areas with moderate current flow. Colonies are slow-growing and extremely fragile, easily damaged by anchors, fishing gear, or careless divers. Their intricate structure provides habitat for many small invertebrates. They are an important indicator of healthy sublittoral rocky habitats in the northeastern Atlantic and are a fascinating subject for divers interested in the diversity of marine colonial organisms.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, North Sea & Baltic
photographyTips: Use a macro lens to reveal the intricate zooid structure, or mid-range to show the full colony form; avoid contact as they are extremely fragile.

name: Patagonian Perch
shortDescription:
The Patagonian perch (Percichthys trucha), also called the creole perch, is a freshwater fish reaching up to 46 cm. It has an olive-green to silvery body with darker spots and a moderately compressed profile. Found in freshwater systems throughout Patagonia in both Argentina and Chile, on both sides of the Andes, it inhabits cold lakes, rivers, and streams at depths of 0 to 30 meters. This predatory species feeds on aquatic invertebrates and small fish.

It spawns in aggregations during spring, gathering at traditional sites in lakes and rivers. Popular as a sport fish in Patagonia's crystal-clear mountain lakes, it is also occasionally encountered by freshwater divers exploring the remarkable underwater landscapes of Patagonian lakes, where volcanic rock formations and clear water create otherworldly dive environments.

imageCredit.artist: This illustration was made by Citron You must credit this : Citron / CC-BY-SA-3.0

shortDescription:
The bay snook (Petenia splendida) is a large, impressive cichlid reaching up to 50 cm. It has an elongated body with a highly protrusible mouth that can extend forward dramatically to engulf prey. Coloration varies from silvery-green to deep red-gold, with specimens from different habitats showing distinct color morphs. Native to the Atlantic drainages of Central America from Mexico to Guatemala and Belize, it inhabits rivers, lagoons, cenotes, and lakes at depths of 0 to 15 meters.

This apex freshwater predator feeds on small fish, catching them with lightning-fast mouth extension strikes. Its large size, striking coloration, and spectacular feeding behavior make it one of the most impressive freshwater fish encountered during cenote and river dives in Central America.
divingRegions: South American Inland
bestSeason: Year-round; most active during warmer months
photographyTips: Use wide-angle for full body shots showing the impressive mouth structure; capture feeding strikes if possible with fast shutter.

name: Flathead Gudgeon
shortDescription:
The flathead gudgeon (Philypnodon grandiceps) is a small freshwater fish in the family Eleotridae, endemic to eastern Australia. Adults reach about 8-12 cm with a broad, distinctively flattened head, wide mouth, and a stout body. Coloration is mottled brown to grey with darker blotches, providing excellent camouflage against rocky and sandy substrates.

This species inhabits rivers, streams, lakes, and lagoons at depths of 0-3 meters throughout the Murray-Darling Basin and in coastal drainages from Queensland to northern Tasmania. Flathead gudgeons are ambush predators that lie motionless on the bottom, waiting to strike at passing invertebrates and small fish. They prefer areas with rocky or gravelly substrates and moderate flow. Their excellent camouflage and bottom-dwelling habits mean they are often overlooked until they make sudden predatory strikes, making them an interesting find for observant freshwater divers.
divingRegions: Australasian Inland
photographyTips: Difficult to spot due to excellent camouflage; use a macro lens and scan rocky bottoms carefully for their flattened profile.

name: Oriental Batfish
shortDescription:
The oriental batfish (Platax orbicularis), also known as the orbicular batfish, is a large, laterally compressed fish reaching up to 50 cm in length. Adults have a nearly circular body profile with a silvery to dusky grey coloration and a dark band through the eye. Juveniles are dramatically different, with extremely elongated dorsal and anal fins and an orange-brown coloration that mimics fallen leaves floating on the surface, providing camouflage from predators. As they grow, the fins become proportionally shorter and the body more rounded.

Batfish are found throughout the Indo-Pacific on coral reefs, lagoons, and around wrecks and artificial structures. They are among the most diver-friendly fish on the reef, frequently approaching divers with apparent curiosity, circling them closely and following for extended periods. They often form small schools of 5-20 individuals that hang in mid-water near drop-offs, wrecks, and cleaning stations. Batfish feed on algae, invertebrates, and jellyfish, and play an important role in reef recovery by consuming seaweed that can overgrow damaged corals.
longDescription: The orbicular batfish (Platax orbicularis) is widespread across the Indo-West Pacific from the Red Sea and East Africa east through Indonesia to Tuamotu, north to southern Japan, and south to New Caledonia. Juveniles mimic floating leaves in mangroves and sheltered lagoons; adults form schools around offshore reefs and wrecks.
divingRegions: Coral Triangle, Great Barrier Reef, Red Sea, Northern Australia, Southern Japan, Sunda Shelf, Micronesia, South Pacific Islands, Japan, India & Sri Lanka, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Wide-angle lens for group portraits; their approachability makes them ideal for close-focus wide-angle shots. Capture the juvenile leaf-mimicry if you find small specimens near the surface.

name: Pinnate Batfish
shortDescription:
The juvenile pinnate batfish (Platax pinnatus) is one of the most visually spectacular fish encountered on Indo-Pacific reefs. While adults are relatively plain silvery-gray, disc-shaped fish reaching about 45 cm, the juveniles are dramatically different and far more prized by divers. Juvenile pinnate batfish are deep black with a continuous bright orange to red-orange margin outlining their extremely elongated dorsal, anal, and pelvic fins. This coloration closely mimics toxic flatworms of the genus Pseudobiceros, providing protection from predators through Batesian mimicry.

Juveniles are typically small, ranging from 3 to 15 cm, and are found in sheltered areas such as lagoons, harbors, and among mangrove roots. They swim with an undulating, flatworm-like motion that reinforces the mimicry. As they grow, the orange edges fade and the fins shorten proportionally. Adult pinnate batfish form schools on deeper reef slopes and wrecks, where they are less secretive. Finding a juvenile is considered a highlight of muck diving, and their willingness to hold position makes them excellent photographic subjects.

bestSeason: Year-round; juveniles most common in sheltered inshore habitats
photographyTips: Use macro lens for small juveniles; black background technique works beautifully to emphasize the orange border; photograph the undulating swimming motion; avoid chasing as they may hide

name: Atka Mackerel
shortDescription:
The Atka mackerel (Pleurogrammus monopterygius) is a species of greenling in the family Hexagrammidae. Adults reach up to 56 cm with an elongated body displaying distinctive dark vertical bars on a lighter background, ranging from olive-green to golden-brown. Males during spawning develop bright yellow coloration.

This species inhabits rocky reefs, kelp forests, and offshore areas at depths of 0-575 meters in the northern Pacific, from the Sea of Japan to the Aleutian Islands and Gulf of Alaska. Atka mackerel are schooling fish that form large aggregations near rocky substrates. Males are nest guarders, defending egg masses deposited on rocky surfaces by multiple females and turning bright yellow during this period.

They feed on zooplankton, small fish, and invertebrates. This species is ecologically significant in the Aleutian Islands ecosystem, serving as important prey for Steller sea lions, seals, and seabirds.

bestSeason: Summer and autumn for shallow-water encounters; nest guarding in summer
photographyTips: Cold-water diving required; use a wide-angle lens to capture the bold vertical barring and, during breeding, the striking yellow male coloration.

name: C-O Sole
shortDescription: A small right-eyed flatfish of the temperate eastern Pacific, the C-O sole takes its name from the pattern on its tail fin: a dark crescent beside a round blotch, which together read as the letters C and O. It lies flat on soft and rocky bottoms from Sitka, Alaska south to San Quintin in Baja California, usually somewhere between 18 and 350 m, and reaches about 36 cm. Both eyes sit on the right side of the head and bulge near the tip of the snout. The upper surface is mottled light to dark brown, frequently with a prominent dark spot at mid-body and a pale patch just behind it, while the blind underside stays cream. It feeds on bottom-living invertebrates, chiefly polychaete worms, bivalves and amphipods. Divers usually find it motionless and part-buried on sand near rocky reef and kelp rather than swimming in the open.
longDescription: A right-eyed flatfish of the temperate northeast Pacific, named for the C- and O-shaped markings on its tail.

name: Yucatan Molly
shortDescription:
The Yucatan molly (Poecilia velifera) is a livebearing freshwater fish reaching up to 18 cm, with males developing a spectacularly large sail-like dorsal fin used in courtship displays. Males are typically greenish-blue with rows of orange and black spots, while the enormous dorsal fin can be as tall as the body when fully extended. Endemic to the coastal lagoons and cenotes of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, it inhabits brackish and freshwater environments at depths of 0 to 5 meters.

Males perform elaborate courtship displays, erecting their sail fin and performing sideways swimming dances to attract females. This species is a popular aquarium fish and the ancestor of many cultivated molly varieties. Cenote divers in the Yucatan regularly encounter these beautiful fish, where the crystal-clear water allows appreciation of their magnificent dorsal fin displays.
divingRegions: Yucatán Freshwater

name: Sheepshead Drum
shortDescription:
The black drum (Pogonias cromis), sometimes called the sheepshead drum, is a large, heavy-bodied fish reaching up to 170 cm and over 50 kg, found in the western Atlantic from Nova Scotia to Argentina including the Gulf of Mexico. Adults are dark gray to black with a high, arched back and a characteristic chin bearing multiple small barbels used for detecting prey on the bottom. Juveniles are silvery with four to five dark vertical bars that fade with age.

This species is named for the drumming sound males produce by vibrating their swim bladder with specialized muscles, particularly during spawning, which can be loud enough for divers to hear underwater. Black drum have powerful pharyngeal teeth (throat teeth) capable of crushing oysters, mussels, crabs, and other hard-shelled prey. Found in coastal waters, estuaries, bays, and over sandy and muddy bottoms from the surface to about 30 meters, they are commonly encountered by divers near jetties, piers, bridges, and artificial reefs along the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
divingRegions: Caribbean, US East Coast
bestSeason: Year-round; spawning aggregations in spring (March-May) in the Gulf of Mexico
photographyTips: Wide-angle for large adults; capture the chin barbels and heavy body profile. Often found near structures where they can be photographed in context with pilings or reef.

name: Sixbar Angelfish
shortDescription:
The sixbar angelfish (Pomacanthus sexstriatus) is a large, impressive angelfish reaching up to 46 cm in length. Adults display a dark grey to brownish body with six bold white vertical bars, a yellow or cream-colored caudal fin, and a distinctive network of pale spots on the rear body. The face features blue markings around the eyes and operculum.

Juveniles are dramatically different, with a dark body adorned with curving white and blue lines, a pattern common to many Pomacanthus angelfish that prevents territorial aggression from adults. This species inhabits coral reefs, lagoons, and reef slopes throughout the western Pacific, from Indonesia and the Philippines to Australia and Fiji. It is typically found in pairs around coral-rich areas with caves and overhangs, feeding on sponges, tunicates, algae, and occasionally coral polyps.

Adults are somewhat wary of divers but can be approached with patience. Their bold barred pattern and large size make them a memorable sighting, particularly on Southeast Asian reef dives.

name: Painted Goby
shortDescription:
The painted goby (Pomatoschistus pictus) is a small, attractively marked fish found in the northeastern Atlantic and western Mediterranean. Adults reach only 4-6 cm and display a sandy to pale brown body with a distinctive row of dark brown double spots along the flanks and two prominent dark spots on the dorsal fins. Males develop more intense markings during breeding season.

They inhabit sandy, shell-gravel, and mixed substrates at depths of 3-55 meters, often associated with maerl beds and coarse sediment. They feed on tiny crustaceans, worms, and other small invertebrates from the substrate. Males construct nests under shells and guard eggs.

Despite their small size, their intricate markings make them rewarding subjects for patient macro photographers who carefully scan the seabed. They are commonly encountered in British, Irish, and Mediterranean waters, adding to the diversity of temperate bottom-dwelling fish communities.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, North Sea & Baltic
photographyTips: Use a macro lens with close-focus capability; look on sandy-gravel substrates and use a patient, low approach to avoid startling them.

name: Freshwater Crab

imageCredit.artist: Photo by Fabio Liverani (http://www.fabioliverani.com) uploaded by Esculapio

shortDescription:
The European freshwater crab (Potamon fluviatile) is a robust decapod crustacean reaching about 5 cm carapace width, found in rivers, streams, and lakes around the Mediterranean basin. Its carapace is dark olive-green to brown, broad and slightly flattened, with strong, slightly unequal chelae (claws) used for feeding and defense. Unlike most crabs, this species completes its entire life cycle in freshwater, with no marine larval stage.

Females carry relatively large eggs and brood them under the abdomen, releasing fully formed miniature crabs rather than planktonic larvae. This species is primarily nocturnal, sheltering under rocks, in burrows along riverbanks, or among root systems during the day. It is omnivorous, feeding on detritus, aquatic plants, invertebrates, and small vertebrates. Freshwater divers in Mediterranean regions may find them in clean, well-oxygenated streams with rocky substrates, particularly at night when they are most active. The species is considered an indicator of good water quality and has declined in many areas due to pollution and habitat modification.
longDescription: 0-5 meters (freshwater rivers and streams)
divingRegions: European Inland
bestSeason: Spring through autumn; night dives or surveys for best activity
photographyTips: Night dives with macro lens; look under rocks and along stream banks. Use a dim red light to avoid disturbing them before getting into position.

name: Lunar-Tailed Bigeye
shortDescription:
The lunar-tailed bigeye (Priacanthus hamrur), also known as the moontail bullseye, is a striking nocturnal reef fish reaching up to 45 cm. It is characterized by enormous, reflective red eyes adapted for night vision and a distinctive crescent-shaped caudal fin. The body color ranges from bright red to silvery-pink depending on the fish's mood.

Found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea and East Africa to French Polynesia, it inhabits outer reef slopes, rocky areas, and lagoons at depths of 8 to 250 meters. During the day it shelters in caves and under ledges, emerging at night to feed on zooplankton, small fish, and crustaceans. It can rapidly change color from deep red to pale silver. Divers frequently encounter small groups hovering near cave ceilings during daytime dives, making it a reliable and photogenic sighting on reef wall dives.
divingRegions: South Africa, Great Barrier Reef, Western Australia, Northern Australia, Micronesia, South Pacific Islands, Japan, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round; best seen during day dives near caves and overhangs, or on night dives
photographyTips: Use controlled flash to capture the vivid red coloration without overexposing; approach cave openings slowly to avoid startling them.

name: Pygmy Whitefish

imageCredit.artist: United States Department of the Interior

shortDescription:
The pygmy whitefish (Prosopium coulterii) is a small freshwater fish in the family Salmonidae. Adults typically reach only 10-15 cm, making them one of the smallest salmonids. They have a slender, silvery body with an olive-brown back and a small adipose fin.

This species inhabits deep, cold lakes and occasionally streams at depths of 10-100 meters across northwestern North America, from Alaska and British Columbia to Montana and the Great Lakes region. Pygmy whitefish are glacial relicts, persisting in cold, deep lake habitats since the last ice age. They feed primarily on small crustaceans, insect larvae, and zooplankton near the lake bottom. Due to their small size and deep-water habits, they are rarely encountered by divers but are ecologically significant as indicators of pristine glacial-origin water bodies and as prey for larger predatory fish including lake trout and bull trout.
divingRegions: North American Inland
bestSeason: Year-round; rarely encountered due to deep-water habits
photographyTips: Extremely difficult to photograph in the wild; found in deep, cold lakes requiring cold-water diving gear and patience.

name: Round Whitefish

imageCredit.artist: The original uploader was Oniongirl at English Wikipedia.

shortDescription:
The round whitefish (Prosopium cylindraceum) is a slender freshwater fish reaching up to 56 cm. It has a distinctive cylindrical body shape, small downward-pointing mouth, silvery sides, and a dark olive-brown back. Found across northern North America from Alaska and Canada to the northern United States, with an outlying population in New England, it inhabits cold, clear lakes and rivers at depths of 0 to 100 meters.

This species feeds on benthic invertebrates including aquatic insects, snails, and clams, using its small mouth to pick prey from rocky and gravel substrates. It spawns in autumn over gravel shoals. Freshwater divers in northern lakes encounter these elegant fish gliding through crystal-clear water, where their silvery forms reflect light beautifully against dark lake bottoms.
divingRegions: North American Inland
bestSeason: Year-round; autumn spawning provides active behavior; summer for best water conditions
photographyTips: Use wide-angle to capture their sleek form in clear lake water; natural light provides the best silvery coloration.

name: Florida Red-Bellied Cooter
shortDescription:
The Florida red-bellied cooter (Pseudemys nelsoni) is a large freshwater turtle in the family Emydidae. Adults reach 30-37 cm carapace length with a dark olive to black carapace featuring red or yellow markings, and a distinctive reddish-orange plastron (belly). The head displays yellow stripes on a dark background.

This species is native to the southeastern United States, primarily Florida and southern Georgia, inhabiting springs, rivers, lakes, and ponds at depths of 0-5 meters. They are herbivorous, feeding primarily on aquatic vegetation. Florida red-bellied cooters are commonly encountered by divers in Florida's famous spring systems, where crystal-clear water provides exceptional visibility.

They bask on logs and rocks during the day and are often surprisingly tolerant of divers in well-visited springs. Their bright red belly is visible when they swim overhead, creating a memorable sight for freshwater divers.

name: Shovelnose Guitarfish
shortDescription:
The shovelnose guitarfish (Pseudobatos productus) is a distinctive ray found along the Pacific coast of North America. Adults reach 100-170 cm in length and display a unique body plan that is intermediate between sharks and rays, with a flattened, pointed snout, guitar-shaped body, and a powerful shark-like tail used for propulsion. Their dorsal surface is sandy-brown to olive, providing excellent camouflage on sandy bottoms.

They inhabit sandy and muddy beaches, bays, and estuaries at depths of 0-15 meters, often resting partially buried in sand during the day. They feed on crabs, worms, clams, and small fish, using their flattened body to pin prey against the substrate. They are ovoviviparous, with females giving birth to live young. Their unusual body shape, approachable nature, and tendency to rest in shallow water make them an accessible and fascinating encounter for divers and snorkelers in Southern California and Baja California.
divingRegions: Eastern Tropical Pacific, California & Baja

name: Western Blue-spot Goby
shortDescription:
The Swan River goby (Pseudogobius olorum), also known as the bluespot goby, is a small fish in the family Oxudercidae. Adults reach only about 5 cm with a slender body showing mottled pale brown to yellowish-brown coloration with darker blotches. Males display a diagnostic blue spot on the rear of the first dorsal fin and a blue margin on the anal fin.

This species inhabits estuaries, river mouths, and coastal lagoons at depths of 0-3 meters around most of Australia except the northwest. They are commonly found in muddy areas and seagrass beds in the upper reaches of estuaries, and can penetrate upstream into freshwater. Swan River gobies are carnivorous, feeding on small invertebrates.

Males guard and fan eggs deposited on the underside of shells and debris. Originally described from the Swan River in Perth, Western Australia, they are one of the most common small fish in Australian estuaries.

name: West African Goatfish

It has a reddish to pink body with a distinctive dark lateral spot and a pair of long, flexible barbels under the chin used for detecting prey in sandy substrates. Found in the eastern Atlantic from Portugal to Angola, including the Mediterranean Sea, Madeira, and the Canary Islands, it inhabits rocky reefs, sandy bottoms, and seagrass beds at depths of 5 to 100 meters.

This species uses its chemosensory barbels to probe sand and rubble for buried crustaceans, worms, and mollusks, creating small sediment clouds that attract follower fish seeking escaped prey. It is often seen in small groups methodically working across sandy patches between reef areas, providing entertaining behavioral observations for divers.

name: Yellow-Banded Fusilier
shortDescription:
The yellow-banded fusilier (Pterocaesio chrysozona), also known as the goldband fusilier, is a species of fusilier in the family Caesionidae. Adults reach about 21 cm with a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body, silvery-blue coloration, and a distinctive golden-yellow horizontal band running along the midline. This species inhabits coral reefs and reef slopes at depths of 5-35 meters across the Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea and East Africa to the western Pacific. Yellow-banded fusiliers are highly gregarious, forming large, fast-moving schools that sweep across reef walls feeding on zooplankton in the water column.

Their coordinated schooling behavior creates spectacular underwater displays as hundreds of fish move in synchronized patterns. They play an important ecological role as planktivores and as prey for larger predators including trevally and tuna.

name: Devil Firefish
shortDescription:
The devil firefish (Pterois mombasae), also known as the frillfin turkeyfish, is a venomous scorpionfish found in the Indian Ocean and western Pacific. Adults reach 18-25 cm and display a darker overall coloration than more common lionfish species, with brown to reddish-brown banding and elaborate pectoral and dorsal fin rays that are heavily fringed with membrane webbing. They inhabit coral reefs, rocky outcrops, and rubble areas at depths of 5-60 meters, typically in deeper or more cryptic locations than their more conspicuous relatives.

They are nocturnal predators, emerging at night to hunt small fish and crustaceans using their fan-like pectoral fins to corner prey. Their venomous dorsal spines can deliver extremely painful stings. Their relative rarity compared to common lionfish species makes every encounter noteworthy, and their darker, more dramatic appearance creates striking photographic opportunities for experienced underwater photographers.

name: Stone Carp
shortDescription:
The stone carp (Puntius sophore), also known as the pool barb or spotfin swamp barb, is a small freshwater cyprinid in the family Cyprinidae. Adults reach about 13 cm with a deep, laterally compressed body showing silvery to golden coloration with a dark blotch near the tail base and often an orange tinge on the fins. This species inhabits rivers, streams, ponds, floodplain pools, and rice paddies at depths of 0-3 meters throughout the Indian subcontinent, including India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, and Pakistan. Stone carp are found in both clear and turbid waters, forming loose schools in vegetated areas.

They are omnivorous, feeding on algae, aquatic plants, insects, and detritus. This species has high economic value as a food fish and is also popular in the ornamental fish trade. Their resilient nature and ability to thrive in diverse habitats make them one of the most commonly encountered small fish in South Asian freshwater systems.

name: Pale Catfish
shortDescription:
The pale catfish (Rhamdia guatemalensis) is a freshwater catfish reaching up to 30 cm, with long barbels and a body that ranges from normal dark coloring in surface populations to pale, depigmented forms in cave-dwelling populations. Found from central Mexico through Central America to northern South America, it inhabits rivers, lagoons, cenotes, and underground cave systems at depths of 0 to 30 meters. Some cave populations show incipient troglomorphism with reduced pigmentation and smaller eyes, representing early stages of cave adaptation.

It is an omnivorous and opportunistic feeder, consuming invertebrates, plant matter, and detritus. Cenote divers in Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula regularly encounter this species in the crystal-clear waters of cenotes and the entrance zones of underwater caves, where its pale form gliding through sunlit cavern passages creates ethereal photographic opportunities.
divingRegions: South American Inland
bestSeason: Year-round; cenote diving excellent from November to May
photographyTips: Use wide-angle with natural cenote light for environmental shots; the contrast between pale fish and dark cave walls is dramatic.

name: Jack Dempsey Cichlid
shortDescription:
The Jack Dempsey cichlid (Rocio octofasciata) is a colorful freshwater cichlid reaching up to 25 cm. Adults display a dark body covered with iridescent blue-green spangles, with 6 to 8 faint dark bars. Named after the famous boxer Jack Dempsey due to its aggressive territorial behavior and strong facial features, it is native to Atlantic slope drainages from Mexico to Honduras.

It inhabits slow-moving rivers, cenotes, lagoons, and swampy areas at depths of 0 to 10 meters. Both parents guard their eggs and fry aggressively, with breeding pairs displaying intensified coloration. An electric blue morph is popular in the aquarium trade. Cenote and river divers in Mexico encounter this species regularly, where its spangled blue coloring creates stunning photographic opportunities in the clear freshwater environment.
divingRegions: Mexico & Central America Freshwater, Florida Inland, North American Inland
bestSeason: Year-round; breeding pairs most colorful during warm months
photographyTips: Use macro for the iridescent blue spangles; natural light in cenotes brings out the best colors.

name: Freshwater Blenny
shortDescription:
The freshwater blenny (Salaria fluviatilis) is a small, characterful fish reaching about 15 cm in length, native to rivers and lakes of the Mediterranean basin. It has a robust, elongated body with a blunt head, large eyes, and a fleshy tentacle-like structure (supraorbital tentacle) above each eye that gives it an expressive, almost comical appearance. Coloration is variable, typically olive-brown to dark grey with darker bars or mottling that provides camouflage among stones and gravel.

Males develop more intense coloration and larger head crests during the breeding season. Unlike most blennies which are marine, this species has fully adapted to freshwater life. It inhabits clean, well-oxygenated rivers and lakes with rocky or pebbly substrates, where it lives on and among stones in shallow water.

It feeds on algae, small invertebrates, and insect larvae, scraping food from rock surfaces. Males guard eggs deposited under stones by females. Freshwater divers in Mediterranean countries may find these charming fish perched on or peeking out from beneath stones in clear streams.
divingRegions: European Inland
bestSeason: Spring through autumn; breeding behavior visible in late spring and summer
photographyTips: Macro lens essential for this small subject; photograph from the front to capture the expressive face and tentacles. Patience is rewarded as they peep out from hiding spots.

name: Sabre Squirrelfish
shortDescription:
The sabre squirrelfish (Sargocentron spiniferum) is the largest species of squirrelfish, reaching up to 51 cm in length. Found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to Hawaii and the Tuamotu Islands, it is named for its prominent preopercular spine which can inflict a painful wound. It has a bright red body with white highlights on the fin edges and very large eyes adapted for nocturnal activity.

During the day it shelters in caves and under ledges on coral reefs, emerging at night to hunt crabs, shrimp, and small fish. Its robust size and vivid coloration make it one of the most impressive squirrelfish species encountered by divers.

bestSeason: Year-round; most active on night dives
photographyTips: Use strobes to bring out the red coloration; approach caves and ledges carefully; night dives provide active swimming shots rather than static shelter poses.

name: Black Butterfish
shortDescription:
The black butterfish (Schedophilus medusophagus), also known as the cornish blackfish, is a medusafish reaching about 50 cm in length, found in the eastern Atlantic from Scandinavia to West Africa and the Mediterranean. Its body is deep and laterally compressed with a dark blue-black to brown coloration and a rounded profile. The skin has a smooth, somewhat slimy texture. As its scientific name suggests (medusophagus means jellyfish-eater), this species has a strong association with jellyfish throughout its life.

Juveniles shelter among the tentacles of large pelagic jellyfish, gaining protection from predators while feeding on the jellyfish tissue and associated organisms. Adults become more free-swimming and are found at depths of 50 to 500 meters in midwater, though they occasionally appear in shallower coastal waters. They feed on jellyfish, salps, small fish, and crustaceans. Encounters with this species are uncommon for divers, making sightings particularly memorable. When juveniles are found sheltering beneath compass jellyfish or barrel jellyfish in temperate waters, they provide fascinating behavioral photography opportunities showing this unusual symbiotic relationship.
longDescription: 50-500 meters, juveniles occasionally shallower with jellyfish
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean, US East Coast
bestSeason: Summer and autumn when jellyfish blooms bring juveniles into shallower waters
photographyTips: Wide-angle lens for jellyfish association shots; natural light for open water ambiance; fast shutter speed in current; patience needed for rare encounters; photograph the fish within jellyfish tentacles for behavioral context; rarely encountered so be ready

name: Snow Trout
shortDescription:
The snow trout (Schizothorax richardsonii), also known as the common snowtrout, is a freshwater cyprinid in the family Cyprinidae. Adults reach about 30-60 cm with a streamlined body adapted for fast-flowing mountain waters, displaying olive-brown to silvery coloration with scattered dark spots. They have small scales and a distinctive fleshy lower lip adapted for scraping algae from rocks.

This species inhabits fast-flowing, cold mountain streams and rivers at depths of 0-5 meters throughout the Himalayan region, from Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh to Uttarakhand and Assam in India, as well as Nepal, Bhutan, and Afghanistan. Snow trout are omnivorous, feeding primarily on algae, aquatic insects, and plant detritus. They require clear, cold, well-oxygenated waters below 15C and are important bioindicators of healthy Himalayan stream ecosystems. Their presence in pristine mountain waters makes them symbols of healthy aquatic habitats in the Hindu Kush-Himalayan region.
divingRegions: South Asia Inland, North & Central Asian Inland
photographyTips: Found in clear, cold mountain streams; underwater housing needed for shallow, fast-flowing habitats with rocky substrates.

name: Bridled Monocle Bream
shortDescription:
The bridled monocle bream (Scolopsis bilineata), also known as the two-lined monocle bream, is a species of threadfin bream in the family Nemipteridae. Adults reach about 23 cm with a laterally compressed body showing silvery-white coloration, two distinctive dark horizontal lines on the face (the 'bridle'), and yellowish fins. A notable feature is a small backward-pointing spine on the cheek below the eye.

This species inhabits sandy and rubble areas adjacent to coral reefs at depths of 1-25 meters throughout the Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea and East Africa to the western Pacific. They are typically found in small groups or pairs hovering near the substrate, picking small invertebrates from the sand. Bridled monocle bream are common on Indo-Pacific reefs and their distinctive facial markings make them easy to identify. They are often among the first fish encountered when moving from reef to sand habitats.

name: Cero Mackerel
shortDescription:
The cero mackerel (Scomberomorus regalis) is a streamlined, fast-swimming predator reaching up to 91 cm and 5.4 kg. It has an elongated body with a dark blue-green back, silvery sides marked with distinctive rows of golden-yellow spots and streaks along the lateral line, and a deeply forked tail. Found in the western Atlantic from Massachusetts to Brazil, including the Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico, it inhabits coral reefs, rocky coastlines, and offshore waters at depths of 1 to 20 meters.

This species is a visual predator that hunts small fish, squid, and shrimp at high speed. Often seen in small groups patrolling reef edges and drop-offs, it can be distinguished from other mackerels by its prominent golden lateral stripe. Divers on Caribbean reef walls frequently encounter these sleek hunters as they cruise along the edge of the reef.
divingRegions: Caribbean
bestSeason: Year-round in tropical waters; summer in northern range
photographyTips: Use fast shutter speeds with wide-angle to freeze their rapid movements; best captured as they cruise along reef walls.

name: Windowpane Flounder
shortDescription:
The windowpane flounder (Scophthalmus aquosus) is a left-eyed flatfish reaching up to 46 cm in length. Its name derives from its extremely thin, nearly translucent body that allows light to pass through, making it appear like a window pane. Found in the western Atlantic from the Gulf of St. Lawrence to Florida, it inhabits sandy and muddy bottoms at depths of 5 to 73 meters.

This species is remarkably well camouflaged, lying flat on the substrate and changing color to match the bottom. Both eyes are positioned on the left side of its body, and it feeds on small fish, shrimp, and crabs. When disturbed, it can bury itself rapidly in sand with only its eyes protruding. Its extreme flatness and near-transparency make it a fascinating subject for divers interested in cryptic marine life and natural camouflage strategies.
divingRegions: US East Coast
bestSeason: Spring through autumn; most active in warmer months
photographyTips: Scan sandy bottoms carefully and use side-lighting to reveal their nearly transparent body outline against the substrate.

name: Bull Huss
shortDescription:
The bull huss (Scyliorhinus stellaris), also known as the nursehound or greater spotted catshark, is a large catshark reaching up to 170 cm found in the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean. It has a stocky body covered in large dark spots and blotches on a sandy-brown background. Found on rocky reefs, kelp forests, and boulder fields from 1-125 m depth, it is nocturnal, hiding in crevices and caves during the day.

It feeds on crabs, mollusks, and smaller fish. Females lay distinctive mermaid's purse egg cases attached to seaweed and gorgonians. A highlight for divers in British and European temperate waters, it is generally docile and approachable.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean
bestSeason: May-October in British waters; year-round in Mediterranean
photographyTips: Best photographed resting in crevices or caves using wide-angle with strobes; night dives offer best encounters when they are actively hunting.

name: Vermilion Rock Cod
shortDescription:

It has a bright vermilion to orange-red body with grey mottling on the back and a rounded body profile. Found on rocky reefs, pinnacles, and kelp forests from 50-300 m, it forms loose aggregations near rocky structure, often hovering above the reef.

It is a slow-growing, long-lived species that can reach over 60 years of age. A common and impressive sight for deeper recreational divers in California and Oregon waters.

name: Asian Sheepshead Wrasse
shortDescription:
The Asian sheepshead wrasse (Semicossyphus reticulatus) is a large, unmistakable wrasse reaching up to 100 cm and 14 kg. Mature males develop a massively enlarged, bulbous forehead and prominent chin that give them a grotesque yet fascinating appearance. Found in the northwestern Pacific from Japan to Korea and China, it inhabits rocky reefs, kelp forests, and temperate coastal waters at depths of 5 to 30 meters. This protogynous hermaphrodite begins life as female and the dominant individual transforms into a large male.

It feeds on shellfish, sea urchins, and crabs, crushing hard-shelled prey with powerful jaws. The species has gained worldwide attention through viral photographs of its extraordinary facial features. Divers in Japan particularly seek encounters with known individuals that have become local celebrities at dive sites.

bestSeason: Year-round; best from spring through autumn in Japanese waters
photographyTips: Use wide-angle for full face portraits; the bulbous forehead is best captured from a slightly low angle.

name: Reef Cuttlefish
shortDescription:
The reef cuttlefish (Sepia latimanus), also known as the broadclub cuttlefish, is the largest tropical cuttlefish species, reaching up to 50 cm mantle length and 10 kg. It has a broad, flattened body with undulating lateral fins, W-shaped pupils, and remarkable color-changing ability through millions of chromatophore cells. Found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to Australia, it inhabits coral reefs, seagrass beds, and sandy areas at depths of 0 to 30 meters. This intelligent predator uses mesmerizing pulsating color displays to hypnotize prey before striking with its tentacles.

During mating season, males perform spectacular competitive displays, alternating between aggressive patterns toward rivals and gentle patterns toward females. It is the most commonly encountered cuttlefish species on Indo-Pacific coral reefs and one of the most intelligent invertebrates that divers can interact with.

name: Blacktail Comber
shortDescription:
The blacktail comber (Serranus atricauda) is a small grouper-like fish found in the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Adults reach 25-35 cm in length and display a reddish-brown body with 7-9 darker vertical bars and a distinctive dark blotch or bar on the tail, which gives the species its common name. They are synchronous hermaphrodites, possessing both male and female reproductive organs simultaneously.

Found on rocky reefs, boulder fields, and Posidonia seagrass beds at depths of 5-70 meters, they are ambush predators feeding on small fish, crustaceans, and cephalopods. They tend to be solitary and territorial, often seen resting on or near rocky outcrops. Their curious nature means they often approach divers, making them one of the more interactive fish species encountered on Mediterranean dives. They are particularly common around the Canary Islands, Azores, and Madeira.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean
photographyTips: Their curious nature allows close approach; use a macro or mid-range lens and wait for them to settle on a perch for a natural portrait.

The brown comber (Serranus hepatus) is a small marine fish of the family Serranidae, reaching about 13 cm. It has a brownish body with 4 to 5 dark vertical bars and a characteristic dark blotch on the belly. Found in the eastern Atlantic from Portugal to Angola and throughout the Mediterranean Sea, it inhabits sandy and muddy bottoms, seagrass beds, and rocky areas at depths of 5 to 100 meters.

This species is a simultaneous hermaphrodite, possessing functional male and female reproductive organs at the same time. It feeds on small crustaceans, worms, and tiny fish. Despite its small size, it is an interesting find for divers exploring Mediterranean rocky reefs and Posidonia meadows. Its cryptic coloration helps it blend with the substrate, making careful observation rewarding for observant divers.

name: Yellowfin Whiting
shortDescription:
The yellowfin whiting (Sillago schomburgkii) is a species of inshore fish in the family Sillaginidae, native to southern Australia. Adults reach up to 41 cm with a slender, elongated body displaying silvery-grey coloration with distinctive yellow-tinged pectoral and caudal fins. This species inhabits sandy and silty bottoms in shallow coastal waters, estuaries, and bays at depths of 0-20 meters from southern Queensland to the central coast of Western Australia.

They are often found in schools over sandy flats, seagrass meadows, and near reef edges. Yellowfin whiting feed on small crustaceans, worms, and mollusks by probing the substrate with their sensitive snout. They are highly valued by recreational anglers throughout southern Australia and are an important component of the inshore ecosystem.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Western Australia, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia
bestSeason: Year-round; more active and visible in warmer months
photographyTips: Best captured schooling over sandy flats; use natural light in shallow water for their silvery body reflections.

name: Spiny Sea Dragon
shortDescription:
The spiny sea dragon (Solegnathus spinosissimus), also known as the spiny pipehorse, is a deep-water syngnathid in the family Syngnathidae. Adults can reach up to 49 cm with an elongated body covered in prominent bony plates with projecting spines, a long tubular snout, and a coiled, prehensile tail. Coloration is typically reddish-brown to yellowish.

This species inhabits deep rocky reefs and rocky substrates at depths of 20-450 meters in the waters of southern Australia and New Zealand. They use their prehensile tail to anchor to sponges, bryozoans, and other structure on the seafloor. Like seahorses, males brood the eggs on their body. Spiny sea dragons are rarely encountered by divers due to their deep-water habitat, making any sighting exceptional. They represent one of the most unusual and poorly understood members of the syngnathid family.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, New Zealand, Western Australia, Southern Australia
bestSeason: Year-round; rarely encountered due to depth preferences
photographyTips: A deep-water specialty requiring technical diving; use a macro lens and strobe to capture the intricate spiny armor and coiled tail.

name: Violet Sea Urchin
shortDescription:
The violet sea urchin (Sphaerechinus granularis) is one of the most visually striking sea urchins in the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic. Adults reach 10-13 cm in diameter and display a gorgeous purple to violet test covered with short, stout spines that are typically purple with distinctive white tips, though all-white and brownish variations exist. They inhabit rocky reefs, seagrass meadows, and sandy bottoms at depths of 1-100 meters, most commonly between 5-30 meters.

They are omnivorous grazers feeding on algae, bryozoans, sponges, and organic detritus. They frequently carry small pieces of shell, seagrass, or debris on their upper surface using their tube feet, likely for UV protection and camouflage. Their large size, beautiful coloration, and common occurrence make them one of the most recognizable invertebrates on Mediterranean dives. They often occur in aggregations on seagrass meadow edges, creating colorful underwater landscapes.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean

It has a mottled brownish body with darker marbling patterns that provide excellent camouflage against rocky and sandy substrates. Found in the eastern Atlantic from Portugal to Angola, including Madeira, the Azores, Cape Verde, and the Canary Islands, it inhabits rocky bottoms, sandy areas, and seagrass beds at depths of 5 to 100 meters.

Like all pufferfish, it can inflate its body by swallowing water when threatened, and it contains tetrodotoxin, a potent neurotoxin. It feeds on crustaceans, mollusks, and small invertebrates. Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic divers encounter this species on rocky reef dives and sandy bottoms, where its marbled pattern makes it a challenge to spot until it moves.

name: Scalloped Bonnethead
shortDescription: Probably the smallest hammerhead — a rare, little-known species of the eastern Pacific. Its mallet-shaped head and small size set it apart from other Sphyrna.
longDescription:
The scalloped bonnethead (Sphyrna corona) is a rare, little-known hammerhead and probably the smallest species in the family, reaching up to 92 cm (36 in) in total length. Its mallet-shaped cephalofoil is moderately wide (24–29% of total length) and elongated, with a broadly arched front margin and shallow lateral and medial indentations. Coloration is gray above and white below.

It is found in tropical and subtropical waters of the eastern Pacific from Mexico to Peru, possibly as far north as the Gulf of California. It frequents inshore soft bottoms — mud, sand, and gravel — to depths of 100 m, and also enters mangroves and estuaries. Diet is benthic: crustaceans, molluscs, cephalopods, echinoderms, and bony fishes. Viviparous with presumably two pups per litter, born at 23 cm or above. Other common names include mallethead shark and crown shark.
divingRegions: Eastern Tropical Pacific (Mexico to Peru), possibly Sea of Cortez

name: Freshwater Sponge
shortDescription:
The freshwater sponge (Spongilla lacustris) is one of the most widespread freshwater sponge species, found in lakes, rivers, and canals throughout the Northern Hemisphere. It forms encrusting or branching growths on submerged rocks, wood, and other hard surfaces, typically reaching 10-30 cm across though larger colonies exist. Its color ranges from white to grey, but most commonly appears bright green due to symbiotic algae (zoochlorellae) living within its tissues, which photosynthesize and provide the sponge with additional nutrients. The texture is soft and slightly fuzzy, supported internally by microscopic siliceous spicules.

Like all sponges, it is a filter feeder, drawing water through countless pores and extracting bacteria, algae, and organic particles. Freshwater sponges reproduce both sexually through tiny larvae and asexually through gemmules, tough resistant buds that survive winter freezing and drought before germinating in favorable conditions. Freshwater divers may encounter these sponges on submerged logs, bridge pilings, and rocky surfaces in clean lakes and rivers, where they indicate good water quality.

name: Blue Sprat
shortDescription:
The Rottnest Island herring (Spratelloides robustus), also known as the blue sprat, is a small herring in the family Clupeidae. Adults reach about 12 cm with a slender, streamlined body displaying a dark blue upper body and silvery lower body with a pair of horizontal dark blue streaks near the caudal fin. This species inhabits coastal waters around southern Australia from the Dampier Archipelago to southern Queensland, including Tasmania, at depths of 0-30 meters.

They form enormous schooling aggregations numbering in the thousands near rocky reefs, jetties, and coastal structures. Blue sprats are planktivorous filter feeders consuming small crustaceans and phytoplankton. Their dense schools attract predators including larger fish, dolphins, and seabirds, creating dynamic feeding events. At Rottnest Island near Perth, large schools are a regular feature of dive sites.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Western Australia, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia
bestSeason: Year-round; large schools common in temperate waters
photographyTips: Wide-angle lens captures the shimmering school formations; position yourself between the school and predators for dramatic hunting shots.

name: Pacific Gregory

imageCredit.artist: (c) Susan Prior, some rights reserved (CC BY)

shortDescription:
The Pacific gregory (Stegastes fasciolatus) is a species of damselfish in the family Pomacentridae. Adults reach about 16 cm with a deep, compressed body displaying dark brown to olive coloration with indistinct darker barring and a small dark spot at the base of the pectoral fin. This species inhabits reef flats, shallow reef crests, and rocky areas at depths of 1-12 meters throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific, from East Africa to Hawaii and French Polynesia. Pacific gregorys are highly territorial herbivores that actively cultivate and defend algae gardens on the reef, aggressively chasing away much larger fish and even approaching divers who venture too close.

They feed primarily on filamentous algae grown within their defended territories. Their bold, aggressive territorial behavior makes them entertaining to observe, as these small fish fearlessly confront intruders many times their own size.

name: Posidonia Seagrass Pipefish
shortDescription:
The Posidonia seagrass pipefish (Syngnathus typhle), also known as the broadnosed pipefish, is a slender, elongated fish reaching up to 35 cm in length. It is superbly camouflaged among the blades of Posidonia oceanica and other seagrass beds throughout the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic. Its body is covered in bony rings, and its coloration ranges from green to brown, perfectly matching its seagrass habitat.

Like its seahorse relatives, the male carries fertilized eggs in a ventral brood pouch until they hatch. It feeds by sucking tiny crustaceans and zooplankton through its tubular snout with a rapid snap of its jaws. This species is an indicator of healthy seagrass ecosystems and is often found hovering vertically among grass blades, swaying gently with the current. Observing one requires patience and a keen eye, as their camouflage is remarkably effective. They are typically solitary or found in loose pairs during breeding season.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean, North Sea & Baltic
bestSeason: Spring through autumn when seagrass beds are most lush; breeding peaks May-August
photographyTips: Use a macro lens and look carefully among Posidonia blades; slow approach is essential as they drift away when disturbed. Natural light can help capture their camouflage context.

name: Chinese Horseshoe Crab
shortDescription:
The Chinese horseshoe crab (Tachypleus tridentatus), also known as the tri-spine horseshoe crab, is a large chelicerate arthropod reaching up to 60 cm in body length including the telson (tail spine). It has a distinctive horseshoe-shaped carapace, six pairs of legs, book gills for breathing, and three telson spines that give it its scientific name. Found in Southeast and East Asia from Japan to Indonesia and Vietnam, it inhabits sandy and muddy coastal areas, estuaries, and shallow waters at depths of 0 to 30 meters.

As a living fossil virtually unchanged for 450 million years, it represents one of the oldest surviving animal lineages on Earth. Its blue, copper-based blood contains LAL (Limulus Amebocyte Lysate), used to test for bacterial contamination in pharmaceuticals. Now endangered due to habitat loss and overharvesting, encountering one while diving is increasingly rare and ecologically significant.

name: Long-Spined Sea Scorpion
shortDescription:
The long-spined sea scorpion (Taurulus bubalis) is a small sculpin found in the northeastern Atlantic. Adults reach 15-25 cm and display highly variable coloration including brown, green, red, and orange with mottled patterns that provide excellent camouflage against rocky substrates. They have a large, flattened head armed with prominent spines, including a distinctive long preopercular spine that gives the species its common name.

They inhabit rocky shores, tide pools, kelp forests, and boulder fields at depths of 0-30 meters. As ambush predators, they lie motionless on the substrate waiting to strike at passing prey including small fish, crustaceans, and worms. Males guard egg masses laid under rocks during winter.

Their elaborate camouflage means they are often overlooked by divers, but careful observation reveals their intricate color patterns and fascinating behavioral adaptations. They are one of the most commonly encountered sculpin species in UK and northern European waters.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, North Sea & Baltic
photographyTips: Use a macro lens and search rocky substrates carefully; once spotted, they often remain still, allowing detailed close-up portraits.

name: Noronha Wrasse
shortDescription:
The Noronha wrasse (Thalassoma noronhanum) is a colorful wrasse reaching up to 13 cm. Males display vivid green bodies with pink to red lateral stripes and a blue-green head, while females and juveniles are more subdued brownish-yellow. Found exclusively in the western Atlantic around Brazilian oceanic islands including Fernando de Noronha, Atol das Rocas, Trindade, and other offshore islands, it inhabits coral reefs and rocky substrates at depths of 2 to 60 meters.

This species feeds on small invertebrates and zooplankton. As an endemic species restricted to Brazil's offshore islands, encountering the Noronha wrasse is a unique experience available only to divers visiting these remote and pristine marine environments. Its vibrant coloring against the clear Brazilian island waters makes it a memorable photographic subject.
divingRegions: Brazil Coast
bestSeason: Year-round; best diving conditions from September to November
photographyTips: Use macro for terminal male coloration detail; the clear water of Brazilian islands provides excellent natural light.

name: Easter Island Wrasse
shortDescription:
The Easter Island wrasse (Thalassoma purpureum), also called the surge wrasse, is a robust wrasse reaching up to 43 cm. Terminal phase males are spectacularly colored with a green body, reddish stripes along the flanks, and a greenish-blue head with pink-purple markings. Found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to Easter Island and Hawaii, it inhabits surge zones on outer reefs and reef crests at depths of 1 to 45 meters. This active predator feeds on sea urchins, crabs, and other hard-shelled invertebrates.

On Easter Island, it is one of the most commonly encountered and recognizable reef fish, often seen boldly swimming through surge zones and reef flats. Its vivid coloration and energetic behavior make it a reliable photographic subject on Easter Island reef dives.

bestSeason: Year-round; active in surge zones during daylight hours
photographyTips: Use wide-angle to capture terminal males in their surge zone habitat; fast shutter speeds needed in surge conditions.
