name: St Helena Wrasse
shortDescription:
The St. Helena wrasse (Thalassoma sanctaehelenae) is a poorly known species of wrasse in the family Labridae, endemic to St. Helena island in the South Atlantic.

Adults reach up to about 19 cm with greenish to bluish coloration typical of Thalassoma. This species inhabits shallow coastal waters near rocks and rocky reefs at depths of 1-20 meters. Like other Thalassoma wrasses, they are active diurnal swimmers feeding on small invertebrates and zooplankton.

Their extreme geographic isolation means they have evolved independently for millions of years. As one of approximately 18 endemic fish species found only around St. Helena, this wrasse represents a unique piece of oceanic island biodiversity. The remoteness of St. Helena means very few divers have observed this species in the wild.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, South Atlantic Islands
photographyTips: Active and fast-swimming; use a fast shutter speed and anticipate their movements along the reef.

name: European Flying Squid

It is a fast-swimming pelagic predator feeding on fish, crustaceans, and other squid.

While primarily a deep-water species, it may be encountered by divers during night dives when individuals or schools come into shallower water attracted by lights. Its rapid color-changing ability and jet-propelled swimming make encounters exciting.

name: Mahseer Barb
shortDescription:
The mahseer barb (Tor khudree), also known as the Deccan mahseer, is a large freshwater cyprinid fish native to rivers and lakes of the Indian subcontinent. Adults can reach impressive sizes of up to 150 cm and weigh over 25 kg, making them among the largest freshwater fish in their range. They display a robust, deep body with large golden to silvery scales, a subterminal mouth with thick fleshy lips adapted for scraping algae and invertebrates from rocks, and powerful tail fins suited for navigating fast-flowing rivers.

The species inhabits clear, well-oxygenated rivers, streams, and reservoirs in peninsular India, particularly in the Western Ghats region. Mahseer are omnivorous, feeding on algae, aquatic plants, insects, crustaceans, and small fish. They are highly valued as sport fish, often called the 'Tiger of the River' for their powerful fighting ability. Mahseer populations have declined significantly due to dam construction, pollution, habitat degradation, and overfishing, and several species within the genus are considered endangered. Divers in clear Indian river pools occasionally encounter these magnificent fish, which can be surprisingly approachable in protected waters.
longDescription: Surface to 10 meters in freshwater pools and rivers
divingRegions: South Asia Inland
bestSeason: October to March (post-monsoon) when rivers are clearest
photographyTips: Wide-angle lens captures the full size of large individuals; natural light works well in shallow clear pools; approach slowly as mahseer can be wary; underwater housing essential for river diving

name: Tor Putitora
shortDescription:
The golden mahseer (Tor putitora) is one of the largest and most magnificent freshwater fish in South Asia, reaching up to 2.75 meters in length and over 50 kg in weight, though fish over 100 kg have been historically reported. It is named for its stunning golden to yellowish-bronze coloration, with large, thick scales that gleam in the water. The body is powerful and streamlined, adapted for navigating fast-flowing Himalayan rivers.

Its large, rubbery lips are adapted for feeding on algae, aquatic plants, insects, crustaceans, and small fish from rocky substrates. The golden mahseer is found in rivers and lakes of the Himalayan region, from Afghanistan through Pakistan, India, Nepal, and Bangladesh, preferring clear, cool, well-oxygenated mountain rivers with rocky pools. It is considered sacred in some Hindu traditions and is protected at temple pools in several locations.

The species is classified as endangered due to dam construction, pollution, habitat degradation, and overfishing. Conservation efforts including breeding programs are underway. Encountering one while diving in clear Himalayan rivers is a rare and extraordinary experience.
longDescription: 1-10 meters (freshwater mountain rivers and lakes)
divingRegions: South Asia Inland, SE Asia Freshwater, African Inland
bestSeason: October-March when rivers are clearest after monsoon; avoid monsoon season (June-September)
photographyTips: Wide-angle for full-body shots in clear mountain pools; the golden scales reflect beautifully in natural light. Snorkeling may be more practical than diving in shallow rivers.

name: Mahseer
shortDescription:
The mahseer (Tor tor), also known as the tor mahseer or red-finned mahseer, is a large freshwater cyprinid in the family Cyprinidae. Adults can reach over 150 cm and 50 kg with a powerful, torpedo-shaped body, large golden scales, and distinctive red to blood-red fins. The head is relatively large with thick, fleshy lips and barbels.

This species inhabits fast-flowing rivers and deep rocky pools at depths of 0-15 meters in the rivers of central India, particularly in the Narmada, Mahanadi, and other central Indian river systems. Tor tor are omnivorous, feeding on fruits, algae, insects, crustaceans, and small fish. They are considered sacred in some Hindu traditions and are important culturally. As apex freshwater predators, they require clean rivers with rocky substrates and sufficient flow. Their impressive size, fighting ability, and declining populations make conservation efforts critical across their range.
divingRegions: South Asia Inland
photographyTips: Found in deep river pools with clear water; their red fins photograph dramatically against rocky river substrates.

name: Weeping Toadfish
shortDescription:
The common blowfish (Torquigener pleurogramma), also known as the weeping toadfish, is a small pufferfish reaching up to 22 cm. It has a brownish-green body with a distinctive dark lateral stripe and scattered spots providing camouflage against sandy and rocky substrates. Found in the eastern Indian Ocean and southwestern Pacific around Australia, it inhabits sandy areas, seagrass beds, and rocky reefs at depths of 1 to 50 meters.

Like all pufferfish, it can inflate its body with water when threatened and contains tetrodotoxin. It feeds on small invertebrates and algae. This is one of the most commonly encountered pufferfish in Australian waters, often seen resting on sandy bottoms or swimming with its characteristic slow, hovering gait. Its relative abundance and approachable nature make it a frequent and cooperative photographic subject.

name: Cape Horse Mackerel

imageCredit.artist: Frederick Hermanus Van der Bank, University of Johannesburg

shortDescription:
The cape horse mackerel (Trachurus capensis) is a pelagic schooling fish reaching up to 60 cm. It has a streamlined silvery body with a distinct lateral line of enlarged scutes and a greenish-blue back. Found in the southeastern Atlantic and southwestern Indian Ocean from Angola to Mozambique, it inhabits continental shelf waters at depths of 0 to 300 meters.

This species forms enormous schools that can contain millions of individuals, creating spectacular bait balls that attract marine predators including dolphins, seals, sharks, and seabirds. It feeds on small crustaceans, fish larvae, and zooplankton. Divers along the South African coast, particularly during the Sardine Run and other seasonal events, may encounter massive aggregations of horse mackerel being driven into bait balls by predators, creating some of the most action-packed diving experiences in the world.
divingRegions: South Africa, Southwest Africa
bestSeason: Year-round; June–July for Sardine Run along South Africa's east coast
photographyTips: Use wide-angle for schooling and bait ball action; fast shutter speeds essential for capturing predator interactions.

name: Florida Horse Conch
shortDescription:
The Florida horse conch (Triplofusus giganteus) is one of the largest gastropods in the world, with a spindle-shaped shell reaching up to 60 cm in length. The shell is orange-brown with a bright orange aperture, and the animal itself has a vivid orange-red body. Found in the western Atlantic from North Carolina to Mexico and the Caribbean, it inhabits sandy and grassy areas, oyster reefs, and rocky substrates at depths of 0 to 20 meters. This predatory snail feeds on other large gastropods and bivalves, enveloping them with its muscular foot and forcing open their shells.

It can live for decades and grows slowly throughout its life. Encountering a large horse conch plowing through sand on a Florida dive is an impressive sight, as the vivid orange body contrasts dramatically with the sandy substrate.

name: Great Crested Newt
shortDescription:
The great crested newt (Triturus cristatus), also known as the warty newt, is the largest European newt reaching up to 17 cm. Breeding males develop a spectacular jagged crest along the back and tail, with a dark brown to black warty skin above and a vivid orange belly with black blotches. Found across Europe from the UK to western Siberia, it inhabits ponds, lakes, and slow-moving ditches at depths of 0 to 2 meters.

This species spends most of the year on land under logs and in burrows, returning to water from March to June for breeding. Males perform elaborate courtship dances, waving their crests and releasing pheromones. Strictly protected under European law, encountering one during a pond dive or snorkel is a privilege. Its dramatic crest and vivid belly coloring make it one of Europe's most impressive amphibians.

name: Blue-Lined Goatfish
shortDescription:
The blue-lined goatfish (Upeneichthys lineatus) is a species of goatfish in the family Mullidae, native to the temperate waters of southern and eastern Australia. Adults grow to about 35 cm in length and display a reddish to pinkish body adorned with distinctive blue horizontal stripes along the flanks. Like all goatfish, they possess a pair of sensory barbels on the chin used to probe sandy and silty substrates for hidden prey including small crustaceans, worms, and mollusks.

They inhabit rocky reefs and sandy areas at depths of 5-100 meters, though they are more commonly found above 40 meters. Blue-lined goatfish are often seen singly or in small groups foraging over the seafloor, frequently followed by other fish species that scavenge disturbed prey. Their bright coloration and active foraging behavior make them a visually appealing and interesting species to observe during temperate water dives in Australia.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Western Australia, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia
bestSeason: Year-round; best visibility in Australian autumn (March-May)
photographyTips: Capture them while actively foraging with barbels extended; a macro lens works well for close-up shots of their blue-striped pattern.

name: Blue-Spotted Goatfish
shortDescription:
The blue-spotted goatfish (Upeneichthys vlamingii) is a species of goatfish in the family Mullidae, native to the temperate coast of southern Australia. Adults reach about 30 cm with a pinkish to reddish body marked with distinctive blue spots and stripes. Like all goatfish, they possess a pair of sensory barbels on the chin used to probe sandy substrates for hidden prey.

This species inhabits rocky reefs and sandy areas at depths of 5-80 meters from southern New South Wales around to Western Australia. They feed on small crustaceans, worms, and mollusks detected using their sensitive barbels. Blue-spotted goatfish are often seen foraging in loose groups, attracting other fish species that feed on disturbed prey. Their active foraging behavior and attractive coloration make them engaging subjects for underwater observation on temperate Australian dives.
divingRegions: Eastern Australia, Western Australia, Southern Australia, Southwestern Australia
photographyTips: Capture them with barbels extended during foraging; a macro lens works well for their blue-spotted pattern.

name: White-Margin Stargazer
shortDescription:
The white-margin stargazer (Uranoscopus sulphureus) is a distinctive ambush predator found throughout the Indo-Pacific. Adults reach 30-45 cm and have a large, blocky head with dorsally positioned eyes that peer upward from their sandy burial position, and a large, upward-opening mouth. They are yellowish-brown to grey with a white margin on the fins that gives them their name.

They bury themselves in sandy and silty substrates at depths of 1-30 meters, waiting to ambush passing fish and crustaceans with explosive suction strikes. They possess venomous spines behind the gill covers and electric organs behind the eyes capable of delivering shocks up to 50 volts. A worm-like lure inside the mouth attracts prey. Despite their sedentary nature, spotting a buried stargazer is an exciting discovery for observant divers scanning sandy areas on Indo-Pacific reefs, revealing one of the ocean's most bizarre and well-armed ambush predators.
divingRegions: Great Barrier Reef, Red Sea, South Pacific Islands, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
photographyTips: Use a macro lens and scan sandy bottoms for protruding eyes; maintain safe distance as they are venomous, and shoot from a low angle for dramatic perspective.

SIO 190L

shortDescription: Not a true squid — a living fossil in its own order. Turns inside-out to reveal vivid red cloak lined with spiny filaments. Lives in the oxygen minimum zone at 600-900m.
longDescription: The Vampire Squid is neither a squid nor an octopus — it occupies its own taxonomic order as the sole surviving member of an ancient lineage. name: Yellow-edged Lyretail Grouper
shortDescription:
The yellow-edged lyretail grouper (Variola louti), also known as the lunar-tail grouper, is a colorful species reaching about 80 cm found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to the Pitcairn Islands. Its body is reddish to pink covered with small blue spots, and its tail is distinctively crescent-shaped (lyrate) with bright yellow margins. It inhabits coral reef slopes, channels, and drop-offs, often at moderate depths. A solitary predator, it feeds on fish and crustaceans.

Unlike many groupers that are sedentary, it is often seen actively swimming along reef walls. It is a protogynous hermaphrodite, with females changing to males as they grow larger.

name: Firefly Squid
shortDescription:
The firefly squid (Watasenia scintillans) is a small, bioluminescent squid reaching only 7 to 8 cm in mantle length. Its body is equipped with thousands of photophores that produce intense blue light, particularly concentrated on the tips of the tentacles. Found in the western Pacific Ocean around Japan, it inhabits deep waters at depths of 200 to 400 meters during the day, migrating to the surface at night. Each spring, massive aggregations of firefly squid gather in Toyama Bay, Japan, for spawning, creating one of the most spectacular natural light shows in the ocean.

The bioluminescence serves for counter-illumination camouflage and mate attraction. The Toyama Bay firefly squid spawning events draw divers, photographers, and tourists from around the world. It is the sole species in the genus Watasenia and is commercially harvested as a delicacy in Japan.
longDescription: 0–400 m (vertical migration)

bestSeason: March–June for spawning season in Toyama Bay
photographyTips: Use long exposures with high ISO to capture the bioluminescence; surface shots during spawning events are the most dramatic.

name: Gilded Triggerfish
shortDescription:
The gilded triggerfish (Xanthichthys auromarginatus), also known as the blue-throat triggerfish, is a species in the family Balistidae. Adults reach up to 30 cm with a spotted brownish-gray body sometimes showing a bluish or lavender tint. Males develop a distinctive bright blue chin and throat, and the tail has golden-yellow margins.

This species inhabits steep outer reef slopes and drop-offs at depths of 10-150 meters across the Indo-Pacific. Unlike most triggerfish, gilded triggerfish are planktivorous, feeding on zooplankton in the water column above the reef. They are relatively shy and non-aggressive, quite different from the territorial behavior typical of most triggerfishes. Their preference for deeper outer reef habitats means they are less commonly encountered than shallow-water triggerfish species, making them a special find for experienced divers.
divingRegions: Polynesia, Hawaii, Western Australia, Micronesia, South Pacific Islands, Coral Triangle, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round; best on current-swept outer reef walls
photographyTips: Look for males displaying their blue throat; use available light at depth for a natural look that highlights the golden tail margins.

name: Striped Triggerfish
shortDescription:
The striped triggerfish (Xanthichthys lineopunctatus) is a species of triggerfish in the family Balistidae. Adults reach up to 30 cm in length and display a grayish to brownish body covered with distinctive rows of small spots arranged in horizontal lines. Males may develop a brighter yellowish hue on the lower body and tail margins.

This species inhabits outer reef slopes, steep drop-offs, and current-swept channels at depths of 15-100 meters across the Indo-Pacific, from East Africa and the Red Sea to the western Pacific. Unlike many triggerfish that are territorial and aggressive, the striped triggerfish is generally shy and retreats when approached. They feed on zooplankton in the water column, often hovering above the reef. Their preference for deep outer reef habitats and elusive nature make them a special sighting for experienced divers.
divingRegions: South Africa, Western Australia, South China Sea, Southern Japan, Eastern Tropical Pacific, Western Indian Ocean
bestSeason: Year-round; best on current-rich outer reef walls
photographyTips: Often encountered at depth on outer walls; approach very slowly as they tend to retreat quickly, and use available light for a natural look.

name: Green Swordtail
shortDescription:
The green swordtail (Xiphophorus hellerii) is a small freshwater livebearer in the family Poeciliidae. Adult males reach about 14 cm including the distinctive sword-like extension of the lower caudal fin, while females reach about 16 cm without a sword. Wild-type fish display olive-green coloration with a reddish-brown lateral stripe, though aquarium-bred varieties come in many colors.

Males use the sword extension in courtship displays. This species is native to freshwater streams and rivers at depths of 0-3 meters in Central America from Mexico to Honduras, but has been introduced worldwide. Green swordtails inhabit vegetated streams, springs, and river margins, preferring areas with moderate flow and abundant plant growth.

They are omnivorous, feeding on algae, insects, and organic detritus. As livebearers, females give birth to fully formed fry. Their adaptability has led to established feral populations in many tropical regions worldwide.
divingRegions: Australasian Inland, East Asia Inland, Florida Inland, North American Inland, Hawaii, Mexico & Central America Freshwater, Indonesian/Malay Inland, South American Inland
photographyTips: Use a macro lens to capture the male's distinctive sword extension; natural light in clear streams highlights the green coloration.

name: Platy Fish
shortDescription:
The platy fish (Xiphophorus maculatus), also known as the southern platyfish, is a small freshwater livebearer in the family Poeciliidae. Adults reach about 6 cm with a deep, laterally compressed body. Wild-type fish display variable coloration from olive to grey with a dark lateral spot, though captive-bred varieties come in virtually every color.

This species is native to freshwater and brackish habitats at depths of 0-2 meters in Central America from southern Mexico to Belize and Guatemala. Platy fish inhabit warm, slow-moving or still waters with abundant vegetation, including ditches, canals, springs, and river backwaters. They are omnivorous, feeding on algae, aquatic invertebrates, and detritus. As livebearers, females give birth to free-swimming young without laying eggs.

Established feral populations exist in many tropical regions worldwide due to aquarium releases. They are commonly encountered during freshwater dives in Florida and other warm-water destinations.

name: Marmalade Razorfish
shortDescription:
The marmalade razorfish (Xyrichtys blanchardi) is a slender wrasse in the family Labridae found in the southeastern Atlantic Ocean. Adults reach about 15-20 cm and display warm orange to marmalade-colored flanks with subtle barring and a compressed, blade-like body profile. The head has a steep, nearly vertical profile.

This species inhabits sandy and rubble areas adjacent to reefs at depths of 5-40 meters. Like other razorfishes, it can dive headfirst into sand when threatened, completely burying itself in an instant. They emerge to feed on small benthic invertebrates including worms, crustaceans, and mollusks. Their camouflage coloration blends with sandy substrates, and they are often overlooked until they make sudden movements.
divingRegions: Eastern Atlantic, South Atlantic Islands
photographyTips: Move slowly over sandy areas to spot them before they dive into sand; pre-focus and be ready for their rapid burial behavior.

name: Patagonian Scallop
shortDescription:
The Patagonian scallop (Zygochlamys patagonica) is a commercially important bivalve mollusk reaching up to 8 cm in shell height. It has a rounded, fan-shaped shell with fine ribs and a coloration ranging from pink to reddish-brown. Found in the southwestern Atlantic from about 36 to 55 degrees south latitude around southern South America and into the southeastern Pacific, it inhabits sandy and muddy bottoms at depths of 50 to 200 meters.

This species forms dense beds on the continental shelf of Argentina, where it is the target of a major fishery. Like other scallops, it can swim by jet propulsion, clapping its valves together to escape predators such as sea stars. It is a filter feeder, drawing in water to capture phytoplankton and organic particles. Divers in Patagonian waters may encounter large aggregations of these scallops on sandy substrates during deep dives.

bestSeason: Southern hemisphere summer (December–March) for best conditions
photographyTips: Use macro to capture shell detail and wide-angle for bed formations; they may swim away if disturbed, creating action shots.
